Interactive module

Spring Data JPA

The same warehouse, now a Spring Boot application — repositories, derived and declared queries, transactions as a cross-cutting concern, projections, auditing, pagination, validation and testing — with every statement on the page emitted by Spring Boot 4.1 and Hibernate 7.4 at build time.

Start here

How to use this module

Work through it at your own pace. Your section checkmarks, quiz answers, flashcard marks and notes are saved in this browser under a key scoped to this file, so closing the tab loses nothing and the earlier modules cannot overwrite it. Nothing is sent anywhere — this page makes no network requests at all. Press ? at any time for the keyboard shortcuts, and use Reset progress in the sidebar to start over.

Every program in this module is a complete Spring Boot application, compiled and executed as part of the build against a pinned stack: Spring Boot 4.1.1, Spring Data JPA 4.1.1, Hibernate ORM 7.4.5 and an in-memory H2 database, on JDK 21 — the versions Spring Boot's own dependency management selects, resolved by Maven when the page was built. As in the JPA module, every line beginning Hibernate: in an Expected output block is a statement that was actually sent to the database, and the prose reads those statements one by one. When a section says a repository method ran two queries, the build counted them. Widgets that animate something — the autoconfiguration order, a save decision, a transaction proxy — carry the Simulated badge.

Why every program looks the same at the bottom

A Spring Boot application normally prints a banner, a dozen INFO lines with timestamps and the process id, and a "Started in 2.31 seconds" line. None of that is repeatable, and the build diffs standard output byte for byte. So every program here sets the same small property map before it starts, and it is worth knowing what each entry does, because you will want most of them in a test suite too:

The deterministic property set used by every program in this module
PropertyWhy it is set
spring.main.web-application-type=noneNo embedded server. The application runs its runners and exits; nothing listens on a port.
spring.main.banner-mode=offNo ASCII-art banner on standard output.
spring.main.log-startup-info=falseNo "Starting BootAnatomy using Java 21 with PID …" lines, which carry the process id and the machine name.
logging.level.root=WARNLogback writes to standard output by default. At WARN the startup chatter is gone; anything that still prints is a real warning the program should fix.
logging.pattern.console=%level %logger{0}: %msg%nIf a warning does appear, it carries no timestamp, so the output is still comparable run to run.
spring.jpa.show-sql=trueEcho every SQL statement — the point of the module.
spring.jpa.open-in-view=falseSection 6 explains why you want this off anyway; here it also silences the warning Spring Boot prints when it is left on.
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=create-dropBuild the schema from the mappings at start and drop it at close — which is why every output ends with drop table lines.
The warehouse as a Spring Boot application

The JPA module mapped the warehouse and drove it through an EntityManager by hand. This module keeps the same entities and lets Spring generate the boilerplate — and then shows what that costs when you stop paying attention:

  • ProductRepository is the first repository: an interface with no implementation, whose save, findById and findBySkuStartingWith all turn into SQL you can read (§2, §3, §4).
  • InventoryService is where @Transactional lives, and where a method that calls itself quietly runs outside any transaction (§5).
  • Order and OrderLine return for the N+1 problem — this time counted through Spring's statistics, with open-in-view switched off (§6).
  • The reports become pageable repository methods, projections, specifications and a keyset scroll (§7, §9).
  • StockLevel gains auditing columns and a domain event that fires only after the reservation commits (§8).

Before you begin

Prerequisites

This module assumes JPA & Hibernate, and through it the earlier modules. It does not re-teach mapping: when a section shows an entity, it reads as a reminder, not an introduction. Spring Data is a thin layer, and almost every surprise in it is a JPA fact wearing a Spring stack trace, so the items below are leaned on constantly:

Prerequisite skills, where they were taught, and what depends on them here
You should already be able to…Taught inBecause this module…
Map an entity: @Id, a generation strategy, @Column, enums as strings, embeddablesJPA §2declares entities without comment and spends its attention on the repository that wraps them (§1, §2)
Trace an entity through transient, managed and detached, and say when dirty checking writesJPA §3explains what save actually does — persist or merge — in terms of those states (§2)

What you need installed

A JDK 21 or newer, plus the Spring Boot jars — 61 of them once the transitive graph is resolved, which is why this module's dependency list is not pinned by hand but resolved by Maven against Spring Boot's bill of materials. If you are working from the course repository, one command does it (it needs a Maven on your PATH, in MAVEN_HOME, or in the Maven Wrapper's cache under ~/.m2/wrapper):

node tools/fetch-deps.mjs java-spring-data     # resolves Spring Boot 4.1.1's graph into build/lib/java-spring-data/
javac -cp "build/lib/java-spring-data/*" -d classes BootAnatomy.java
java  -cp "classes;build/lib/java-spring-data/*" lm.anatomy.BootAnatomy   # : instead of ; on Linux/macOS

In a project of your own, the same stack is three starters under the Spring Boot parent — the parent is what pins every version:

<parent>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
  <version>4.1.1</version>
</parent>
<dependencies>
  <dependency><groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId><artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-jpa</artifactId></dependency>
  <dependency><groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId><artifactId>spring-boot-starter-validation</artifactId></dependency>
  <dependency><groupId>com.h2database</groupId><artifactId>h2</artifactId><scope>runtime</scope></dependency>
</dependencies>

No versions on the starters: the parent's dependencyManagement supplies them, and that is exactly the mechanism fetch-deps reproduces by importing spring-boot-dependencies as a BOM. Every program in this module names its own package (lm.anatomy, lm.repos, …) because Spring component-scans the package of the application class, and the build compiles all programs into one directory.

Three habits to unlearn

Spring Data removes so much code that it is easy to stop thinking about what the remaining code does. Three habits in particular survive every code review and fail in production:

  • "@Transactional on the method is enough." The annotation does nothing by itself; a proxy around the bean does the work, and a call that does not pass through the proxy — a private method, a method the same object calls on itself — gets no transaction at all. Section 5 proves it with a transaction-name check that prints null.
  • "Lazy loading just works in Spring." It works in a web request because open-in-view keeps a persistence context open from controller to template, which hides every N+1 behind a working page. Switch it off and the same code throws. Section 6 does exactly that.
  • "ddl-auto=update keeps the schema in sync." Spring Boot defaults it to create-drop for an embedded database and none otherwise, and the JPA module already explained why update is a development convenience and never a deployment. Section 12 shows where Flyway slots in.

The contract

Learning objectives

By the end of this module you will be able to do each of the following without reaching for a reference. The final quiz tests exactly these twelve.

  1. Explain what spring-boot-starter-data-jpa auto-configures, in what order, and how the default property set (naming strategy, ddl-auto, open-in-view) differs from plain Hibernate.
  2. Choose the right repository interface and predict what save does for a new versus an existing entity, including the role of @Version and Persistable.
  3. Derive a query from a method name using the keyword grammar, predict its SQL, and know when a derived name has become unreadable.
  4. Declare queries with @Query (JPQL and native), write @Modifying updates safely, and choose between interface, class and dynamic projections.
  5. Draw the transaction boundary of a request through the @Transactional proxy, name each propagation level's effect, explain the self-invocation trap and the checked-exception rollback rule.
  6. Diagnose N+1 in a Spring service from statement counts and fix it with @EntityGraph or a fetch query, with open-in-view off.
  7. Paginate with Pageable/Page/Slice, explain the count query, and choose keyset scrolling for deep pages.
  8. Audit entities with @CreatedDate/@LastModifiedDate/@CreatedBy and publish domain events that fire after commit.
  9. Compose dynamic filters with Specification and Query by Example, and say where each stops being the right tool.
  10. Validate entities and service inputs with Bean Validation and map Spring's translated DataAccessException hierarchy to causes.
  11. Test the data layer with @DataJpaTest, TestEntityManager, @Sql and Testcontainers, and explain why test transactions roll back.
  12. Configure profiles, @ConfigurationProperties, the Hikari pool and production-safe JPA settings.
Deliberately out of scope

Spring MVC and REST controllers get one paragraph on DTOs at the boundary; the programs here have no web layer at all. Spring Security, Spring Data REST, the reactive stack and R2DBC are not covered. Spring Data JDBC gets a comparison paragraph in §1, Querydsl a mention in §9, and Hibernate Envers a mention in §8. Everything that is covered runs in the programs on this page.

Section 1

A Spring Boot data application, dissected

The JPA module ended with a program that built a PersistenceConfiguration, opened an EntityManagerFactory, began a transaction, persisted a product and committed. Fifteen lines of plumbing around three lines of intent. Spring Boot's promise is that the plumbing is inferred: put spring-boot-starter-data-jpa and a JDBC driver on the class path, and the pool, the EntityManagerFactory, the transaction manager and a working repository all exist before your first line of code runs. The promise is kept, and the cost is that the plumbing is now invisible — which is fine right up to the moment it does something you did not expect. This section makes it visible once, so that every later section can refer back to a specific piece.

The mechanism is autoconfiguration. A starter is an empty jar whose only purpose is to bring other jars in; spring-boot-starter-data-jpa pulls Spring Data JPA, Hibernate, Spring's JDBC and transaction support and HikariCP. Spring Boot then evaluates a long list of @AutoConfiguration classes, each guarded by conditions — @ConditionalOnClass (is Hibernate on the class path?), @ConditionalOnMissingBean (did the user already declare a DataSource?), @ConditionalOnProperty — and registers beans for the ones whose conditions hold. Your own @Bean always wins over an autoconfigured one of the same type, because the autoconfiguration runs after your configuration and checks for a missing bean first.

Worked example: ask the context what it built

This is the shape every program in this module follows: one @SpringBootApplication class, nested entities and repository interfaces, a CommandLineRunner bean for the demonstration, and the property map explained in "How to use this module". The runner here injects the infrastructure beans and prints facts about them, then performs one save and one query so the SQL can be read.

javaBootAnatomy.java
package lm.anatomy;
 
import jakarta.persistence.*;
import jakarta.persistence.metamodel.EntityType;
import org.springframework.aop.support.AopUtils;
import org.springframework.boot.CommandLineRunner;
import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.core.env.Environment;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaRepository;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.config.EnableJpaRepositories;
import org.springframework.transaction.PlatformTransactionManager;
import javax.sql.DataSource;
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;
 
@SpringBootApplication
@EnableJpaRepositories(considerNestedRepositories = true)   // the repositories below are nested interfaces
public class BootAnatomy {
 
    @Entity(name = "Product")                                // nested entities need an explicit JPQL name
    @Table(name = "product")
    public static class Product {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE) Long id;
        @Column(nullable = false, unique = true, length = 16) String sku;
        int priceInCents;                                    // becomes price_in_cents — read on
        protected Product() {}
        Product(String sku, int priceInCents) { this.sku = sku; this.priceInCents = priceInCents; }
        @Override public String toString() { return "Product[" + id + ", " + sku + ", " + priceInCents + "c]"; }
    }
 
    public interface ProductRepository extends JpaRepository<Product, Long> {
        List<Product> findBySkuStartingWithOrderBySku(String prefix);   // no body: derived from the name (§3)
    }
 
    @Bean
    CommandLineRunner demo(DataSource dataSource, PlatformTransactionManager txManager,
                           EntityManagerFactory emf, ProductRepository repo, Environment env) {
        return args -> {
            System.out.println("-- what the starter configured --");
            System.out.println("DataSource          = " + dataSource.getClass().getSimpleName());
            System.out.println("TransactionManager  = " + txManager.getClass().getSimpleName());
            System.out.println("repository is proxy = " + AopUtils.isAopProxy(repo));
            System.out.println("proxy interfaces    = " + Arrays.stream(repo.getClass().getInterfaces())
                    .map(Class::getSimpleName).filter(n -> n.contains("Repository")).sorted().toList());
            System.out.println("entities            = " + emf.getMetamodel().getEntities().stream()
                    .map(EntityType::getName).sorted().toList());
            System.out.println("naming strategy     = " + String.valueOf(emf.getProperties().get("hibernate.physical_naming_strategy"))
                    .replaceAll(".*\\.", ""));
            System.out.println("ddl-auto            = " + env.getProperty("spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto"));
            System.out.println("open-in-view        = " + env.getProperty("spring.jpa.open-in-view"));
 
            System.out.println("-- one save, one derived query --");
            repo.save(new Product("BOLT-7", 80));
            repo.save(new Product("NUT-3", 25));
            repo.save(new Product("BOLT-9", 95));
            System.out.println("count = " + repo.count());
            System.out.println("bolts = " + repo.findBySkuStartingWithOrderBySku("BOLT"));
        };
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication app = new SpringApplication(BootAnatomy.class);
        app.setDefaultProperties(Map.of(
            "spring.main.web-application-type", "none",
            "spring.main.banner-mode", "off",
            "spring.main.log-startup-info", "false",
            "logging.level.root", "WARN",
            "logging.pattern.console", "%level %logger{0}: %msg%n",
            "spring.datasource.url", "jdbc:h2:mem:anatomy;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1",
            "spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto", "create-drop",
            "spring.jpa.show-sql", "true",
            "spring.jpa.open-in-view", "false"));
        app.run(args).close();
    }
}

Read it top to bottom; every line is evidence of a decision Spring Boot made without being asked:

  • The DDL ran before the runner. Five Hibernate: lines precede the first -- heading: the schema is generated while the EntityManagerFactory is being built, which happens during context refresh, before any runner. The HTE_product temporary table is Hibernate 7's scratch table for bulk HQL on H2 (JPA §1); it will appear in every output here.
  • price_in_cents, not priceInCents. Plain Hibernate kept the Java name. Spring Boot sets Hibernate's hibernate.physical_naming_strategy to the snake-case strategy — the program read the resolved property back from the factory and printed its class, PhysicalNamingStrategySnakeCaseImpl. The sequence is product_seq for the same reason. If you ever port an application from plain Hibernate to Boot, this is the first thing that breaks against an existing schema.
  • HikariDataSource. Hibernate's built-in pool (the one JPA §1 warned about) is never used: Boot's DataSourceAutoConfiguration saw HikariCP on the class path and built a pooled data source from spring.datasource.*. The embedded H2 URL was supplied explicitly; without it, Boot would have invented a random in-memory database name.
  • JpaTransactionManager. The @Transactional machinery of §5 is already wired to the EntityManagerFactory. Nothing in the program mentioned transactions, and yet each repo.save ran in one.
  • The repository is a proxy implementing ProductRepository and Spring Data's marker Repository. There is no class called ProductRepositoryImpl anywhere; §2 opens the proxy up.
  • ddl-auto = create-drop and open-in-view = false are the values from the property map. Leave both unset and Boot would choose create-drop here too — because H2 is an embedded database — but none against PostgreSQL, and it would leave open-in-view on and print a warning about it. Those three defaults (naming, ddl-auto, open-in-view) are the whole difference between "plain Hibernate" and "Hibernate inside Boot".
  • Two sequence calls for three inserts. product_seq increments by 50, so one call should cover fifty ids. The pooled optimiser makes an extra call the first time to establish the low end of its block; after that it is one call per fifty rows (JPA §2, §9).
  • The derived query. findBySkuStartingWithOrderBySku has no body. Spring Data parsed the method name into sku like ? escape '\' order by sku — the escape clause is there because a prefix containing % or _ must not become a wildcard. Section 3 is about that grammar.

Where does a property come from?

Every program here calls setDefaultProperties, which is the lowest-priority source Spring Boot has: anything else that sets the same key wins. That is deliberate — a reader who runs these programs with --spring.jpa.show-sql=false gets what they asked for. The order itself is long and worth having internalised, because "why is this setting not taking effect?" is the most common configuration question there is.

Which source of spring.jpa.show-sql wins?

Tick the places where the property is set. Each source sets the value shown beside it; the readout names the winner and shows the full precedence order.

The pieces, named

@SpringBootApplication is three annotations: @SpringBootConfiguration (a @Configuration), @ComponentScan rooted at the class's package, and @EnableAutoConfiguration. It implies nothing about JPA — @EnableJpaRepositories and @EnableTransactionManagement arrive through autoconfiguration, conditionally, and only because the starter is present. Put the class at the top of your package tree; everything below it is scanned, everything beside it is not.

The programs here add @EnableJpaRepositories(considerNestedRepositories = true) explicitly. Repositories are normally top-level interfaces and Spring Data skips nested ones by default; one file per program forces them to be nested. Writing the annotation yourself replaces Boot's — the attributes you omit (base packages) fall back to the application package, as before.

Two ways to make a bean. Stereotype scanning: annotate a class @Component, @Service or @Repository and let the scan find it — the usual choice for your own classes, and the only way @Transactional proxies (§5) get created. @Bean methods in a configuration class: you construct the object; the usual choice for third-party types and for small runners like demo() above. Both end up as singletons in the same container; both can inject anything by constructor or method parameter.

@Service                                       // found by scanning; proxied if it has @Transactional methods
public class InventoryService {
    private final ProductRepository products;  // constructor injection: final, testable, no @Autowired needed
    InventoryService(ProductRepository products) { this.products = products; }
}
 
@Bean CommandLineRunner demo(ProductRepository repo) { return args -> { ... }; }   // runs once, after refresh

CommandLineRunner receives the raw String[]; ApplicationRunner receives parsed ApplicationArguments. Several runners execute in @Order. A runner is ordinary code: no transaction, no persistence context — every repository call it makes is its own unit of work, which is the behaviour the SQL above shows.

The spring.jpa properties that matter and their defaults
PropertyDefaultEffect
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-autocreate-drop for an embedded DB, else noneMaps to hibernate.hbm2ddl.auto. The embedded detection is what makes "works on H2, no tables on Postgres" happen.
spring.jpa.hibernate.naming.physical-strategysnake-casepriceInCents → price_in_cents. Set it to org.hibernate.boot.model.naming.PhysicalNamingStrategyStandardImpl to keep Java names, as plain Hibernate does.
spring.jpa.open-in-viewtrue (with a warning)Keeps a persistence context open for the whole web request. §6 argues for false.
spring.jpa.show-sqlfalseEcho SQL to standard output via hibernate.show_sql. For real logging use the org.hibernate.SQL logger instead (JPA §12).
spring.jpa.properties.*—Passthrough: anything after properties. reaches Hibernate untouched — spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50, …hibernate.generate_statistics=true.
spring.datasource.url / username / passwordembedded if a driver is foundFeeds the pool. spring.datasource.hikari.* tunes HikariCP (§12).

Run any Boot application with --debug and it prints the condition evaluation report: every autoconfiguration that matched, with the condition that let it in, and every one that did not, with the condition that kept it out. Reading it answers "why is there no DataSource?" in seconds. The shape (abbreviated; the real report is hundreds of lines and is not part of the verified output):

Shape of the --debug condition report
Positive matches:
-----------------
   DataSourceAutoConfiguration matched:
      - @ConditionalOnClass found required classes 'javax.sql.DataSource', 'EmbeddedDatabaseType'
   HibernateJpaAutoConfiguration matched:
      - @ConditionalOnClass found required classes 'LocalContainerEntityManagerFactoryBean', 'EntityManager', 'SessionImplementor'
   JpaRepositoriesAutoConfiguration matched:
      - @ConditionalOnMissingBean (types: JpaRepositoryFactoryBean, JpaRepositoryConfigExtension) did not find any beans

Negative matches:
-----------------
   DataSourceTransactionManagerAutoConfiguration:
      - @ConditionalOnMissingBean found bean 'transactionManager' (JpaTransactionManager)   -- JPA's won
   FlywayAutoConfiguration:
      - @ConditionalOnClass did not find required class 'org.flywaydb.core.Flyway'

The second negative match is the one to remember: Flyway is not configured because it is not on the class path. Add the dependency and the same report flips to a positive match, with no other change (§12).

Spring Data JDBC, briefly

Spring Data JPA is not the only Spring Data module that talks to a relational database. Spring Data JDBC offers the same repository interfaces over plain JDBC with no persistence context, no lazy loading, no dirty checking and no caching: an aggregate is loaded whole and saved whole. It is simpler to reason about and has none of the N+1 and LazyInitializationException failure modes of §6 — and, by the same token, none of the first-level cache, the automatic update-on-commit or the mapping flexibility of JPA. If your domain is a set of small aggregates and you are tired of ORM surprises, it is worth a look. This module stays with JPA because the warehouse's associations, locking and batching are exactly the territory where JPA earns its complexity.

Autoconfiguration gotchas
  • The application class's package is the scan root. Entities and repositories in a sibling package are invisible — the symptom is "Not a managed type" for an entity, or a NoSuchBeanDefinitionException for a repository. Fix with @EntityScan / @EnableJpaRepositories(basePackages), or move the class.
  • ddl-auto changes meaning with the database. The embedded-database default silently becomes none the day you point at PostgreSQL. Set it explicitly in every profile (§12).
  • Declaring a bean replaces the autoconfigured one — entirely. A hand-written DataSource bean means spring.datasource.* is now ignored, including the Hikari tuning you set in properties.
  • Runners run with no transaction. Each repository call commits on its own. A LazyInitializationException in a runner is this, not a mapping bug.
  • Boot's naming strategy is not Hibernate's default. Against an existing schema with camel-case columns, either set the standard physical strategy or add @Column(name) everywhere.

Check yourself

1.An entity field int priceInCents produced the column price_in_cents above, while the same entity in the JPA module produced priceInCents. What changed?

B. The program printed the resolved property: hibernate.physical_naming_strategy is PhysicalNamingStrategySnakeCaseImpl, set by HibernateJpaAutoConfiguration. Hibernate on its own uses the standard strategy, which keeps the Java name.

A is wrong: Hibernate's default has not changed between patch releases, and the JPA module's 7.4.1 output is the proof that the default keeps camel case. C describes H2's case folding of unquoted identifiers, which would give PRICEINCENTS, not add underscores. D confuses two unrelated mechanisms: method-name derivation (§3) reads entity property names and never influences the schema.

2.You remove spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto from a project that works against H2 and point spring.datasource.url at PostgreSQL. The first query fails with "relation product does not exist". Why?

C. The default is computed from the data source: embedded (H2, HSQLDB, Derby in memory) gets create-drop, everything else gets none. It is the single most common "works locally, fails in staging" cause, and the fix is to set the property explicitly per profile — validate in production with a migration tool owning the schema.

A is wrong: both spellings reach Hibernate; spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto is the documented one. B is invented — there is no such misdetection. D is wrong: the snake-case strategy emits lower case, and the error says the relation does not exist at all, which is a missing table rather than a case mismatch.

3.Which of these does @SpringBootApplication itself imply, without any starter on the class path? Select all that apply.

A, B and D. Those three are the annotation's definition. Everything JPA-specific — repositories, transaction management, the entity manager — is added by autoconfiguration, conditionally, when the starter's classes are present.

C is the trap: @EnableJpaRepositories is applied for you by JpaRepositoriesAutoConfiguration, which is why removing the starter silently removes your repositories rather than failing to compile. The programs here write it explicitly only to set considerNestedRepositories.

4.Every program in this module calls setDefaultProperties rather than shipping an application.properties. A reader runs one with --spring.jpa.show-sql=false. What happens?

D. Command-line arguments sit near the top of the precedence order; setDefaultProperties sits at the very bottom, below application.properties and even below @PropertySource. That is why the programs use it: anything the reader sets, anywhere, overrides it.

A inverts the order — "programmatic" is not "specific"; the method's name says what it is. B is wrong: multiple sources for one key are the normal case, resolved by precedence, never an error. C is wrong because a property has exactly one effective value for the lifetime of the environment.

Section 2

Repositories: from CrudRepository to JpaRepository

In §1 the repository was an interface with no implementation, and yet repo.save inserted a row. Somebody wrote that body. At startup Spring Data finds every interface that extends Repository, and for each one builds a JDK proxy whose method calls are routed to one of three places: a base implementation (SimpleJpaRepository, which holds an EntityManager and implements save, findById, delete and the rest), a query method generated from the method's name or annotation (§3, §4), or a fragment you implement by hand. Knowing which of the three is behind a call is most of what there is to know about repositories — because the base implementation is ordinary JPA code, and every one of its decisions is something the JPA module already taught.

The interfaces form a ladder. You pick the rung whose methods you want to expose, not the most powerful one available:

Spring Data repository interfaces and what each adds
InterfaceAddsUse it when
Repository<T, ID>nothing — a markeryou want to expose only the query methods you declare, e.g. a read-only reference-data repository
CrudRepository / ListCrudRepositorysave, findById, findAll, count, delete*, existsById (the List variant returns List instead of Iterable)the usual aggregate root
PagingAndSortingRepository / List…findAll(Sort), findAll(Pageable)you page or sort the whole table (§7)
JpaRepositoryflush, saveAndFlush, saveAllAndFlush, getReferenceById, deleteAllInBatch, deleteAllByIdInBatch, plus Query by Exampleyou need JPA-specific operations — which in practice is most of the time

Every method you inherit is a method a caller can use. A repository for an append-only audit log that extends JpaRepository has a deleteAllInBatch() on it, whether you meant to offer one or not. Narrowing the interface is cheap API design.

Worked example: what each method actually sends

One application, two entities, and a runner that calls the repository methods people most often misjudge. Product has a generated id and a @Version; Tag has an assigned String id and implements Persistable. The runner is not transactional, so unless a TransactionTemplate wraps a block, every repository call is its own transaction — a detail that explains several lines of the output.

javaRepositories.java
package lm.repos;
 
import jakarta.persistence.*;
import org.springframework.boot.CommandLineRunner;
import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.data.domain.Persistable;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaRepository;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.config.EnableJpaRepositories;
import org.springframework.data.repository.NoRepositoryBean;
import org.springframework.transaction.support.TransactionTemplate;
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
 
@SpringBootApplication
@EnableJpaRepositories(considerNestedRepositories = true)
public class Repositories {
 
    @Entity(name = "Product")
    @Table(name = "product")
    public static class Product {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE) Long id;
        @Version Long version;                                   // save() looks at this first
        @Column(nullable = false, unique = true, length = 16) String sku;
        int priceInCents;
        protected Product() {}
        Product(String sku, int priceInCents) { this.sku = sku; this.priceInCents = priceInCents; }
        static Product detached(Long id, Long version, String sku, int price) {   // a row we hold without a context
            Product p = new Product(sku, price); p.id = id; p.version = version; return p;
        }
        String sku() { return sku; }
        @Override public String toString() { return "Product[" + id + ", v" + version + ", " + sku + ", " + priceInCents + "c]"; }
    }
 
    /* An assigned id gives save() nothing to go on: id is never null, there is
       no @Version. Persistable lets the entity say whether it is new. */
    @Entity(name = "Tag")
    @Table(name = "tag")
    public static class Tag implements Persistable<String> {
        @Id String code;
        String label;
        @Transient private boolean isNew = true;
        protected Tag() {}
        Tag(String code, String label) { this.code = code; this.label = label; }
        @Override public String getId() { return code; }
        @Override public boolean isNew() { return isNew; }
        @PostPersist @PostLoad void markNotNew() { isNew = false; }
    }
 
    @NoRepositoryBean
    public interface BaseRepository<T, ID> extends JpaRepository<T, ID> {   // shared signatures, no bean of its own
        List<T> findAllSortedById();
    }
 
    public interface ProductRepositoryCustom { List<Product> cheaperThan(int cents); }
 
    public static class ProductRepositoryCustomImpl implements ProductRepositoryCustom {   // a fragment: hand-written body
        @PersistenceContext EntityManager em;
        @Override public List<Product> cheaperThan(int cents) {
            return em.createQuery("select p from Product p where p.priceInCents < :c order by p.sku", Product.class)
                     .setParameter("c", cents).getResultList();
        }
    }
 
    public interface ProductRepository extends JpaRepository<Product, Long>, ProductRepositoryCustom {}
    public interface TagRepository extends JpaRepository<Tag, String> {}
 
    @Bean
    CommandLineRunner demo(ProductRepository products, TagRepository tags, TransactionTemplate tx) {
        return args -> {
            System.out.println("-- the hierarchy --");
            System.out.println("JpaRepository extends " + Arrays.stream(JpaRepository.class.getInterfaces())
                    .map(Class::getSimpleName).sorted().toList());
 
            System.out.println("-- save: new entity (id null) --");
            Product bolt = products.save(new Product("BOLT-7", 80));
            System.out.println("saved " + bolt);
 
            System.out.println("-- save: detached entity (id and version set) --");
            Product copy = Product.detached(bolt.id, bolt.version, "BOLT-7", 85);
            Product merged = products.save(copy);
            System.out.println("merged == copy: " + (merged == copy) + ", merged = " + merged);
 
            System.out.println("-- save: looks detached, but the row does not exist --");
            try {
                products.save(Product.detached(404L, 0L, "GHOST-1", 1));
            } catch (RuntimeException e) {
                System.out.println("threw " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " caused by " + rootCause(e).getClass().getSimpleName());
            }
 
            System.out.println("-- save: Persistable decides --");
            Tag fast = tags.save(new Tag("FAST", "fast mover"));
            fast.label = "fast-moving";
            tags.save(fast);
            System.out.println("tags = " + tags.count());
 
            System.out.println("-- reads --");
            System.out.println("findById       = " + products.findById(bolt.id).map(Product::toString).orElse("none"));
            System.out.println("findById(404)  = " + products.findById(404L).isPresent());
            tx.executeWithoutResult(status -> {
                Product ref = products.getReferenceById(bolt.id);
                System.out.println("reference type = " + (ref.getClass() == Product.class ? "Product" : "a Hibernate proxy") + " (no select yet)");
                System.out.println("field read     = " + ref.sku + " (a field read bypasses the proxy)");
                System.out.println("getter read    = " + ref.sku());
            });
            System.out.println("existsById     = " + products.existsById(bolt.id));
 
            System.out.println("-- saveAndFlush inside a transaction --");
            tx.executeWithoutResult(status -> {
                products.save(new Product("NUT-3", 25));
                System.out.println("after save: nothing sent yet");
                products.saveAndFlush(new Product("CAM-9", 2300));
                System.out.println("after saveAndFlush: both inserts sent");
            });
 
            System.out.println("-- the custom fragment --");
            System.out.println("cheaperThan(100) = " + products.cheaperThan(100));
 
            System.out.println("-- deletes --");
            products.deleteById(bolt.id);
            System.out.println("remaining = " + products.count());
            products.deleteAllInBatch();
            System.out.println("remaining = " + products.count());
        };
    }
 
    static Throwable rootCause(Throwable t) { while (t.getCause() != null) t = t.getCause(); return t; }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication app = new SpringApplication(Repositories.class);
        app.setDefaultProperties(Map.of(
            "spring.main.web-application-type", "none",
            "spring.main.banner-mode", "off",
            "spring.main.log-startup-info", "false",
            "logging.level.root", "WARN",
            "logging.pattern.console", "%level %logger{0}: %msg%n",
            "spring.datasource.url", "jdbc:h2:mem:repos;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1",
            "spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto", "create-drop",
            "spring.jpa.show-sql", "true",
            "spring.jpa.open-in-view", "false"));
        app.run(args).close();
    }
}

Read it block by block:

  • The hierarchy. JpaRepository extends ListCrudRepository, ListPagingAndSortingRepository and QueryByExampleExecutor (§9) — the table above, read off the class itself.
  • A new entity: sequence call, insert, no select. save asked "is this entity new?", decided yes, and called em.persist. The insert appears straight away rather than at some later flush because the call was its own transaction, and the transaction committed as save returned. The returned object is the same instance you passed in, now with id = 1 and version = 0.
  • A detached copy: select, then update. The copy carried an id and a version, so save decided it was not new and called em.merge — which loads the row (the select), copies your state onto the managed instance, and the commit's dirty check writes it (the update, guarded by and version=?). Note merged == copy: false: merge returns a different, managed instance, exactly as JPA §3 showed. The version is now 1 on the returned object; the copy you still hold says 0.
  • A copy whose row does not exist. Same decision — id and version set, so merge — but the select finds nothing. Because the entity is versioned, Hibernate does not treat the missing row as "insert it": it concludes another transaction deleted it and throws StaleObjectStateException, which Spring translates into its own ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException (§10 covers the translation). Without @Version, the same call would have inserted a new row with whatever id the copy carried — usually not what anybody wanted.
  • Persistable decides for Tag. An assigned id is never null, and Tag has no version, so neither of the usual signals can tell a new tag from an existing one. Implementing Persistable hands the decision to the entity: isNew() starts true, so the first save is a plain insert with no select. A @PostPersist/@PostLoad callback flips the flag, so the second save merges — select, then update.
  • findById always selects, and returns Optional; a missing id is an empty Optional, not an exception. Each call ran in a separate transaction with a fresh persistence context, so the second read of the same id hit the database again.
  • getReferenceById sent nothing. It returned a Hibernate proxy — a generated subclass of Product — without touching the database. Then the surprise: reading the field ref.sku printed null. The proxy is a subclass instance whose own fields are never populated; only method calls are intercepted and forwarded to the real, lazily loaded entity. The getter ref.sku() triggered the select and returned BOLT-7. The block needed a TransactionTemplate: outside a transaction the persistence context would be gone before the getter ran (JPA §5).
  • existsById is a count(*), never a full row load.
  • save inside a transaction defers the insert. Within the template, save(NUT-3) fetched an id (the sequence call) but sent no insert — persist only queues the action. saveAndFlush(CAM-9) then flushed the whole persistence context, and both inserts went out. CAM-9 needed no sequence call of its own: the block of fifty fetched for NUT-3 covered it.
  • The fragment. cheaperThan is a method no naming convention could produce. ProductRepositoryCustomImpl holds its body; Spring Data found it by the interface name plus the Impl postfix and wired it into the proxy, so callers see one repository.
  • Two deletes, two shapes. deleteById loads the entity (select) and removes it through the persistence context, so the delete carries and version=? and any cascades, orphan removal and @PreRemove callbacks run. deleteAllInBatch is a single bulk delete from product: no select, no version check, no cascades, no callbacks.

Watch save decide

persist or merge? Simulated ← → to step
SimpleJpaRepository.save, simplified
public <S extends T> S save(S entity) {
    if (entityInformation.isNew(entity)) {
        em.persist(entity);
        return entity;
    }
    return em.merge(entity);
}
 
// isNew(entity), in order:
//   1. implements Persistable?           -> entity.isNew()
//   2. @Version of a wrapper type?       -> version == null
//   3. otherwise the id                   -> id == null (or 0 for a primitive id)
The entity and the decision
SQL

Proxies, transactions and fragments

Every repository method is transactional. SimpleJpaRepository is annotated @Transactional(readOnly = true) at class level and plain @Transactional on its write methods. Called from code that has no transaction, each call opens and commits its own — which is why every save in the worked example produced SQL at once. Called from inside a @Transactional service (§5), the repository joins the caller's transaction and the SQL waits for that transaction's flush. Same call, different timing, and the difference is entirely in the caller. Your own query methods inherit the read-only default; a @Modifying query method needs its own @Transactional (§4).

Fragments compose. A repository interface may extend any number of fragment interfaces; for each, Spring Data looks for a class named after the fragment interface plus Impl (the postfix is configurable) and routes those methods to it. Fragments are ordinary beans, so they can inject an EntityManager, a JdbcClient or anything else. A fragment method with the same signature as a base method overrides it — which is how you replace, say, save for one aggregate without touching the others.

Shared signatures without a bean. BaseRepository in the example is marked @NoRepositoryBean: it is a building block that other repository interfaces extend, and Spring Data must not try to create a repository for it on its own (it has no concrete entity type). Nothing in this program extends it; it is there to show the shape. @RepositoryDefinition(domainClass = …, idClass = …) is the opposite tool: it makes a plain interface a repository without extending anything, so it exposes exactly the methods you write.

Return types. Single results come back as Optional<T> or as T (then null for "no row"); collections as List, Iterable, Streamable or Stream (the last one must be consumed inside a transaction and closed — §4). Prefer Optional for anything a caller might look up by user input. An application with two databases declares two @EnableJpaRepositories blocks, each with its own basePackages, entityManagerFactoryRef and transactionManagerRef; that is the only time the repository infrastructure needs configuring by hand.

Why flush is on the interface. Most code never needs it: the commit flushes. You need it when the database must see the change before the transaction ends — to trip a unique constraint now rather than at commit, so the exception surfaces where you can handle it, or before a native query that reads the same table. saveAndFlush is save followed by flush; as the output showed, it flushes everything pending, not just the entity you passed.

Match the method to its SQL

Drag a method onto its SQL shape, or click one then click the other

Each method is called on its own, outside any transaction, for a versioned Product.

All four correct. The pattern: anything that goes through the persistence context (save, deleteById) behaves like the JPA operation underneath it, with its callbacks, cascades and version checks; anything named …InBatch is a bulk statement that bypasses the context entirely; and getReferenceById defers the database until the data is actually needed.

Repository gotchas
  • Use the object save returns. For a new entity it is the same instance; for anything merged it is a different one. Code that ignores the return value works for inserts and silently keeps a stale, detached object for updates.
  • Calling save on a managed entity is redundant. Inside a transaction, a loaded entity is already tracked; changing a field is enough and the commit's dirty check writes it. The extra save is harmless but suggests the author thinks it is required — and in a long loop with detached entities it turns into a select per row.
  • Assigned ids need Persistable or a @Version. Otherwise every save of a new entity is a merge: one extra select per insert, and a batch import twice as chatty as it needs to be.
  • A proxy's fields are empty. Code that reads entity fields directly — from equals, from a mapper, from a test — sees null on a reference or a lazy association. Access state through methods; it is one more reason entity equals should use getters (§11 of the JPA module).
  • deleteAllInBatch and deleteAllByIdInBatch skip the domain model. No cascades, no orphan removal, no @PreRemove, no auditing — and managed instances of the deleted rows stay in any open persistence context, stale. Fast, and only correct when nothing depends on those hooks.

Check yourself

1.A web handler receives a Product with id = 7 and version = 3 deserialised from JSON, calls repo.save(product) and then returns product.version to the client. The database row ends with version 4. What does the client receive?

B. A non-null version means "not new", so save called merge, which copied the state onto a managed instance and returned that. The worked example printed merged == copy: false for exactly this reason. The client is told version 3, sends it back on its next edit, and gets an optimistic-locking failure for a conflict that never happened. Return the value save returns.

A is true only for new entities, where persist manages the instance you passed. C is wrong: an id is precisely what makes save choose merge. D is invented; merge never writes to its argument.

2.An entity has an assigned String id, no @Version, and does not implement Persistable. What SQL does repo.save(new Country("NO", "Norway")) send for a code that is not yet in the table?

C. With no Persistable and no version, the id decides — and an assigned id is never null, so the entity looks existing and save calls merge. Merge selects, finds nothing, and treats the object as new: an insert. The result is correct; the select is wasted. That is the case Persistable exists for, as Tag showed.

A is what happens with Persistable reporting new. B describes a hand-written update, not merge; merge reads before it writes. D is wrong: save always ends in persist or merge, and both write.

3.Inside a transaction, Product ref = repo.getReferenceById(1L); then System.out.println(ref.sku); prints null although the row's SKU is BOLT-7. Why?

A. Hibernate builds the reference as a ByteBuddy subclass of Product holding an interceptor and the id. Calling a method runs the interceptor, which loads the real entity and delegates; reading a field goes straight to the proxy object's own, never-populated field. The worked example printed null for the field and BOLT-7 for the getter.

B is wrong: the getter in the same block loaded the data, because a transaction was open. C is wrong: the proxy points at the existing row; it is not a new entity. D is wrong: basic columns are eagerly loaded by default, and the problem is the proxy, not column fetching.

4.An Order has @OneToMany(cascade = ALL, orphanRemoval = true) lines and a @PreRemove audit callback. Which statements about orderRepo.deleteAllInBatch() are true? Select all that apply.

A, C and D. deleteAllInBatch issues a single JPQL bulk delete — the worked example's delete from product p1_0 — which runs in the database and bypasses the persistence context. Nothing is loaded, so no lifecycle callback can run and no cascade is applied; the database's foreign key then rejects deleting orders that still have lines.

B describes deleteById and delete(entity), which load the entity and remove it through the context, version check included. Use those when the domain model's hooks matter; use the batch variants for tables where they do not.

Section 3

Derived queries: method names that become SQL

A repository interface in §2 had no implementation and still worked, because Spring Data generated a proxy for it. This section is about the part of that proxy that reads your mind: declare List<Product> findByCategoryAndPriceInCentsLessThan(Category c, int max) with no body and no annotation, and at startup Spring Data parses the method name into a predicate tree, checks every property against the entity's metamodel, builds a JPQL query from it, and from then on every call runs that query. The name is the specification. Get it wrong and the application refuses to start, which is the best place to be wrong.

The grammar is small. A subject (find…By, count…By, exists…By, delete…By, with optional Distinct, First/Top and a limit), then a predicate made of property names, comparison keywords and And/Or, then an optional OrderBy with properties and directions. Parameters are bound to the predicate's placeholders by position, left to right, so the parameter order must follow the name. Everything else — the SQL, the parameter escaping, the fetch first clause, the upper() for a case-insensitive match — is derived.

Worked example

One repository with eighteen derived methods, exercised over seven products. Two of them have no name on purpose (findByNameIsNull), two are inactive, and the SKUs are chosen so that each string keyword matches something different. Read the Hibernate: line above each result: it is the SQL the name became.

javaDerivedQueries.java
package lm.derived;
 
import jakarta.persistence.*;
import org.springframework.boot.CommandLineRunner;
import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.data.domain.Sort;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaRepository;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.config.EnableJpaRepositories;
import org.springframework.transaction.PlatformTransactionManager;
import org.springframework.transaction.support.TransactionTemplate;
import java.util.Collection;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Optional;
import java.util.stream.Stream;
 
@SpringBootApplication
@EnableJpaRepositories(considerNestedRepositories = true)
public class DerivedQueries {
 
    public enum Category { FASTENER, STRUCTURAL, MOTION }
 
    @Entity(name = "Product")
    @Table(name = "product")
    public static class Product {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE) Long id;
        @Column(nullable = false, unique = true, length = 16) String sku;
        String name;                                        // nullable on purpose: see findByNameIsNull
        @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING) @Column(nullable = false, length = 16) Category category;
        int priceInCents;
        boolean active;
        protected Product() {}
        Product(String sku, String name, Category category, int priceInCents, boolean active) {
            this.sku = sku; this.name = name; this.category = category; this.priceInCents = priceInCents; this.active = active;
        }
        @Override public String toString() { return sku; }
    }
 
    // Every method below is implemented by Spring Data from its NAME alone.
    public interface ProductRepository extends JpaRepository<Product, Long> {
        List<Product> findByCategoryOrderBySkuAsc(Category category);
        List<Product> findByCategoryAndPriceInCentsLessThanOrderBySku(Category category, int max);
        List<Product> findByPriceInCentsBetweenOrderByPriceInCents(int low, int high);
        List<Product> findBySkuStartingWithOrderBySku(String prefix);
        List<Product> findBySkuContainingOrderBySku(String part);
        List<Product> findBySkuEndingWithOrderBySku(String suffix);
        Optional<Product> findByNameIgnoreCase(String name);
        List<Product> findBySkuInOrderBySku(Collection<String> skus);
        List<Product> findByActiveTrueOrderBySku();
        List<Product> findByNameIsNullOrderBySku();
        List<Product> findFirst3ByOrderByPriceInCentsDesc();
        Optional<Product> findTopByCategoryOrderByPriceInCentsAsc(Category category);
        long countByCategory(Category category);
        boolean existsBySku(String sku);
        long countByActiveFalse();
        long deleteBySku(String sku);                        // derived delete: needs a transaction
        List<Product> findByCategory(Category category, Sort sort);
        Stream<Product> findByPriceInCentsGreaterThanOrderBySku(int min);   // needs an open transaction
    }
 
    @Bean TransactionTemplate tx(PlatformTransactionManager manager) { return new TransactionTemplate(manager); }
 
    @Bean CommandLineRunner demo(ProductRepository repo, TransactionTemplate tx) {
        return args -> {
            repo.saveAll(List.of(
                new Product("BOLT-7", "Hex bolt M8", Category.FASTENER, 80, true),
                new Product("NUT-3", "Hex nut M8", Category.FASTENER, 25, true),
                new Product("PIN-2", null, Category.FASTENER, 15, false),
                new Product("GIRD-1", "Steel girder 6m", Category.STRUCTURAL, 120_000, true),
                new Product("ROD-4", "Threaded rod 1m", Category.STRUCTURAL, 4_500, true),
                new Product("CAM-9", "Cam follower", Category.MOTION, 2_300, true),
                new Product("HUB-8", null, Category.MOTION, 7_900, false)));
 
            System.out.println("-- equality, comparison, range --");
            System.out.println("fasteners         = " + repo.findByCategoryOrderBySkuAsc(Category.FASTENER));
            System.out.println("cheap fasteners   = " + repo.findByCategoryAndPriceInCentsLessThanOrderBySku(Category.FASTENER, 50));
            System.out.println("2000..8000        = " + repo.findByPriceInCentsBetweenOrderByPriceInCents(2_000, 8_000));
 
            System.out.println("-- string matching --");
            System.out.println("starts BOLT       = " + repo.findBySkuStartingWithOrderBySku("BOLT"));
            System.out.println("contains -        = " + repo.findBySkuContainingOrderBySku("D-"));
            System.out.println("ends 9            = " + repo.findBySkuEndingWithOrderBySku("9"));
            System.out.println("name ignore case  = " + repo.findByNameIgnoreCase("hex BOLT m8").map(p -> p.sku).orElse("none"));
 
            System.out.println("-- collections, booleans, nulls --");
            System.out.println("in list           = " + repo.findBySkuInOrderBySku(List.of("NUT-3", "CAM-9", "NOPE")));
            System.out.println("active            = " + repo.findByActiveTrueOrderBySku());
            System.out.println("unnamed           = " + repo.findByNameIsNullOrderBySku());
 
            System.out.println("-- limiting and ordering --");
            System.out.println("top 3 by price    = " + repo.findFirst3ByOrderByPriceInCentsDesc());
            System.out.println("cheapest motion   = " + repo.findTopByCategoryOrderByPriceInCentsAsc(Category.MOTION).map(p -> p.sku).orElse("none"));
            System.out.println("sorted by param   = " + repo.findByCategory(Category.STRUCTURAL, Sort.by(Sort.Direction.DESC, "priceInCents")));
 
            System.out.println("-- counts and existence --");
            System.out.println("count structural  = " + repo.countByCategory(Category.STRUCTURAL));
            System.out.println("exists ROD-4      = " + repo.existsBySku("ROD-4"));
            System.out.println("inactive          = " + repo.countByActiveFalse());
 
            System.out.println("-- streaming and deleting need a transaction --");
            tx.executeWithoutResult(status -> {
                try (Stream<Product> s = repo.findByPriceInCentsGreaterThanOrderBySku(1_000)) {
                    System.out.println("streamed          = " + s.map(p -> p.sku).toList());
                }
                System.out.println("deleted           = " + repo.deleteBySku("PIN-2"));
            });
            System.out.println("remaining         = " + repo.count());
        };
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication app = new SpringApplication(DerivedQueries.class);
        app.setDefaultProperties(Map.of(
            "spring.main.web-application-type", "none",
            "spring.main.banner-mode", "off",
            "spring.main.log-startup-info", "false",
            "logging.level.root", "WARN",
            "logging.pattern.console", "%level %logger{0}: %msg%n",
            "spring.datasource.url", "jdbc:h2:mem:derived;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1",
            "spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto", "create-drop",
            "spring.jpa.show-sql", "true",
            "spring.jpa.open-in-view", "false"));
        app.run(args).close();
    }
}

Six things in that output are worth reading twice:

  • like ? escape '\'. StartingWith, Containing and EndingWith all become like, but Spring Data builds the pattern itself (BOLT%, %D-%, %9) and escapes any % or _ in your argument first. A user searching for 50% finds SKUs containing "50%", not everything starting with 50. §4 shows the declared-query version, which does not escape for you.
  • in (?,?,?). In with a three-element collection expands to three placeholders. A different collection size is a different SQL string, which matters for statement caching and for the database's bind limit (Oracle stops at 1,000).
  • fetch first ? rows only. First3 and Top become the dialect's limit clause. H2 and PostgreSQL say fetch first; MySQL would say limit. You wrote neither.
  • upper(p1_0.name)=upper(?). IgnoreCase wraps both sides in upper(), which also means the index on name is useless for that query unless it is a functional index. Think before adding IgnoreCase to a hot path.
  • exists is a select p1_0.id … fetch first ? rows only, not a count. It stops at the first match.
  • The derived deleteBySku ran a select before its delete. A derived delete loads the entities and removes them one by one through the persistence context, so cascades and lifecycle callbacks fire. A @Modifying @Query("delete …") (§4) is one statement and fires nothing.

Build a method name and watch it parse

From method name to SQL

The keyword table

Derived-query keywords and the JPQL they produce
KeywordExampleJPQL fragment
Is, Equals, or nothingfindBySkup.sku = ?1
NotfindByCategoryNotp.category <> ?1
LessThan, LessThanEqual, GreaterThan, GreaterThanEqualfindByPriceInCentsLessThanp.priceInCents < ?1
BetweenfindByPriceInCentsBetweenp.priceInCents between ?1 and ?2 (two parameters, inclusive)
After, BeforefindByPlacedAfterp.placed > ?1 — comparison keywords for dates
IsNull, IsNotNullfindByNameIsNullp.name is null (no parameter)
Like, NotLikefindBySkuLikep.sku like ?1 — you supply the %
StartingWith, EndingWith, ContainingfindBySkuContainingp.sku like %?1% with the argument escaped
In, NotInfindBySkuIn(Collection)p.sku in ?1
True, FalsefindByActiveTruep.active = true (no parameter)
IgnoreCase, AllIgnoreCasefindByNameIgnoreCaseupper(p.name) = upper(?1)
OrderBy…Asc/DescfindByCategoryOrderBySkuAscorder by p.sku asc
DistinctfindDistinctByCategoryselect distinct p
First/Top + numberfindFirst3ByOrderByPriceInCentsDescdialect limit clause, 1 if no number

Parsing rules you will hit

findByOrderCustomerName(String name) is resolved greedily: Spring Data first looks for a property called orderCustomerName, then splits from the right — orderCustomer.name, then order.customerName, then order.customer.name — until a path through the metamodel matches. Each association in the path becomes a join in the SQL.

List<OrderLine> findByOrderCustomerName(String name);     // order.customer.name — two joins
List<OrderLine> findByOrder_Customer_Name(String name);   // the same, written unambiguously

The underscore is the disambiguator for when the greedy split would pick the wrong path — an entity with both an address association and a addressZip field, for example. Use it whenever the name has more than one plausible reading, and never rely on the reader guessing the same way the parser did.

Or splits the name first, then And inside each part: findByCategoryAndActiveTrueOrPriceInCentsLessThan means (category = ?1 and active = true) or priceInCents < ?2. There are no parentheses in a method name, so you cannot express category = ?1 and (active = true or priceInCents < ?2) at all — that is a @Query.

Parameters bind by position to the predicate parts that take one: Category for part one, nothing for ActiveTrue, int for part three. Put the parameters in a different order and the application starts, the types coerce, and the query is silently wrong — the only keyword-grammar mistake that is not caught at boot.

Return types of derived queries
Declared return typeWhat you get
Productthe one result, null if none, IncorrectResultSizeDataAccessException if several
Optional<Product>the same, with an empty Optional for none — prefer this
List, Set, Collection, Streamableall results, loaded
Stream<Product>results pulled from an open cursor — needs a surrounding transaction and try-with-resources, as the worked example shows
Page, Slice, Windowone page of results plus metadata, driven by a Pageable or ScrollPosition parameter — §7
an interface, record or class that is not the entitya projection — §4
long, intfor count…By and delete…By (rows affected)
booleanfor exists…By

A derived method may also take a trailing Sort, Pageable or Limit parameter; it is applied after the name's own OrderBy. Combining OrderBy in the name with a Sort parameter sorts by both, name first.

Every method name is parsed when the repository bean is created. A property that does not exist stops the application before it serves a request, with a message that names the type and the property:

Startup failure (illustrative)
Caused by: org.springframework.data.mapping.PropertyReferenceException:
  No property 'pricelnCents' found for type 'Product'
  Did you mean 'priceInCents'?
  at org.springframework.data.mapping.PropertyPath.<init>(PropertyPath.java:91)
  at org.springframework.data.repository.query.parser.Part.<init>(Part.java:81)
  at org.springframework.data.repository.query.parser.PartTree$Predicate.buildTree(…)

The "did you mean" is computed by edit distance against the entity's properties. This fail-fast check is a large part of the value of derived queries: a renamed field breaks the build of every query that used it, which a string inside @Query only does if query validation at startup is on (it is, by default — §4).

When a derived name is the wrong tool
  • It no longer reads as a sentence. findByCategoryAndActiveTrueAndPriceInCentsBetweenAndSupplierCountryInOrderByPriceInCentsDescSkuAsc is a 90-character specification nobody will review. Past roughly forty characters, or past two Ands, write a @Query and give the method a name that says what it is for.
  • It needs an aggregate, a group, a join on a non-association, or a projection with expressions. The grammar has none of these. sum, group by, case, coalesce are @Query territory.
  • It needs a fetch join. A derived method can declare @EntityGraph (§6), but a JPQL join fetch cannot be derived.
  • It hides a scan. findByNameContaining is a leading-wildcard like: no B-tree index helps it. The name looks innocent; the plan is a full table scan.
  • It is a derived delete over many rows. It loads each entity first. Use a @Modifying delete, or a batch job, past a few hundred rows.

Check yourself

1.List<Product> findBySkuContaining(String part) is called with "50%". Which rows match?

C. The worked example's SQL says like ? escape '\': Spring Data wraps the argument in %…% and escapes any % or _ inside it, so the user's percent sign is matched literally.

A and D would be true of a @Query("… like ?1") where you pass the pattern yourself — §4 shows that version emits escape '', no escaping. B invents a validation that does not exist; any string is a valid argument.

2.A repository declares findByCategoryAndActiveTrueOrPriceInCentsLessThan(Category c, int max). Which predicate does it run?

B. The parser splits on Or first, then on And within each part — the only precedence a method name can express.

A needs parentheses, which the grammar has no syntax for; that query must be a @Query. C is wrong: mixing is allowed, with exactly this precedence. D is wrong because True/False/IsNull are the keywords that take no parameter; the two parameters bind to Category and LessThan.

3.Which of these would be caught when the application starts, before any request? Select all that apply.

A and D. Both are PropertyReferenceExceptions: the name is parsed against the metamodel when the repository bean is built, and a property or path that does not exist fails there.

B starts fine — parameters bind by position and the types are checked only loosely — and returns wrong results, which is why the positional rule deserves care. C is a performance problem the parser cannot see; the query is valid, the plan is the issue.

Section 4

@Query, modifying queries and projections

A derived name is a specification written in a tiny language. When the language runs out — an aggregate, parentheses around an or, a fetch join, a constructor expression, a vendor function — you write the query yourself and put it on the method with @Query. Spring Data still does the plumbing: it binds the parameters, appends a Sort, derives or uses a count query for a Page, and maps the result to whatever return type you declared. The query string is still parsed at startup, so a misspelt attribute in JPQL fails the boot exactly as a misspelt derived name does.

This section also covers the other half of "I do not want the whole entity": projections. A read screen that shows a SKU and a price does not need a managed Product with its snapshot, its dirty check and its lazy associations; it needs two columns. Spring Data offers three ways to ask for them, and they do not all do what they look like they do.

Worked example

Seven declared queries, five projections and the two forms of @Modifying, over six products. The SQL line above each result is the evidence for every claim in the rest of the section.

javaDeclaredQueries.java
package lm.declared;
 
import jakarta.persistence.*;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Value;
import org.springframework.boot.CommandLineRunner;
import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.data.domain.Page;
import org.springframework.data.domain.PageRequest;
import org.springframework.data.domain.Pageable;
import org.springframework.data.domain.Sort;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaRepository;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.Modifying;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.Query;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.config.EnableJpaRepositories;
import org.springframework.data.repository.query.Param;
import org.springframework.transaction.PlatformTransactionManager;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;
import org.springframework.transaction.support.TransactionTemplate;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
 
@SpringBootApplication
@EnableJpaRepositories(considerNestedRepositories = true)
public class DeclaredQueries {
 
    public enum Category { FASTENER, STRUCTURAL, MOTION }
 
    @Entity(name = "Product")
    @Table(name = "product")
    @NamedQuery(name = "Product.cheaperThan",
                query = "select p from Product p where p.priceInCents < :max order by p.sku")
    public static class Product {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE) Long id;
        @Column(nullable = false, unique = true, length = 16) String sku;
        @Column(nullable = false) String name;
        @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING) @Column(nullable = false, length = 16) Category category;
        int priceInCents;
        boolean active;
        protected Product() {}
        Product(String sku, String name, Category category, int priceInCents, boolean active) {
            this.sku = sku; this.name = name; this.category = category; this.priceInCents = priceInCents; this.active = active;
        }
        public String getSku() { return sku; }
        public int getPriceInCents() { return priceInCents; }
        @Override public String toString() { return sku + "@" + priceInCents; }
    }
 
    /* Projections: three ways to say "I do not want the whole entity". */
    public interface SkuAndPrice { String getSku(); int getPriceInCents(); }              // closed: only these columns
    public interface SkuLabel { @Value("#{target.sku + ' @ ' + target.priceInCents + 'c'}") String getLabel(); }  // open: all columns
    public record SkuPrice(String sku, int priceInCents) {}                                // DTO: only these columns
    public interface SkuCents { String getSku(); int getCents(); }                         // for the native query's aliases
 
    public interface ProductRepository extends JpaRepository<Product, Long> {
 
        @Query("select p from Product p where p.category = :category and p.priceInCents <= :max order by p.sku")
        List<Product> affordable(@Param("category") Category category, @Param("max") int max);
 
        @Query("select p from Product p where p.sku like ?1 order by p.sku")
        List<Product> skuLike(String pattern);
 
        @Query("select p from Product p where p.category = :category")
        List<Product> byCategory(@Param("category") Category category, Sort sort);
 
        @Query(value = "select p from Product p where p.active = true",
               countQuery = "select count(p) from Product p where p.active = true")
        Page<Product> activePage(Pageable pageable);
 
        @Query(value = "select sku, price_in_cents as cents from product where price_in_cents > :min order by sku",
               nativeQuery = true)
        List<SkuCents> nativeAbove(@Param("min") int min);
 
        List<Product> cheaperThan(@Param("max") int max);          // resolved to the @NamedQuery "Product.cheaperThan"
 
        @Query("select count(p) from #{#entityName} p")
        long total();
 
        @Modifying @Transactional
        @Query("update Product p set p.priceInCents = p.priceInCents + :delta where p.category = :category")
        int repriceStale(@Param("category") Category category, @Param("delta") int delta);
 
        @Modifying(clearAutomatically = true) @Transactional
        @Query("update Product p set p.priceInCents = p.priceInCents + :delta where p.category = :category")
        int repriceClearing(@Param("category") Category category, @Param("delta") int delta);
 
        @Modifying @Transactional
        @Query("delete from Product p where p.active = false")
        int purgeInactive();
 
        List<SkuAndPrice> findByCategoryOrderBySku(Category category);                       // closed projection
        List<SkuLabel> findByPriceInCentsGreaterThanOrderBySku(int min);                      // open projection
        List<SkuPrice> findByCategoryAndActiveTrueOrderBySku(Category category);              // DTO, derived
        @Query("select new lm.declared.DeclaredQueries$SkuPrice(p.sku, p.priceInCents) from Product p where p.category = :category order by p.sku")
        List<SkuPrice> prices(@Param("category") Category category);                          // DTO, declared
        <T> List<T> findByCategoryOrderBySkuDesc(Category category, Class<T> type);           // dynamic projection
    }
 
    @Bean TransactionTemplate tx(PlatformTransactionManager manager) { return new TransactionTemplate(manager); }
 
    @Bean CommandLineRunner demo(ProductRepository repo, TransactionTemplate tx) {
        return args -> {
            repo.saveAll(List.of(
                new Product("BOLT-7", "Hex bolt M8", Category.FASTENER, 80, true),
                new Product("NUT-3", "Hex nut M8", Category.FASTENER, 25, true),
                new Product("PIN-2", "Split pin", Category.FASTENER, 15, false),
                new Product("GIRD-1", "Steel girder 6m", Category.STRUCTURAL, 120_000, true),
                new Product("ROD-4", "Threaded rod 1m", Category.STRUCTURAL, 4_500, true),
                new Product("CAM-9", "Cam follower", Category.MOTION, 2_300, true)));
 
            System.out.println("-- declared JPQL --");
            System.out.println("affordable        = " + repo.affordable(Category.FASTENER, 50));
            System.out.println("positional like   = " + repo.skuLike("%-%"));
            System.out.println("sort appended     = " + repo.byCategory(Category.STRUCTURAL, Sort.by("priceInCents").descending()));
            Page<Product> page = repo.activePage(PageRequest.of(1, 2, Sort.by("sku")));
            System.out.println("page 2 of active  = " + page.getContent() + " of " + page.getTotalElements() + " in " + page.getTotalPages() + " pages");
            System.out.println("native            = " + repo.nativeAbove(1_000).stream().map(r -> r.getSku() + "=" + r.getCents()).toList());
            System.out.println("named query       = " + repo.cheaperThan(100));
            System.out.println("#{#entityName}    = " + repo.total());
 
            System.out.println("-- projections --");
            System.out.println("closed interface  = " + repo.findByCategoryOrderBySku(Category.FASTENER).stream().map(p -> p.getSku() + "/" + p.getPriceInCents()).toList());
            System.out.println("open interface    = " + repo.findByPriceInCentsGreaterThanOrderBySku(2_000).stream().map(SkuLabel::getLabel).toList());
            System.out.println("record, derived   = " + repo.findByCategoryAndActiveTrueOrderBySku(Category.FASTENER));
            System.out.println("record, declared  = " + repo.prices(Category.STRUCTURAL));
            System.out.println("dynamic -> record = " + repo.findByCategoryOrderBySkuDesc(Category.FASTENER, SkuPrice.class));
            System.out.println("dynamic -> entity = " + repo.findByCategoryOrderBySkuDesc(Category.FASTENER, Product.class));
 
            System.out.println("-- @Modifying without clearAutomatically: the managed copy goes stale --");
            tx.executeWithoutResult(status -> {
                Product bolt = repo.findById(1L).orElseThrow();
                int changed = repo.repriceStale(Category.FASTENER, 10);
                Product again = repo.findById(1L).orElseThrow();
                System.out.println("rows updated      = " + changed);
                System.out.println("managed copy says = " + bolt.priceInCents + " (same instance: " + (bolt == again) + ")");
            });
            System.out.println("database says     = " + repo.findById(1L).orElseThrow().priceInCents);
 
            System.out.println("-- @Modifying(clearAutomatically = true): the context is emptied, so the next read hits the database --");
            tx.executeWithoutResult(status -> {
                Product bolt = repo.findById(1L).orElseThrow();
                int changed = repo.repriceClearing(Category.FASTENER, 10);
                Product again = repo.findById(1L).orElseThrow();
                System.out.println("rows updated      = " + changed);
                System.out.println("stale copy says   = " + bolt.priceInCents + ", fresh copy says " + again.priceInCents + " (same instance: " + (bolt == again) + ")");
            });
 
            System.out.println("-- @Modifying delete --");
            System.out.println("purged            = " + repo.purgeInactive());
            System.out.println("remaining         = " + repo.total());
        };
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication app = new SpringApplication(DeclaredQueries.class);
        app.setDefaultProperties(Map.of(
            "spring.main.web-application-type", "none",
            "spring.main.banner-mode", "off",
            "spring.main.log-startup-info", "false",
            "logging.level.root", "WARN",
            "logging.pattern.console", "%level %logger{0}: %msg%n",
            "spring.datasource.url", "jdbc:h2:mem:declared;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1",
            "spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto", "create-drop",
            "spring.jpa.show-sql", "true",
            "spring.jpa.open-in-view", "false"));
        app.run(args).close();
    }
}
