Reading the output

  • Named and positional parameters. affordable binds :category and :max through @Param; skuLike binds ?1 by position. Both become plain ? placeholders in the SQL, so neither can be injected into. Never build JPQL by string concatenation to "add a parameter".
  • escape '' on the declared like. Compare it with §3's escape '\'. In a declared query you supply the pattern ("%-%") and nothing is escaped for you: a user-supplied % is a wildcard here. If the value comes from a user, either escape it yourself or use a derived Containing.
  • A Sort parameter is appended. byCategory's JPQL has no order by; the SQL has order by p1_0.price_in_cents desc. Spring Data rewrote the query string before handing it to Hibernate. It validates the sort property against the entity, which is why an unknown property in a client-supplied sort fails instead of injecting SQL.
  • A Page costs two statements. activePage ran the offset … fetch first select and then the countQuery. Give a declared paged query its own countQuery whenever the select has joins or fetches; the count Spring Data would otherwise derive by rewriting your select can be wrong or slow (§7 goes deeper).
  • Native SQL goes through untouched. nativeAbove's SQL is exactly the string in the annotation, aliases and all, and its result maps to the SkuCents interface by alias name. You give up portability, entity graphs and automatic count derivation; you gain every feature of your database.
  • A named query is found by convention. cheaperThan has no annotation; Spring Data looked up Product.cheaperThan among the entity's @NamedQuerys before trying to derive the name. #{#entityName} in total() is SpEL substituted with the entity name, so a query in a generic base repository works for every entity.

Projections: what the SQL actually selects

The five projection lines are the most instructive part of the output, because the method signatures look alike and the SQL does not.

Projection types and the columns they select
Return typeExampleSQL selectsManaged entities?
Closed interfaceSkuAndPrice { getSku(); getPriceInCents(); }only sku, price_in_centsno
Open interface@Value("#{target.sku + …}") getLabel()every column — the SpEL needs a whole targetyes, behind a proxy
Record / DTO, derivedList<SkuPrice> findBy…only the constructor's columnsno
Record / DTO, declaredselect new lm.declared.DeclaredQueries$SkuPrice(…)only the listed expressionsno
Dynamic<T> List<T> findBy…(…, Class<T> type)depends on the class passed at the callonly if you pass the entity

Two details from the output: the open projection's SQL selects id, active, category, name, price_in_cents, sku even though the label uses two of them, so it saves nothing over loading the entity. And the declared constructor expression names the record by its binary name, DeclaredQueries$SkuPrice, because it is nested; a top-level record would be lm.declared.SkuPrice. Spring Data's derived DTO projection needed no such string — it inspected the record's constructor itself.

Drag a projection onto what its SQL selects, or click one then click the other

All four correct. The practical rule: for a read model, use a closed interface or a record; reach for an open projection only when the computed value needs data you would have loaded anyway; load the entity only when you intend to change it.

@Modifying: one statement, and a stale persistence context

An update or delete in JPQL is a bulk operation: Hibernate turns it into one SQL statement (update product p1_0 set price_in_cents=(p1_0.price_in_cents+cast(? as integer)) where p1_0.category=?) and the database changes every matching row. The persistence context is not consulted and not updated (JPA §6). The output shows the consequence exactly:

  • Without clearAutomatically, BOLT-7 was loaded at 80, the update raised it to 90 in the database, and the second findById returned the same instance from the first-level cache — no select was emitted for it — still saying 80. Only after the transaction ended did a fresh read say 90. Any business logic after the update in that transaction worked on wrong numbers, and had the code then modified that entity, the flush would have written the stale price back over the update.
  • With clearAutomatically = true, Spring Data calls EntityManager.clear() after the update. The next findById emitted a select and got a new instance at 100, while the old reference still said 90. Clearing detaches everything, so unflushed changes to other entities would be lost — pair it with flushAutomatically = true when the transaction has pending writes.
  • The delete is one delete from product p1_0 where p1_0.active=false: no select, no cascades, no @PreRemove. That is the point of it, and also the risk.

A @Modifying method must run inside a writable transaction. A declared query method gets none of its own, so it needs @Transactional on the method (as here) or a caller's transaction (§5). Without one you get TransactionRequiredException: Executing an update/delete query.

Choosing the form

  • Derive when the name reads as a sentence: one or two conditions, a sort, maybe a limit.
  • Declare when you need parentheses, aggregates, group by, case, a fetch join, a subquery, or a constructor expression — or when the derived name would pass forty characters.
  • Name the method for its purpose once you declare: affordable(category, max) says why the query exists; findByCategoryAndPriceInCentsLessThanEqualOrderBySku only says how.
  • A Specification (§9) is the answer when the conditions are chosen at run time from a filter form.
JPQL versus native queries in Spring Data
JPQL @QuerynativeQuery = true
Validated at startupyes, against the entity modelno — errors appear on first call
Portable across databasesyesno
Sort parameterappended safelyappended as raw SQL column names, limited
Pagecount derived if absentcountQuery effectively required
@EntityGraphappliesignored
Window functions, CTEs, JSON operators, hintssome (Hibernate 6+ HQL has many)all of them

Hibernate 6 and 7's HQL covers window functions, CTEs and set operations, so "I need native for this" is less often true than it used to be. Check the HQL guide before giving up portability.

A Stream<T> return holds a JDBC cursor open. It needs a surrounding transaction and must be closed, or the connection leaks back to the pool late or never:

@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public long exportActive(Writer out) {
    try (Stream<SkuAndPrice> rows = repo.streamAllActive()) {     // @QueryHints fetch size below
        return rows.peek(r -> write(out, r)).count();
    }
}
 
@QueryHints(@QueryHint(name = org.hibernate.jpa.HibernateHints.HINT_FETCH_SIZE, value = "500"))
@Query("select p.sku as sku, p.priceInCents as priceInCents from Product p where p.active = true")
Stream<SkuAndPrice> streamAllActive();

@QueryHints passes JPA or Hibernate hints straight through: HINT_FETCH_SIZE for streaming, HINT_READ_ONLY to skip snapshots for entities you will not change, jakarta.persistence.query.timeout for a statement deadline.

Declared-query gotchas
  • A bulk update leaves managed entities stale in the same transaction, as the output shows. Use clearAutomatically (with flushAutomatically if there are pending changes), or run the update in its own transaction.
  • Bulk operations skip @Version, callbacks, cascades and the second-level cache. An optimistic lock is not checked; increment the version column in the JPQL yourself (set p.version = p.version + 1) if other writers rely on it.
  • A declared like does not escape. escape '' in the output: user input containing % or _ becomes a wildcard.
  • An open projection is not a projection. It loads the entity. Use it for convenience, never for performance.
  • select new needs the fully qualified (binary) class name. A nested record is Outer$Record; a typo fails at startup with a class-resolution error.
  • A native Page without countQuery makes Spring Data guess a count by rewriting your SQL, which fails or lies on anything non-trivial.

Check yourself

1.Inside one transaction: p = repo.findById(1L) (price 80), then a @Modifying query without clearAutomatically adds 10 to every fastener's price, then repo.findById(1L).priceInCents. What does the last read return?

B. The output shows managed copy says = 80 (same instance: true) and no select before it: the second findById was served by the first-level cache.

A is wrong: findById checks the persistence context first. C describes behaviour Hibernate does not have — bulk operations bypass the context entirely, which is why clearAutomatically exists. D: nothing detects the divergence; the stale value is silently used.

2.A report needs only sku and price from a wide table. Which return type keeps the selected columns to those two?

C. The closed interface and the record both produced select p1_0.sku,p1_0.price_in_cents in the output.

A is an open projection: its SQL selected every column, because SpEL may touch any property of target. B skips the dirty-check snapshot but still selects and hydrates whole entities. D is false; nothing analyses which getters you call.

3.Which are true of @Modifying @Query("delete from Product p where p.active = false")? Select all that apply.

A and D. The output's single delete from product p1_0 where p1_0.active=false is the bulk statement; JPA requires a transaction for any bulk update or delete.

B and C describe entity-level removal — what §3's derived deleteBySku did by loading first. A bulk JPQL delete never loads the entities, so there is nothing to call back on and nothing to cascade from; child rows with a foreign key make it fail instead.

Section 5

@Transactional: boundaries, propagation and the proxy

In the JPA module you opened and committed transactions by hand. In a Spring application you almost never do: you put @Transactional on a service method and the transaction begins before the method runs and commits (or rolls back) after it returns. That convenience is implemented by a proxy — an object Spring puts in front of your bean that intercepts each call, consults the annotation, talks to the PlatformTransactionManager, and only then calls your code. Every surprising behaviour of @Transactional follows from that one fact: the annotation does nothing unless the call goes through the proxy.

The boundary matters because the persistence context lives exactly as long as the transaction (JPA §3). Inside it, entities are managed, lazy associations load, and dirty checking writes your changes at commit. Outside it, entities are detached. Where you draw the boundary decides what is consistent, what is atomic, and how long a database connection is held.

Worked example

Ten experiments in one application. show_sql is off here — the evidence is the transaction state itself, read through TransactionSynchronizationManager (the thread-bound registry Spring uses to track the current transaction), Hibernate's transaction counter, and which rows survive.

javaTransactions.java
package lm.tx;
 
import jakarta.persistence.*;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.hibernate.stat.Statistics;
import org.springframework.boot.CommandLineRunner;
import org.springframework.boot.transaction.autoconfigure.TransactionManagerCustomizer;
import org.springframework.orm.jpa.JpaTransactionManager;
import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaRepository;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.config.EnableJpaRepositories;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.transaction.IllegalTransactionStateException;
import org.springframework.transaction.NestedTransactionNotSupportedException;
import org.springframework.transaction.PlatformTransactionManager;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Propagation;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;
import org.springframework.transaction.support.TransactionSynchronizationManager;
import org.springframework.transaction.support.TransactionTemplate;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Optional;
 
@SpringBootApplication
@EnableJpaRepositories(considerNestedRepositories = true)
public class Transactions {
 
    @Entity(name = "StockLevel")
    @Table(name = "stock_level")
    public static class StockLevel {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE) Long id;
        @Column(nullable = false, unique = true, length = 16) String sku;
        int onHand;
        protected StockLevel() {}
        StockLevel(String sku, int onHand) { this.sku = sku; this.onHand = onHand; }
    }
 
    public interface StockRepository extends JpaRepository<StockLevel, Long> {
        Optional<StockLevel> findBySku(String sku);
    }
 
    static String txName() {
        return TransactionSynchronizationManager.isActualTransactionActive()
            ? TransactionSynchronizationManager.getCurrentTransactionName() : "(no transaction)";
    }
 
    /* A second bean: calling it goes through a proxy, so REQUIRES_NEW takes effect. */
    @Service
    public static class Auditor {
        @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
        public String inner() { return txName(); }
 
        @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.NESTED)
        public void stockAndFail(StockRepository repo, String sku) {
            repo.saveAndFlush(new StockLevel(sku, 1));     // flushed so the savepoint rollback has a row to undo
            throw new IllegalStateException("boom inside NESTED");
        }
    }
 
    @Service
    public static class InventoryService {
        private final StockRepository repo;
        private final Auditor auditor;
        InventoryService(StockRepository repo, Auditor auditor) { this.repo = repo; this.auditor = auditor; }
 
        @Transactional
        public void twoCallsOneTransaction() {
            repo.save(new StockLevel("BOLT-7", 100));
            repo.save(new StockLevel("NUT-3", 40));
        }
 
        @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
        public String inner() { return txName(); }
 
        @Transactional
        public void selfInvocation() {
            System.out.println("outer runs in     = " + txName());
            System.out.println("this.inner() in   = " + inner());              // the trap: no proxy, no new transaction
            System.out.println("auditor.inner() in= " + auditor.inner());      // another bean: proxied, REQUIRES_NEW honoured
        }
 
        @Transactional
        public void addThenFail(String sku) {
            repo.save(new StockLevel(sku, 5));
            throw new IllegalStateException("runtime failure after save");
        }
 
        @Transactional
        public void addThenFailChecked(String sku) throws Exception {
            repo.save(new StockLevel(sku, 5));
            throw new Exception("checked failure after save");
        }
 
        @Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class)
        public void addThenFailCheckedRollback(String sku) throws Exception {
            repo.save(new StockLevel(sku, 5));
            throw new Exception("checked failure, rollbackFor set");
        }
 
        @Transactional(readOnly = true)
        public void tryToModify(String sku) {
            StockLevel s = repo.findBySku(sku).orElseThrow();
            s.onHand = 999;                                   // dirty, but a read-only transaction never flushes
            System.out.println("read-only tx      = " + TransactionSynchronizationManager.isCurrentTransactionReadOnly());
        }
 
        @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.MANDATORY)
        public void requiresCaller() { }
 
        @Transactional
        public void nestedSavepoint() {
            repo.save(new StockLevel("CAM-9", 7));
            try { auditor.stockAndFail(repo, "GIRD-1"); }
            catch (NestedTransactionNotSupportedException e) {
                System.out.println("NESTED refused    = " + e.getClass().getSimpleName());   // JPA has no savepoints
            }
            repo.save(new StockLevel("ROD-4", 3));            // the outer transaction carries on and commits
        }
    }
 
    @Bean TransactionTemplate tx(PlatformTransactionManager manager) {
        TransactionTemplate t = new TransactionTemplate(manager);
        t.setName("lm.tx.Transactions.template");            // a template has no method to be named after
        return t;
    }
 
    /* Boot's JpaTransactionManager refuses NESTED unless told otherwise. */
    @Bean TransactionManagerCustomizer<JpaTransactionManager> allowNested() {
        return manager -> manager.setNestedTransactionAllowed(true);
    }
 
    @Bean CommandLineRunner demo(StockRepository repo, InventoryService service, TransactionTemplate tx, EntityManagerFactory emf) {
        Statistics stats = emf.unwrap(SessionFactory.class).getStatistics();
        return args -> {
            System.out.println("-- 1. every repository call outside a service transaction is its own transaction --");
            long before = stats.getTransactionCount();
            repo.count(); repo.count();
            System.out.println("runner runs in    = " + txName());
            System.out.println("transactions used = " + (stats.getTransactionCount() - before));
 
            System.out.println("-- 2. a @Transactional service method: two calls, one transaction --");
            before = stats.getTransactionCount();
            service.twoCallsOneTransaction();
            System.out.println("transactions used = " + (stats.getTransactionCount() - before));
 
            System.out.println("-- 3. self-invocation bypasses the proxy --");
            service.selfInvocation();
 
            System.out.println("-- 4/5/6. what rolls back --");
            try { service.addThenFail("PIN-2"); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { }
            System.out.println("after runtime ex  = " + repo.findBySku("PIN-2").isPresent());
            try { service.addThenFailChecked("HUB-8"); } catch (Exception e) { }
            System.out.println("after checked ex  = " + repo.findBySku("HUB-8").isPresent());
            try { service.addThenFailCheckedRollback("WIDGET-1"); } catch (Exception e) { }
            System.out.println("with rollbackFor  = " + repo.findBySku("WIDGET-1").isPresent());
 
            System.out.println("-- 7. readOnly = true: dirty entities are never flushed --");
            service.tryToModify("BOLT-7");
            System.out.println("BOLT-7 on hand    = " + repo.findBySku("BOLT-7").orElseThrow().onHand);
 
            System.out.println("-- 8. programmatic: TransactionTemplate --");
            String name = tx.execute(status -> { repo.save(new StockLevel("TMPL-1", 1)); return txName(); });
            System.out.println("template tx name  = " + name);
 
            System.out.println("-- 9. MANDATORY outside any transaction --");
            try { service.requiresCaller(); }
            catch (IllegalTransactionStateException e) { System.out.println("threw             = " + e.getClass().getSimpleName()); }
 
            System.out.println("-- 10. NESTED: a savepoint inside the outer transaction --");
            service.nestedSavepoint();
            System.out.println("CAM-9 present     = " + repo.findBySku("CAM-9").isPresent());
            System.out.println("GIRD-1 present    = " + repo.findBySku("GIRD-1").isPresent());
            System.out.println("ROD-4 present     = " + repo.findBySku("ROD-4").isPresent());
            System.out.println("rows              = " + repo.count());
        };
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication app = new SpringApplication(Transactions.class);
        app.setDefaultProperties(Map.ofEntries(                     // Map.of stops at ten pairs
            Map.entry("spring.main.web-application-type", "none"),
            Map.entry("spring.main.banner-mode", "off"),
            Map.entry("spring.main.log-startup-info", "false"),
            Map.entry("logging.level.root", "WARN"),
            Map.entry("logging.pattern.console", "%level %logger{0}: %msg%n"),
            Map.entry("spring.datasource.url", "jdbc:h2:mem:tx;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1"),
            Map.entry("spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto", "create-drop"),
            Map.entry("spring.jpa.show-sql", "false"),
            Map.entry("spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.generate_statistics", "true"),
            Map.entry("spring.jpa.open-in-view", "false")));
        app.run(args).close();
    }
}
Expected output
-- 1. every repository call outside a service transaction is its own transaction --
runner runs in    = (no transaction)
transactions used = 2
-- 2. a @Transactional service method: two calls, one transaction --
transactions used = 1
-- 3. self-invocation bypasses the proxy --
outer runs in     = lm.tx.Transactions$InventoryService.selfInvocation
this.inner() in   = lm.tx.Transactions$InventoryService.selfInvocation
auditor.inner() in= lm.tx.Transactions$Auditor.inner
-- 4/5/6. what rolls back --
after runtime ex  = false
after checked ex  = true
with rollbackFor  = false
-- 7. readOnly = true: dirty entities are never flushed --
read-only tx      = true
BOLT-7 on hand    = 100
-- 8. programmatic: TransactionTemplate --
template tx name  = lm.tx.Transactions.template
-- 9. MANDATORY outside any transaction --
threw             = IllegalTransactionStateException
-- 10. NESTED: a savepoint inside the outer transaction --

GIRD-1 present    = false
ROD-4 present     = true
rows              = 6

Reading the output, experiment by experiment

  1. No service, no shared transaction. The runner itself is in (no transaction), and two repo.count() calls used two transactions. Every SimpleJpaRepository method carries its own @Transactional (read-only for reads), so a repository called directly from outside a transaction opens and commits one per call. Two calls are not atomic together, and entities returned by the first are detached before the second runs.
  2. A service method draws the boundary. twoCallsOneTransaction made two save calls and Hibernate counted one transaction: the repository's own @Transactional uses the default propagation REQUIRED, which joins the transaction the service already opened.
  3. Self-invocation. this.inner() is annotated REQUIRES_NEW and still ran in …InventoryService.selfInvocation — the outer transaction. this is the target object, not the proxy, so nothing intercepted the call and the annotation was never read. The same method on another bean, auditor.inner(), went through that bean's proxy and got its own transaction, named after itself.
  4. An unchecked exception rolls back. PIN-2 was saved, then an IllegalStateException left the method: the proxy rolled back and the row is absent.
  5. A checked exception commits. HUB-8 survived a thrown Exception. Spring's default rollback rule — inherited from EJB — is "roll back on RuntimeException and Error, commit on checked exceptions", on the theory that a checked exception is an expected business outcome. Very few teams want that; most set a rule.
  6. rollbackFor = Exception.class changes the rule for that method: WIDGET-1 was rolled back.
  7. readOnly = true suppresses the flush. The method changed a managed entity's onHand to 999, and the database still says 100. Spring tells Hibernate the session is read-only, which sets the flush mode to manual and skips dirty-check snapshots; the change is simply never written. It also passes the read-only flag to the JDBC driver, which some databases and routing data sources use to send the work to a replica.
  8. TransactionTemplate is the programmatic form: the same begin/commit/rollback logic around a lambda, with no proxy involved. Use it where an annotation cannot reach — a runner, a loop that wants one transaction per item, or code that must not be a separate bean.
  9. MANDATORY refuses to run without a caller's transaction: IllegalTransactionStateException. It documents and enforces "this method is only ever a step inside something bigger".
  10. NESTED is not available here. NESTED means "a savepoint inside the current transaction": roll back to it on failure, keep the outer work. Even with nestedTransactionAllowed switched on, Spring's JpaTransactionManager refused it in this stack with NestedTransactionNotSupportedException, so GIRD-1 was never written; the outer transaction carried on and committed CAM-9 and ROD-4. Savepoints are a JDBC feature (DataSourceTransactionManager supports them for plain JDBC work). With JPA, model "try this step, keep the rest" as a REQUIRES_NEW call on another bean, accepting that it commits independently.

Through the proxy, and around it Simulated ← → to step
Source
@Service
class InventoryService {
    @Transactional
    public void reserve(String sku) {
        repo.save(new StockLevel(sku, 5));
        audit();                        // this.audit()
    }
    @Transactional(propagation = REQUIRES_NEW)
    public void audit() { /* ... */ }
}
 
service.reserve("PIN-2");            // service is the PROXY
Transaction state
Effect

Propagation, interactively

Propagation answers one question: when a transactional method is called and a transaction may already exist, what happens? Pick an outer context, an inner propagation and what the inner method does. The case to try first is outer REQUIRED, inner REQUIRED, inner throws a RuntimeException, and the outer catches it.

outer() calls other.inner() through its proxy
Propagation levels
PropagationTransaction existsNo transaction
REQUIRED (default)join itbegin a new one
REQUIRES_NEWsuspend it, begin a new one, resume afterbegin a new one
SUPPORTSjoin itrun without one
MANDATORYjoin itIllegalTransactionStateException
NOT_SUPPORTEDsuspend it, run without onerun without one
NEVERIllegalTransactionStateExceptionrun without one
NESTEDsavepoint inside it — where the transaction manager supports savepoints (JDBC, not JPA here)begin a new one

Where the annotation goes, and what it cannot do

Spring Boot proxies classes with CGLIB by default: it generates a subclass that overrides each public method to add the transaction logic, then delegates to your instance. That design has hard limits:

  • Self-invocation is invisible — experiment 3. Move the method to another bean, inject the bean into itself lazily, or use a TransactionTemplate.
  • private methods cannot be intercepted; a subclass cannot override them. The annotation is silently ignored.
  • final methods and final classes cannot be overridden either. Kotlin classes are final by default, which is why Spring's Kotlin plugin opens them.
  • Calls made before the proxy exists — from a constructor or @PostConstruct on the same bean — run without a transaction.
  • On the service layer, around one use case: "reserve stock and record the reservation" is one transaction. Repositories already have their own; controllers should not hold one.
  • On the class for a default, overridden on methods: a common shape is @Transactional(readOnly = true) on the class and plain @Transactional on the few writing methods.
  • On concrete classes, not interfaces. Interface annotations work for interface-based proxies but are easy to lose with class-based ones.
  • Keep it short. A transaction holds a connection and, for writes, row locks. No remote calls, file uploads or user think-time inside one.

The most confusing exception in Spring transactions comes from catching an inner failure:

@Transactional
public void placeOrder(Order o) {
    orders.save(o);
    try {
        loyalty.addPoints(o.customer(), 10);   // @Transactional (REQUIRED) on another bean; throws
    } catch (RuntimeException e) {
        log.warn("points failed, carrying on");  // looks handled …
    }
}                                              // … UnexpectedRollbackException here

addPoints joined the outer transaction. When it threw, its proxy could not roll back a transaction it does not own, so it marked the shared transaction rollback-only. The catch hid the exception, placeOrder returned normally, its proxy tried to commit, found the mark, rolled back, and threw UnexpectedRollbackException to tell you the order you thought was saved was not. Fixes: let it propagate, make addPoints REQUIRES_NEW so its failure is its own, or decide the call is optional and set noRollbackFor on it.

  • isolation — READ_COMMITTED, REPEATABLE_READ… (JPA §7's table). Only applies when the method begins the transaction; a joining method cannot change it.
  • timeout — seconds; passed to JPA as a query timeout for statements in the transaction.
  • rollbackFor / noRollbackFor — adjust the rule from experiments 4–6.
  • transactionManager — pick one by bean name when the application has several data sources.
  • JTA — for transactions spanning several resources (two databases, a database and a message broker) Spring delegates to a JTA transaction manager instead of JpaTransactionManager. Most applications avoid distributed transactions and use the outbox pattern (§8) instead.
Transaction gotchas
  • Checked exceptions commit by default. Experiment 5. Set rollbackFor = Exception.class, or throw unchecked domain exceptions.
  • Self-invoked and private transactional methods do nothing. No warning, no error; the method just runs in whatever transaction (or none) the caller had.
  • Catching an exception from a joined transaction leaves it rollback-only and ends in UnexpectedRollbackException at commit.
  • Repository calls from a controller or runner are separate transactions. Experiment 1. Two saves there are not atomic, and lazy loads between them fail.
  • readOnly = true silently discards changes to managed entities. That is the feature; it is also a bug if a "read" method is later taught to write.
  • Long transactions are the real performance problem, not their number: a transaction held across a slow HTTP call holds a pooled connection the whole time.

Check yourself

1.In InventoryService, a @Transactional method reserveAll() calls this.reserveOne(sku) in a loop, where reserveOne is annotated @Transactional(propagation = REQUIRES_NEW) so each item commits on its own. One item fails with a RuntimeException that reserveAll lets propagate. What happens?

C. Experiment 3 shows this.inner() running in the outer method's transaction despite REQUIRES_NEW. The per-item transactions never existed, so the exception rolls back the whole loop.

A is what the author intended, and what happens if reserveOne moves to another bean. B: mixing propagations is normal and nothing is checked at startup. D assumes the annotation took effect, which is precisely what self-invocation prevents.

2.A @Transactional method saves an order and then throws OutOfStockException extends Exception. No rollbackFor is set. Is the order in the database afterwards?

B. Experiment 5: after checked ex = true. The default rule rolls back only on RuntimeException and Error.

A is the rule most people assume and the reason for rollbackFor. C: whether the insert was flushed is irrelevant — the proxy commits, which flushes. D: the decision is made by the proxy when the exception passes through it, before the caller sees it.

3.Which of these run without the transaction behaviour their annotation asks for? Select all that apply.

A and C. Both are calls that never pass through the proxy: a private method cannot be overridden by the CGLIB subclass and is called on this; @PostConstruct runs on the target during initialisation, also via this.

B works as asked: an external call through the proxy, read-only transaction begun. D also behaves exactly as its annotation says — experiment 9 shows MANDATORY throwing IllegalTransactionStateException, which is the requested behaviour, not a bypass.

Section 6

Fetching and N+1 in a Spring application

JPA §5 showed the N+1 problem with a bare EntityManager: one query for the parents, one more per parent the moment a lazy collection is touched. Spring changes nothing about the mechanism and everything about where it bites, because Spring decides where the persistence context begins and ends. In a plain JPA program you open and close the EntityManager yourself. In a Spring application the context is opened by the @Transactional proxy when a service method starts and closed when it returns — unless spring.jpa.open-in-view is on, in which case it stays open for the whole web request, including view rendering, which is where the lazy loads then quietly run.

So the question "will this lazy collection load?" has a Spring-specific answer: only inside the transaction that loaded its owner. Touch it in the service and you get an N+1; touch it after the service returned and you get a LazyInitializationException; touch it in a template with open-in-view on and you get an N+1 you cannot see in any Java file. This section measures all of those with Hibernate's statistics, then shows the two tools Spring Data adds for fixing them at the repository: @EntityGraph and fetch queries in @Query.

Worked example: six ways to read the same report

Five orders, two lines each, totalling 65 units. The ReportService is @Transactional(readOnly = true), so every method runs inside one transaction and one persistence context. The runner clears the statistics before each phase and prints the prepared-statement count after it.

javaSpringFetching.java
package lm.fetching;
 
import jakarta.persistence.*;
import org.hibernate.Hibernate;
import org.hibernate.LazyInitializationException;
import org.hibernate.Session;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.hibernate.stat.Statistics;
import org.springframework.boot.CommandLineRunner;
import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.EntityGraph;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaRepository;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.Query;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.config.EnableJpaRepositories;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
 
@SpringBootApplication
@EnableJpaRepositories(considerNestedRepositories = true)
public class SpringFetching {
 
    @Entity(name = "Product")
    @Table(name = "product")
    public static class Product {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE) Long id;
        @Column(nullable = false, unique = true, length = 16) String sku;
        protected Product() {}
        Product(String sku) { this.sku = sku; }
        String getSku() { return sku; }
    }
 
    @Entity(name = "Order")
    @Table(name = "orders")
    public static class Order {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE) Long id;
        @Column(nullable = false, unique = true) String reference;
        @OneToMany(mappedBy = "order", cascade = CascadeType.ALL)        // LAZY by default
        List<OrderLine> lines = new ArrayList<>();
        protected Order() {}
        Order(String reference) { this.reference = reference; }
        String getReference() { return reference; }
        List<OrderLine> getLines() { return lines; }
        void addLine(Product p, int qty) { OrderLine l = new OrderLine(p, qty); l.order = this; lines.add(l); }
    }
 
    @Entity(name = "OrderLine")
    @Table(name = "order_line")
    public static class OrderLine {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE) Long id;
        @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false) Order order;
        @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false) Product product;
        int qty;
        protected OrderLine() {}
        OrderLine(Product product, int qty) { this.product = product; this.qty = qty; }
        int getQty() { return qty; }
        Product getProduct() { return product; }
    }
 
    public interface ProductRepository extends JpaRepository<Product, Long> {}
 
    public interface OrderRepository extends JpaRepository<Order, Long> {
        List<Order> findAllByOrderByReference();                                  // lazy: the N+1 shape
 
        @EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"lines", "lines.product"})
        List<Order> findWithGraphByOrderByReference();                            // one statement
 
        @Query("select distinct o from Order o join fetch o.lines l join fetch l.product order by o.reference")
        List<Order> findAllFetched();                                             // one statement, explicit
    }
 
    public record OrderSummary(String reference, int lineCount, int totalQty) {}
 
    @Service
    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public static class ReportService {
        private final OrderRepository orders;
        @PersistenceContext private EntityManager em;
        ReportService(OrderRepository orders) { this.orders = orders; }
 
        public int totalQtyLazy() { return sum(orders.findAllByOrderByReference()); }
        public int totalQtyGraph() { return sum(orders.findWithGraphByOrderByReference()); }
        public int totalQtyFetchQuery() { return sum(orders.findAllFetched()); }
        public int totalQtyBatched() {
            em.unwrap(Session.class).setFetchBatchSize(8);                        // what default_batch_fetch_size does globally
            return sum(orders.findAllByOrderByReference());
        }
        public Order firstOrder() { return orders.findAllByOrderByReference().get(0); }           // entity escapes the transaction
        public OrderSummary firstOrderSummary() {                                                // DTO: nothing lazy escapes
            Order o = orders.findWithGraphByOrderByReference().get(0);
            return new OrderSummary(o.getReference(), o.getLines().size(), sum(List.of(o)));
        }
        private static int sum(List<Order> os) {
            int t = 0;
            for (Order o : os) for (OrderLine l : o.getLines()) t += l.getQty();
            return t;
        }
    }
 
    @Bean CommandLineRunner demo(ProductRepository products, OrderRepository orders, ReportService report, EntityManagerFactory emf) {
        return args -> {
            Product bolt = products.save(new Product("BOLT-7"));
            Product nut = products.save(new Product("NUT-3"));
            for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
                Order o = new Order("ORD-" + i);
                o.addLine(bolt, i);
                o.addLine(nut, 10);
                orders.save(o);
            }
            Statistics stats = emf.unwrap(SessionFactory.class).getStatistics();
 
            System.out.println("-- A: lazy collection in a loop --");
            stats.clear();
            System.out.println("total = " + report.totalQtyLazy() + ", statements = " + stats.getPrepareStatementCount());
 
            System.out.println("-- B: @EntityGraph --");
            stats.clear();
            System.out.println("total = " + report.totalQtyGraph() + ", statements = " + stats.getPrepareStatementCount());
 
            System.out.println("-- C: join fetch in @Query --");
            stats.clear();
            System.out.println("total = " + report.totalQtyFetchQuery() + ", statements = " + stats.getPrepareStatementCount());
 
            System.out.println("-- D: batch fetching, size 8 --");
            stats.clear();
            System.out.println("total = " + report.totalQtyBatched() + ", statements = " + stats.getPrepareStatementCount());
 
            System.out.println("-- E: an entity leaves the transaction (open-in-view=false) --");
            Order escaped = report.firstOrder();
            System.out.println("lines initialised = " + Hibernate.isInitialized(escaped.getLines()));
            try {
                System.out.println("line count = " + escaped.getLines().size());
            } catch (LazyInitializationException e) {
                System.out.println("caught " + e.getClass().getSimpleName());
            }
 
            System.out.println("-- F: a DTO leaves instead --");
            System.out.println(report.firstOrderSummary());
        };
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication app = new SpringApplication(SpringFetching.class);
        app.setDefaultProperties(Map.of(
            "spring.main.web-application-type", "none",
            "spring.main.banner-mode", "off",
            "spring.main.log-startup-info", "false",
            "logging.level.root", "WARN",
            "logging.pattern.console", "%level %logger{0}: %msg%n",
            "spring.datasource.url", "jdbc:h2:mem:fetching;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1",
            "spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto", "create-drop",
            "spring.jpa.show-sql", "true",
            "spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.generate_statistics", "true",
            "spring.jpa.open-in-view", "false"));
        app.run(args).close();
    }
}

Read the phases against the statement counts; the SQL between them is the evidence.

  • A, six statements. One for the orders, then where l1_0.order_id=? five times as getLines() initialises each proxy collection. This is N+1 at N = 5, inside a transaction that was opened for exactly this method. At N = 500 it is 501 round trips, and nothing in totalQtyLazy() looks wrong.
  • B, one statement. @EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"lines", "lines.product"}) on the repository method turns the derived query into a left join over lines and products. The method name still drives the where and order by; the graph only says what to fetch. Note the left join: a graph keeps orders that have no lines.
  • C, one statement, by hand. The @Query with join fetch produces the same shape with an inner join and a distinct (Hibernate 6+ deduplicates the parent entities without passing distinct to SQL, so it is harmless to write). Prefer B when the fetch plan is the only thing you need to say; prefer C when the query itself is custom.
  • D, two statements. With a fetch batch size of 8 the first touched collection loads the lines for up to eight orders in one in (?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?). Set globally as spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size it is the safety net that turns every forgotten N+1 into N/8+1; it does not replace B and C, it caps the damage when they are missing.
  • E, the exception. firstOrder() returns a managed entity; the transaction commits on return and the persistence context closes. Back in the runner, Hibernate.isInitialized(lines) is false and size() throws LazyInitializationException. With spring.jpa.open-in-view=true (the default in a web application) the context would still be open here and the call would silently run the collection query — which is the whole open-in-view argument in one line.
  • F, the right shape. firstOrderSummary() fetches what it needs inside the transaction and returns a record. Nothing lazy crosses the boundary, so nothing can throw later, and the caller cannot accidentally trigger a query from a template.

Where will the lazy load run?

What happens when the collection is touched

Open-in-view: why it is on, and why you turn it off

In a web application Spring Boot registers an OpenEntityManagerInViewInterceptor. It binds an EntityManager to the request thread before the controller runs and closes it after the view has rendered. Every @Transactional service call in between reuses that same persistence context, and after the last transaction commits the context stays open — detached entities are not detached, lazy collections still load, and a template can walk order.lines[i].product.name without anyone having planned a fetch.

That is why it is on by default: it makes naive code work. Spring Boot logs a warning at startup (spring.jpa.open-in-view is enabled by default) precisely because "works" and "scales" are different claims. Setting the property to false, as every program in this module does, makes E above throw instead of query — which is the behaviour you want to find in development, not in production under load.

  • A connection for the whole request. The first lazy load after the service returns needs a JDBC connection; Hibernate takes one from the pool and, with the context still open, keeps it until the view is rendered. Slow templates and slow clients now hold pool connections. Under load the pool empties and unrelated requests queue on HikariPool … connection is not available.
  • N+1 in places that are not Java. The loop in A at least sits in a method you can profile. The same loop in a template is invisible to statistics taken in the service, so the fix (B or C) is never applied where it is needed.
  • Reads after the transaction are not transactional. Lazy loads outside the @Transactional method run in auto-commit mode on whatever the database shows now, so a page can show an order from one moment and its lines from another.
  • The fix is a shape, not a flag. With open-in-view off, every read method must fetch what its caller needs (B, C) or return a DTO (F). That constraint is the design: it makes each query's cost visible at the method that runs it.
// attribute paths, nested with dots — the usual form
@EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"lines", "lines.product"})
List<Order> findWithGraphByOrderByReference();
 
// a named graph declared on the entity, reused by several methods
@NamedEntityGraph(name = "Order.full", attributeNodes = {
    @NamedAttributeNode(value = "lines", subgraph = "lines"),
    @NamedAttributeNode("customer") },
    subgraphs = @NamedSubgraph(name = "lines", attributeNodes = @NamedAttributeNode("product")))
@EntityGraph("Order.full")
Optional<Order> findByReference(String reference);
 
// FETCH (default): listed attributes eager, every other one LAZY regardless of mapping
// LOAD: listed attributes eager, the rest as mapped
@EntityGraph(attributePaths = "lines", type = EntityGraph.EntityGraphType.LOAD)
List<Order> findByReferenceStartingWith(String prefix);

A graph applies to derived queries, findById, findAll and @Query methods alike. Two List collections in one graph throw MultipleBagFetchException exactly as two join fetches would (JPA §5); use a Set for one of them or fetch in two queries. And a graph combined with a Pageable fetches the join in full and pages in memory with Hibernate's HHH90003004 warning — §7 shows the shape that avoids it.

Fetching gotchas specific to Spring
  • Returning entities from a service is the bug, not the symptom. E throws only because open-in-view is off; with it on, the same code runs an unplanned query from the caller. Return DTOs or fetch-complete entities; never let a lazy proxy cross the service boundary.
  • @Transactional(readOnly = true) is not optional on read services. It gives you one context per call (so B and C can dedupe and the identity map works), tells Hibernate to skip dirty-check snapshots, and lets a replica-aware data source route the read. Without it every repository call is its own transaction and its own context, and a loop over two repositories loads the same Product many times.
  • default_batch_fetch_size is a net, not a plan. Set it (8–32) in every application, then still fix the N+1s you find; a page that needs 500 collections still runs 500/16 + 1 statements.
  • Statistics are the test. hibernate.generate_statistics costs little; a @DataJpaTest that asserts getPrepareStatementCount() == 1 after calling the report method is how regressions are caught. §11 shows the harness.
  • Turning open-in-view off is a migration, not a toggle. Every template and serializer that walked a lazy association will start throwing. Do it early in a project, or do it with statistics and a log of LazyInitializationExceptions to drive the fixes.

Check yourself

1.In phase E the runner calls escaped.getLines().size() after firstOrder() returned and gets LazyInitializationException. Which single change makes that call succeed without changing the service?

C — and it is the wrong fix, which is the point. Open-in-view keeps the persistence context open past the service, so the lazy load runs in the caller with an extra query and a connection held for the rest of the request. It only applies to web requests (the interceptor is request-scoped), so in this command-line program even that would not help; in a controller it would.

A: a @Bean method's returned lambda is not a proxied bean, so @Transactional on it does nothing; and even a real transaction in the caller would be a new context that does not contain escaped. B is the wrong association: lines is the collection that is lazy, and making OrderLine.order eager changes how lines load their parent, not how orders load their lines. D: a detached collection can be reattached (merge) or initialised inside a new transaction with Hibernate.initialize after a reload — it is the context that is gone, not the data.

2.A service method is @Transactional(readOnly = true) and runs orders.findAllByOrderByReference() for 400 orders, then touches each getLines(). The application sets spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size=16. How many statements run?

B. Phase D at scale: each time an uninitialised collection is touched, Hibernate loads it together with up to 15 other uninitialised collections of the same role that are already in the persistence context, keyed by the owners' ids. 400 orders, 16 per batch, 25 batches, plus the order query.

A: default_batch_fetch_size is exactly the global form of @BatchSize; the annotation overrides it per collection. C describes @Fetch(FetchMode.SUBSELECT), which re-runs the original query as a subselect — a different, explicit annotation. D: a batch size never changes the shape of the original query; only a graph or a fetch join does that.

3.Which of the following are true of @EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"lines", "notes"}) on a repository method, where both lines and notes are Lists? Select all that apply.

A and D. A graph is translated into joins, so it inherits the join rules from JPA §5: two bags cannot be fetched in one result set, and one bag plus one set can but produces the cartesian product. The practical answers are two queries in one transaction, a batch size, or a DTO.

B is false — the generated SQL in phase B shows the joins. C: graphs apply to findById, findAll, derived and @Query methods alike.

Section 7

Pagination, sorting, slices and keyset scrolling

Nobody wants all 400,000 products. A screen wants twenty, sorted somehow, and a way to ask for the next twenty. JPA gives you setFirstResult/setMaxResults and leaves the rest — the sort, the total, the "is there a next page" — to you. Spring Data turns that into three types you pass in and three you get back: a Pageable (page number, size, Sort) goes into any repository method, and a Page, Slice or Window comes out carrying the content plus exactly as much metadata as you asked to pay for.

"Pay for" is the right phrase. A Page knows the total, which costs a second count query on every request. A Slice knows only whether there is a next page, which costs one extra row. And both use offset, which makes page 5,000 as expensive as reading 100,000 rows the database then throws away. The scrolling API's keyset position fixes that by remembering where the last page ended instead of how many rows to skip. This section runs all of them against 23 products and reads the SQL each one produces.

Worked example: eight ways to ask for a few rows

Twenty-three products, three categories, prices that are deliberately not in SKU order so a two-level sort has something to do.

javaPaging.java
package lm.paging;
 
import jakarta.persistence.*;
import org.springframework.boot.CommandLineRunner;
import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.data.domain.*;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaRepository;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.Query;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.config.EnableJpaRepositories;
import org.springframework.data.repository.query.Param;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
 
@SpringBootApplication
@EnableJpaRepositories(considerNestedRepositories = true)
public class Paging {
 
    public enum Category { FASTENER, STRUCTURAL, TOOLING }
 
    @Entity(name = "Product")
    @Table(name = "product")
    public static class Product {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE) Long id;
        @Column(nullable = false, unique = true, length = 16) String sku;
        @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING) @Column(nullable = false) Category category;
        int priceInCents;
        protected Product() {}
        Product(String sku, Category category, int priceInCents) { this.sku = sku; this.category = category; this.priceInCents = priceInCents; }
        public String getSku() { return sku; }
        public int getPriceInCents() { return priceInCents; }
        @Override public String toString() { return sku + "@" + priceInCents; }
    }
 
    public record ProductView(String sku, int priceInCents) {}
 
    public interface ProductRepository extends JpaRepository<Product, Long> {
        Slice<Product> findByCategory(Category category, Pageable pageable);                     // no count query
 
        @Query(value = "select p from Product p where p.priceInCents > :min",
               countQuery = "select count(p) from Product p where p.priceInCents > :min")
        Page<Product> findExpensive(@Param("min") int min, Pageable pageable);
 
        Window<Product> findFirst5ByCategoryOrderBySkuAsc(Category category, ScrollPosition position);   // scrolling API
 
        List<Product> findByCategory(Category category, Limit limit, Sort sort);
    }
 
    static String skus(Iterable<Product> ps) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("[");
        for (Product p : ps) sb.append(sb.length() > 1 ? ", " : "").append(p.getSku());
        return sb.append("]").toString();
    }
 
    @Bean CommandLineRunner demo(ProductRepository repo) {
        return args -> {
            Category[] cats = Category.values();
            for (int i = 1; i <= 23; i++) {
                repo.save(new Product(String.format("SKU-%02d", i), cats[i % 3], (i * 37) % 100 * 10));
            }
 
            System.out.println("-- A: Page with a two-level sort --");
            Pageable first = PageRequest.of(0, 5, Sort.by("priceInCents").descending().and(Sort.by("sku")));
            Page<Product> page = repo.findAll(first);
            System.out.println("content = " + skus(page));
            System.out.println("totalElements = " + page.getTotalElements() + ", totalPages = " + page.getTotalPages()
                    + ", number = " + page.getNumber() + ", hasNext = " + page.hasNext());
 
            System.out.println("-- B: the last page --");
            Page<Product> last = repo.findAll(PageRequest.of(page.getTotalPages() - 1, 5, first.getSort()));
            System.out.println("content = " + skus(last) + ", numberOfElements = " + last.getNumberOfElements() + ", hasNext = " + last.hasNext());
 
            System.out.println("-- C: Slice, no count --");
            Slice<Product> slice = repo.findByCategory(Category.FASTENER, PageRequest.of(0, 3, Sort.by("sku")));
            System.out.println("content = " + skus(slice) + ", hasNext = " + slice.hasNext());
 
            System.out.println("-- D: @Query with its own countQuery --");
            Page<Product> dear = repo.findExpensive(600, PageRequest.of(0, 4, Sort.by("sku")));
            System.out.println("content = " + skus(dear) + ", total = " + dear.getTotalElements());
 
            System.out.println("-- E: Page.map to a DTO --");
            Page<ProductView> views = page.map(p -> new ProductView(p.getSku(), p.getPriceInCents()));
            System.out.println(views.getContent().get(0) + " of " + views.getTotalElements());
 
            System.out.println("-- F: keyset scrolling --");
            Window<Product> w1 = repo.findFirst5ByCategoryOrderBySkuAsc(Category.STRUCTURAL, ScrollPosition.keyset());
            System.out.println("window 1 = " + skus(w1) + ", hasNext = " + w1.hasNext());
            Window<Product> w2 = repo.findFirst5ByCategoryOrderBySkuAsc(Category.STRUCTURAL, w1.positionAt(w1.size() - 1));
            System.out.println("window 2 = " + skus(w2) + ", hasNext = " + w2.hasNext());
 
            System.out.println("-- G: Limit + Sort on a derived query --");
            System.out.println(skus(repo.findByCategory(Category.TOOLING, Limit.of(3), Sort.by("priceInCents").descending())));
 
            System.out.println("-- H: unpaged --");
            System.out.println("all = " + repo.findAll(Pageable.unpaged()).getTotalElements());
        };
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication app = new SpringApplication(Paging.class);
        app.setDefaultProperties(Map.of(
            "spring.main.web-application-type", "none",
            "spring.main.banner-mode", "off",
            "spring.main.log-startup-info", "false",
            "logging.level.root", "WARN",
            "logging.pattern.console", "%level %logger{0}: %msg%n",
            "spring.datasource.url", "jdbc:h2:mem:paging;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1",
            "spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto", "create-drop",
            "spring.jpa.show-sql", "true",
            "spring.jpa.open-in-view", "false"));
        app.run(args).close();
    }
}

What each phase paid for:

  • A — two statements. The order by price_in_cents desc, sku comes straight from the Sort; offset ? rows fetch first ? rows only is H2's (and SQL:2008's) pagination syntax, which Hibernate picks per dialect. Then select count(p1_0.id) runs so the Page can answer getTotalElements() and getTotalPages(). Every page request pays that count.
  • B — one statement. Spring Data skips the count when it can derive the total: the last page returned 3 rows at offset 20, so the total must be 23. An optimisation, not a promise — do not design around it.
  • C — one statement, size + 1. A Slice asks for fetch first 4 when you wanted 3; if a fourth row comes back, hasNext() is true and the row is dropped. No count, so "page 1 of 937" cannot be shown, but infinite-scroll screens never needed it.
  • D — your own count. A @Query that returns Page needs a countQuery whenever Spring Data cannot derive one (joins, distinct, native SQL — anything beyond a simple select). Without it you get a runtime error on the first call, not at startup.
  • E — no statement. Page.map converts the content and keeps the metadata. Return this from a service, not a page of entities: the DTO page is complete, serialisable, and cannot trigger a lazy load.
  • F — keyset. The first window has no position, so it is a plain order by sku, id fetch first 5 — note that Spring Data appended id to make the sort unique. The second window carries the last row's keys: where sku > ? or (sku = ? and id > ?). The database seeks to that key through the index and reads five rows; it never skips anything, so window 10,000 costs the same as window 1.
  • G — Limit. When you want "the top 3" and nothing else, a Limit parameter plus a Sort is clearer than a Pageable you then ignore.
  • H — Pageable.unpaged(). Accepted everywhere a Pageable is, returns everything, no count query. Useful for the "export all" path of a method that otherwise pages.

What page N costs

Offset versus keyset, by the numbers

Sorting, safely

Sort.by("priceInCents").descending().and(Sort.by("sku"))     // property paths, validated against the entity
Sort.by(Sort.Direction.DESC, "category", "sku")
Sort.by(Sort.Order.asc("sku").ignoreCase())
 
Sort.TypedSort<Product> p = Sort.sort(Product.class);       // refactoring-safe
p.by(Product::getPriceInCents).descending().and(p.by(Product::getSku));
 
JpaSort.unsafe("length(sku)")                               // raw JPQL expression; never from user input
 
// a @Query honours the Pageable's sort by appending it, so the query must not have its own order by
@Query("select p from Product p where p.category = :c")
Page<Product> byCategory(@Param("c") Category c, Pageable pageable);

A Sort built from property names is checked against the entity metamodel at query time; a typo throws PropertyReferenceException rather than producing bad SQL. That check is what makes it safe to build a Sort from a request parameter after validating the property against an allow-list. JpaSort.unsafe skips the check and interpolates the expression, which is why its name says so.

Pagination gotchas
  • Paging a fetch join pages in memory. @Query("select o from Order o join fetch o.lines") with a Pageable cannot apply fetch first in SQL — the join multiplies rows per order — so Hibernate loads everything and pages the list, logging HHH90003004: firstResult/maxResults specified with collection fetch; applying in memory. Page the parent ids first, then fetch the collections for that page (§6).
  • Offset pages drift under writes. If a row is inserted before page 3 while a user reads page 2, page 3 repeats a row and the one after it is skipped. Keyset positions are stable because they remember a key, not a count.
  • An unstable sort makes keyset wrong and offset random. Sorting by a non-unique column only (price) means equal rows have no defined order between queries. Spring Data appends id to keyset sorts (F shows it); for offset paging, add the tiebreaker yourself.
  • The count query is the slow one. On a large table with a filter the count(*) is a full scan the page query avoided through its index. If the UI only needs "next", return a Slice; if it needs totals, cache or estimate them.
  • Do not return Page<Entity> from an API. Serialising a page of entities walks lazy associations and ships internal fields; Page.map to a DTO, then (Spring Data 3.3+) wrap in PagedModel for a stable JSON shape. spring.data.web.pageable.* properties (default size, max size, one-indexed pages) configure the web binding — the web starter is not on this class path, so they are only mentioned.

Check yourself

1.A method returns Page<Product> for PageRequest.of(2, 20, Sort.by("sku")) on a 1,000-row table. How many SQL statements run, and what do they do?

B. Phase A, exactly: a Page promises totals, and totals need a count. The count is skipped only when the returned rows settle it (a short last page, or a first page smaller than its size — phase B).

A cannot know the total from 20 rows. C adds a statement nothing issues; hasNext is computed from the total. D is the Slice technique, which does not produce a total at all.

2.An infinite-scroll feed shows 50,000 events newest-first and users routinely scroll a thousand items deep. Which repository method shape is right?

C. Deep offset is the problem: item 1,000 means offset 1000, which reads and discards a thousand rows per request, and an insert at the top shifts every later page by one. A keyset window on (createdAt, id) uses the index and is immune to inserts above the cursor.

A pays a count of 50,000 rows on every scroll and still has the offset cost. B drops the count — better — but keeps offset, so it still degrades with depth and drifts under inserts. D loads 50,000 entities per request.

3.Which statements about this method are true? Select all that apply.

@Query("select o from Order o join fetch o.lines where o.status = :s")
Page<Order> open(@Param("s") Status s, Pageable pageable);

A and C. Two separate problems. The count: Spring Data rewrites simple queries into counts but refuses a fetch join, so you supply countQuery = "select count(o) from Order o where o.status = :s". The paging: a fetch join returns one row per line, so fetch first 20 rows would cut an order's lines in half; Hibernate therefore fetches all rows and pages the entities in memory, logging the warning. The fix is two queries — page the order ids, then fetch lines for those ids.

B is the misconception the warning exists for. D: a Slice still uses fetch first with a fetch join, so the same in-memory fallback applies.

Section 8

Auditing, lifecycle and domain events

Two questions every warehouse eventually asks of its database: who changed this row and when, and what else should happen when it changes. Both are cross-cutting — they apply to dozens of entities and belong to none of them — and both have a tempting wrong answer: setting updatedAt = Instant.now() by hand in every service method, and calling the e-mail sender from inside the one that saves the order. Spring Data gives each question a declarative answer that sits next to the entity and runs at exactly the right moment in the transaction.

For the first, auditing: four annotations on four fields, an AuditorAware that says who the current user is, and a JPA entity listener that fills them in before every insert and update. For the second, domain events: an aggregate root records that something happened, the repository publishes it when the aggregate is saved, and listeners choose whether to run inside the transaction or only after it has committed — which is the difference between an e-mail about an order that exists and one about an order that was rolled back.

Worked example: stamps and events

The DateTimeProvider bean is the one unusual thing here. Auditing normally calls Instant.now(); this program replaces it with a clock that ticks one second per call so the printed stamps are reproducible. That is not a trick for the page — it is exactly what you do in tests, and it is why the stamps below can be read rather than merely asserted non-null.

javaAuditing.java
package lm.auditing;
 
import jakarta.persistence.*;
import org.springframework.boot.CommandLineRunner;
import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;
import org.springframework.context.ApplicationEventPublisher;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.event.EventListener;
import org.springframework.data.annotation.CreatedBy;
import org.springframework.data.annotation.CreatedDate;
import org.springframework.data.annotation.LastModifiedBy;
import org.springframework.data.annotation.LastModifiedDate;
import org.springframework.data.auditing.DateTimeProvider;
import org.springframework.data.domain.AbstractAggregateRoot;
import org.springframework.data.domain.AuditorAware;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.domain.support.AuditingEntityListener;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaRepository;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.config.EnableJpaAuditing;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.config.EnableJpaRepositories;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;
import org.springframework.transaction.event.TransactionPhase;
import org.springframework.transaction.event.TransactionalEventListener;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.time.temporal.TemporalAccessor;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;
 
@SpringBootApplication
@EnableJpaRepositories(considerNestedRepositories = true)
@EnableJpaAuditing(auditorAwareRef = "auditor", dateTimeProviderRef = "clock")
public class Auditing {
 
    // who: in a real application this reads the security context
    @Bean AuditorAware<String> auditor() { return () -> Optional.of("picker-42"); }
 
    // when: a fixed, ticking clock so the stamps are reproducible (tests do the same)
    @Bean DateTimeProvider clock() {
        AtomicInteger tick = new AtomicInteger();
        return () -> Optional.of(Instant.parse("2026-10-15T09:00:00Z").plusSeconds(tick.getAndIncrement()));
    }
 
    @MappedSuperclass
    @EntityListeners(AuditingEntityListener.class)
    public static abstract class Auditable {
        @CreatedDate Instant createdAt;
        @LastModifiedDate Instant updatedAt;
        @CreatedBy String createdBy;
        @LastModifiedBy String updatedBy;
    }
 
    static final AtomicInteger prePersist = new AtomicInteger(), postLoad = new AtomicInteger();
 
    @Entity(name = "Product")
    @Table(name = "product")
    public static class Product extends Auditable {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE) Long id;
        @Column(nullable = false, unique = true, length = 16) String sku;
        int priceInCents;
        protected Product() {}
        Product(String sku, int priceInCents) { this.sku = sku; this.priceInCents = priceInCents; }
        @PrePersist void beforeInsert() { prePersist.incrementAndGet(); }      // JPA callback, independent of Spring
        @PostLoad void afterLoad() { postLoad.incrementAndGet(); }
        void setPriceInCents(int p) { priceInCents = p; }
    }
 
    public record OrderPlaced(String reference) {}
 
    @Entity(name = "Order")
    @Table(name = "orders")
    public static class Order extends AbstractAggregateRoot<Order> {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE) Long id;
        @Column(nullable = false, unique = true) String reference;
        protected Order() {}
        Order(String reference) { this.reference = reference; }
        Order place() { registerEvent(new OrderPlaced(reference)); return this; }   // collected, published by save()
    }
 
    public interface ProductRepository extends JpaRepository<Product, Long> {}
    public interface OrderRepository extends JpaRepository<Order, Long> {}
 
    @Component
    public static class Listeners {
        final List<String> log = Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>());
        @EventListener
        void inTransaction(OrderPlaced e) { log.add("inside tx: " + e.reference()); }
        @TransactionalEventListener(phase = TransactionPhase.AFTER_COMMIT)
        void afterCommit(OrderPlaced e) { log.add("after commit: " + e.reference()); }
        List<String> drain() { List<String> out = new ArrayList<>(log); Collections.sort(out); log.clear(); return out; }
    }
 
    @Service
    public static class OrderService {
        private final OrderRepository orders;
        OrderService(OrderRepository orders) { this.orders = orders; }
        @Transactional public void place(String ref) { orders.save(new Order(ref).place()); }
        @Transactional public void placeAndFail(String ref) {
            orders.save(new Order(ref).place());
            throw new IllegalStateException("payment declined");                 // RuntimeException → rollback
        }
    }
 
    @Bean CommandLineRunner demo(ProductRepository products, OrderService service, Listeners listeners, ApplicationEventPublisher publisher) {
        return args -> {
            System.out.println("-- A: auditing stamps on insert --");
            Product p = products.save(new Product("BOLT-7", 80));
            Product loaded = products.findById(p.id).orElseThrow();
            System.out.println("createdBy = " + loaded.createdBy + ", createdAt = " + loaded.createdAt);
            System.out.println("updatedAt == createdAt: " + loaded.updatedAt.equals(loaded.createdAt));
 
            System.out.println("-- B: stamps on update --");
            loaded.setPriceInCents(95);
            Product after = products.findById(products.save(loaded).id).orElseThrow();
            System.out.println("updatedBy = " + after.updatedBy + ", updatedAt = " + after.updatedAt);
            System.out.println("updatedAt after createdAt: " + after.updatedAt.isAfter(after.createdAt));
            System.out.println("callbacks: prePersist = " + prePersist.get() + ", postLoad = " + postLoad.get());
 
            System.out.println("-- C: a domain event, committed --");
            service.place("ORD-1");
            System.out.println(listeners.drain());
 
            System.out.println("-- D: a domain event, rolled back --");
            try { service.placeAndFail("ORD-2"); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("caught " + e.getMessage()); }
            System.out.println(listeners.drain());
 
            System.out.println("-- E: published directly, outside any transaction --");
            publisher.publishEvent(new OrderPlaced("ORD-3"));
            System.out.println(listeners.drain());
        };
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication app = new SpringApplication(Auditing.class);
        app.setDefaultProperties(Map.of(
            "spring.main.web-application-type", "none",
            "spring.main.banner-mode", "off",
            "spring.main.log-startup-info", "false",
            "logging.level.root", "WARN",
            "logging.pattern.console", "%level %logger{0}: %msg%n",
            "spring.datasource.url", "jdbc:h2:mem:auditing;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1",
            "spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto", "create-drop",
            "spring.jpa.show-sql", "true",
            "spring.jpa.open-in-view", "false"));
        app.run(args).close();
    }
}

  • A. One save on a new entity: the AuditingEntityListener's @PrePersist callback filled all four fields before the insert ran — look at the insert's column list. The clock was asked once, so createdAt and updatedAt are the same instant: a new row is "last modified" at creation.
  • B. save on an existing entity is a merge (§2): the select loads the current row, the listener's @PreUpdate stamps updatedAt/updatedBy only, and the update writes every column because Hibernate updates all columns by default. The clock ticked once more, so updatedAt is one second later. The counters show plain JPA callbacks running alongside: one @PrePersist, three @PostLoads for the three selects.
  • C. place() only records the event; orders.save() publishes it. The @EventListener ran immediately, inside the still-open transaction; the @TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT) ran after the commit. The output is sorted, because listener order is not a contract.
  • D. Same save, then an exception: the transaction rolled back. Notice there is no insert at all — the flush never happened — yet the in-transaction listener had already run on a row that would never exist. The after-commit listener, correctly, did not. That asymmetry is the whole reason the second phase exists.
  • E. Published by hand with no transaction. The plain listener runs; the transactional one does not, because there is no transaction to attach to. That is the default and it surprises people in batch jobs and tests — see fallbackExecution below.
