When does each one run?

Drag each annotation onto the moment it fires, or click one then the other

All four. The two auditing stamps are JPA callbacks under the hood (AuditingEntityListener implements @PrePersist and @PreUpdate), so they fire at flush time, inside the transaction. The two event listeners differ only in when: one during publication, the other at a transaction phase. Choose the phase by asking "must this only happen if the data is really there?"

The pieces, and the choices inside them

Auditing and event building blocks
PieceWhat it doesDecide
@EnableJpaAuditingRegisters the auditing handler; auditorAwareRef and dateTimeProviderRef name the beans to consultOne per application, on a configuration class
AuditorAware<T>Supplies the current principal as Optional<T>; empty leaves @CreatedBy nullT is a String username or a user entity (then the field is a @ManyToOne); read it from the security context, never pass it around
DateTimeProviderSupplies the timestamp as a TemporalAccessor; defaults to LocalDateTime.now()Override it in tests and for a Clock-driven application; field types can be Instant, LocalDateTime, ZonedDateTime, long, Date
@EntityListeners(AuditingEntityListener.class)Hooks the handler into JPA's @PrePersist/@PreUpdateOn a @MappedSuperclass every audited entity extends, so no entity forgets it
@PrePersist … @PostLoadPlain JPA callbacks on the entity or an @EntityListeners classFor invariants and derived fields; keep them free of repository calls and Spring beans (a JPA listener is not a Spring bean unless you wire it so)
AbstractAggregateRoot / @DomainEventsHolds events until the repository's save/saveAll/delete publishes them, then @AfterDomainEventPublication clears themEvents fire only through the repository — an em.persist bypasses them; publish from the aggregate's behaviour methods, not from services
@TransactionalEventListenerRuns at AFTER_COMMIT (default), AFTER_ROLLBACK, AFTER_COMPLETION or BEFORE_COMMITfallbackExecution = true runs it even with no transaction; an AFTER_COMMIT listener that writes to the database needs its own @Transactional(propagation = REQUIRES_NEW)
Event and auditing gotchas
  • An AFTER_COMMIT listener cannot write in the committed transaction. It runs with the transaction's resources still bound but the transaction finished; a repository call inside it joins a transaction that will never commit again, and the write is silently lost. Annotate the listener @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW), or hand the work to a queue.
  • Phase D is the e-mail bug. An @EventListener that sends "your order is confirmed" has sent it for ORD-2, which was rolled back. Anything with an external side effect belongs in AFTER_COMMIT — or, if it must not be lost when the process dies between commit and send, in an outbox row written inside the transaction and delivered by a separate poller. Spring Modulith's @ApplicationModuleListener packages that pattern.
  • @Async plus @TransactionalEventListener loses the context twice. The listener runs on another thread with no transaction and no security context; AuditorAware returns empty and lazy loading fails. Pass ids in the event, not entities.
  • Events only fire through save. Dirty checking at commit writes the aggregate's changes without calling the repository, so a method that mutates an aggregate and registers an event but never calls save publishes nothing. Call save explicitly when you register events.
  • @CreatedBy is null when nobody is logged in. Batch jobs and startup runners have no principal; either an AuditorAware that falls back to "system", or a nullable column with that meaning. Decide, then write it down.
  • Auditing columns are not history. They say who touched the row last; for what changed and the previous values you need Hibernate Envers (@Audited, shadow _aud tables) or an explicit event log. Envers is not on this class path and is out of scope, but it is the right next tool.

Check yourself

1.In phase D the transaction rolls back after save, yet the output shows inside tx: ORD-2 and no insert statement. Why both?

B. Two JPA facts combine: persist only schedules the insert (JPA §3, write-behind), and the sequence value was fetched eagerly for the id — which is why select next value appears and insert does not. Meanwhile the event was published the moment save returned, inside the transaction, and the plain listener acted on it.

A: show-sql prints every statement Hibernate executes, committed or not; none ran. C: publication happens after the delegate save, in the repository proxy. D: listeners are synchronous on the calling thread unless annotated @Async.

2.An @TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT) receives OrderPlaced and calls auditLog.save(new AuditEntry(…)). No exception is thrown, but the audit table stays empty. What is wrong?

C. The documented trap: at AFTER_COMMIT the synchronization still runs within the scope of the completed transaction, so a plain @Transactional (REQUIRED) joins it and its work is discarded. REQUIRES_NEW opens a real second transaction.

A: they can, with a new transaction. B: clearing the aggregate's list does not affect an event already handed to the publisher. D: AbstractAggregateRoot is about publishing events, not about being saveable.

3.Which of the following are true of Spring Data auditing as configured in the worked example? Select all that apply.

A and D. Bulk JPQL updates bypass the persistence context and its callbacks (JPA §6), so audited columns must be set in the statement itself. And the provider bean is precisely the hook this program uses — the printed stamps are proof.

B: the timestamp comes from the application's DateTimeProvider (JVM clock by default), which is why clock skew between instances is a real concern and why some teams use a database default instead. C: the save would join the finished transaction and be lost, the trap in question 2 — with REQUIRES_NEW it would stamp correctly.

Section 9

Dynamic queries: Specifications and Query by Example

A search screen has six optional filters. A derived query name cannot express "category if given, price range if given, SKU prefix if given": you would need one method per combination, and six filters make sixty-four. A @Query string cannot either, unless you start concatenating JPQL — which is how injection bugs and unreadable code are born. What you need is a query assembled at runtime from whichever criteria are present, with the type checking and parameter binding of a real query.

That is the JPA Criteria API (JPA §6), and Spring Data wraps it in one small idea. A Specification<T> is a function (root, query, cb) -> Predicate: given the query being built, return the condition this criterion contributes. Because each criterion is a value, you can name it, test it, store it in a list and combine it with and, or and not. A repository that also extends JpaSpecificationExecutor<T> gains findAll(spec), count(spec), exists(spec) and delete(spec), and Spring Data turns the composed predicate into one JPQL query. Query by Example is the lighter sibling: hand it a half-filled entity and it builds the equality and string-matching predicates for you.

Worked example: one repository, eight queries, no strings

Six products from two suppliers. Every criterion is a static factory on ProductSpecs; the runner composes them in different ways and the SQL shows exactly what each composition became.

javaSpecifications.java
package lm.specs;
 
import jakarta.persistence.*;
import org.springframework.boot.CommandLineRunner;
import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.data.domain.*;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.domain.Specification;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaRepository;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaSpecificationExecutor;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.config.EnableJpaRepositories;
 
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
 
import static org.springframework.data.domain.ExampleMatcher.GenericPropertyMatchers.startsWith;
 
@SpringBootApplication
@EnableJpaRepositories(considerNestedRepositories = true)
public class Specifications {
 
    public enum Category { FASTENER, STRUCTURAL, MOTION }
 
    @Entity(name = "Supplier")
    @Table(name = "supplier")
    public static class Supplier {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE) Long id;
        @Column(nullable = false, unique = true) String name;
        protected Supplier() {}
        Supplier(String name) { this.name = name; }
    }
 
    @Entity(name = "Product")
    @Table(name = "product")
    public static class Product {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE) Long id;
        @Column(nullable = false, unique = true, length = 16) String sku;
        @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING) @Column(nullable = false) Category category;
        int priceInCents;
        boolean active = true;
        @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY) Supplier supplier;
        protected Product() {}
        Product(String sku, Category category, int priceInCents, boolean active, Supplier supplier) {
            this.sku = sku; this.category = category; this.priceInCents = priceInCents; this.active = active; this.supplier = supplier;
        }
        @Override public String toString() { return sku + "/" + category + "/" + priceInCents + (active ? "" : "/inactive"); }
    }
 
    /* One static factory per criterion. Each returns a Specification, so they compose. */
    public static final class ProductSpecs {
        static Specification<Product> inCategory(Category c) {
            return (root, query, cb) -> cb.equal(root.get("category"), c);
        }
        static Specification<Product> priceBetween(int lo, int hi) {
            return (root, query, cb) -> cb.between(root.get("priceInCents"), lo, hi);
        }
        static Specification<Product> skuStartsWith(String prefix) {
            return (root, query, cb) -> cb.like(root.get("sku"), prefix + "%");
        }
        static Specification<Product> isActive() {
            return (root, query, cb) -> cb.isTrue(root.get("active"));
        }
        static Specification<Product> suppliedBy(String supplierName) {
            return (root, query, cb) -> {
                if (query != null) query.distinct(true);        // query is null for count/exists/delete
                return cb.equal(root.join("supplier").get("name"), supplierName);
            };
        }
        /* The "ignore absent criteria" pattern: every null argument means "no filter". */
        static Specification<Product> filter(Category c, Integer minPrice, Integer maxPrice, String skuPrefix, Boolean activeOnly) {
            List<Specification<Product>> parts = new ArrayList<>();
            if (c != null) parts.add(inCategory(c));
            if (minPrice != null || maxPrice != null) {
                parts.add(priceBetween(minPrice == null ? 0 : minPrice, maxPrice == null ? Integer.MAX_VALUE : maxPrice));
            }
            if (skuPrefix != null) parts.add(skuStartsWith(skuPrefix));
            if (Boolean.TRUE.equals(activeOnly)) parts.add(isActive());
            return Specification.allOf(parts);                   // empty list → no where clause at all
        }
    }
 
    public interface ProductRepository extends JpaRepository<Product, Long>, JpaSpecificationExecutor<Product> {}
    public interface SupplierRepository extends JpaRepository<Supplier, Long> {}
 
    @Bean CommandLineRunner demo(ProductRepository products, SupplierRepository suppliers) {
        return args -> {
            Supplier acme = suppliers.save(new Supplier("Acme"));
            Supplier bolt = suppliers.save(new Supplier("BoltCo"));
            products.saveAll(List.of(
                new Product("BOLT-7", Category.FASTENER, 80, true, bolt),
                new Product("BOLT-9", Category.FASTENER, 95, false, bolt),
                new Product("NUT-3", Category.FASTENER, 25, true, acme),
                new Product("GIRD-1", Category.STRUCTURAL, 120_000, true, acme),
                new Product("ROD-4", Category.STRUCTURAL, 4_500, true, acme),
                new Product("CAM-9", Category.MOTION, 2_300, true, bolt)));
            Sort bySku = Sort.by("sku");
 
            System.out.println("-- 1. one criterion --");
            System.out.println(products.findAll(ProductSpecs.inCategory(Category.FASTENER), bySku));
 
            System.out.println("-- 2. and / or / not --");
            Specification<Product> cheapFasteners = Specification.where(ProductSpecs.inCategory(Category.FASTENER))
                    .and(ProductSpecs.priceBetween(0, 90));
            System.out.println(products.findAll(cheapFasteners.or(ProductSpecs.inCategory(Category.MOTION)), bySku));
            System.out.println(products.findAll(Specification.not(ProductSpecs.isActive()), bySku));
 
            System.out.println("-- 3. allOf / anyOf --");
            System.out.println(products.findAll(Specification.anyOf(
                    ProductSpecs.skuStartsWith("BOLT"), ProductSpecs.skuStartsWith("CAM")), bySku));
 
            System.out.println("-- 4. the null-tolerant filter --");
            System.out.println(products.findAll(ProductSpecs.filter(null, null, null, null, null), bySku));
            System.out.println(products.findAll(ProductSpecs.filter(Category.STRUCTURAL, 1_000, null, null, true), bySku));
 
            System.out.println("-- 5. a page needs two statements --");
            Page<Product> page = products.findAll(ProductSpecs.isActive(), PageRequest.of(0, 2, bySku));
            System.out.println("page 0 of " + page.getTotalPages() + ": " + page.getContent() + " total=" + page.getTotalElements());
 
            System.out.println("-- 6. a join inside a spec --");
            System.out.println(products.findAll(ProductSpecs.suppliedBy("BoltCo"), bySku));
 
            System.out.println("-- 7. count / exists / delete --");
            System.out.println("count structural = " + products.count(ProductSpecs.inCategory(Category.STRUCTURAL)));
            System.out.println("exists inactive = " + products.exists(Specification.not(ProductSpecs.isActive())));
            System.out.println("deleted inactive = " + products.delete((root, cb) -> cb.isFalse(root.get("active"))));
 
            System.out.println("-- 8. Query by Example --");
            Product probe = new Product();
            probe.sku = "bo";
            // one probe field only: with two, the order of the and-ed predicates is not guaranteed
            ExampleMatcher matcher = ExampleMatcher.matching()
                    .withIgnoreNullValues()
                    .withIgnorePaths("id", "priceInCents", "active")   // primitives are never null, so they must be ignored explicitly
                    .withMatcher("sku", startsWith())
                    .withIgnoreCase();
            System.out.println(products.findAll(Example.of(probe, matcher), bySku));
        };
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication app = new SpringApplication(Specifications.class);
        app.setDefaultProperties(Map.of(
            "spring.main.web-application-type", "none",
            "spring.main.banner-mode", "off",
            "spring.main.log-startup-info", "false",
            "logging.level.root", "WARN",
            "logging.pattern.console", "%level %logger{0}: %msg%n",
            "spring.datasource.url", "jdbc:h2:mem:specs;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1",
            "spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto", "create-drop",
            "spring.jpa.show-sql", "true",
            "spring.jpa.open-in-view", "false"));
        app.run(args).close();
    }
}

Hibernate: select p1_0.id,p1_0.active,p1_0.category,p1_0.price_in_cents,p1_0.sku,p1_0.supplier_id from product p1_0 where not(p1_0.active) order by p1_0.sku
[BOLT-9/FASTENER/95/inactive]
-- 3. allOf / anyOf --
Hibernate: select p1_0.id,p1_0.active,p1_0.category,p1_0.price_in_cents,p1_0.sku,p1_0.supplier_id from product p1_0 where p1_0.sku like ? escape '' or p1_0.sku like ? escape '' order by p1_0.sku
[BOLT-7/FASTENER/80, BOLT-9/FASTENER/95/inactive, CAM-9/MOTION/2300]
-- 4. the null-tolerant filter --
Hibernate: select p1_0.id,p1_0.active,p1_0.category,p1_0.price_in_cents,p1_0.sku,p1_0.supplier_id from product p1_0 order by p1_0.sku
[BOLT-7/FASTENER/80, BOLT-9/FASTENER/95/inactive, CAM-9/MOTION/2300, GIRD-1/STRUCTURAL/120000, NUT-3/FASTENER/25, ROD-4/STRUCTURAL/4500]
Hibernate: select p1_0.id,p1_0.active,p1_0.category,p1_0.price_in_cents,p1_0.sku,p1_0.supplier_id from product p1_0 where p1_0.category=? and p1_0.price_in_cents between ? and ? and p1_0.active order by p1_0.sku
[GIRD-1/STRUCTURAL/120000, ROD-4/STRUCTURAL/4500]
-- 5. a page needs two statements --
Hibernate: select p1_0.id,p1_0.active,p1_0.category,p1_0.price_in_cents,p1_0.sku,p1_0.supplier_id from product p1_0 where p1_0.active order by p1_0.sku offset ? rows fetch first ? rows only
Hibernate: select count(p1_0.id) from product p1_0 where p1_0.active
page 0 of 3: [BOLT-7/FASTENER/80, CAM-9/MOTION/2300] total=5
-- 6. a join inside a spec --
Hibernate: select distinct p1_0.id,p1_0.active,p1_0.category,p1_0.price_in_cents,p1_0.sku,p1_0.supplier_id from product p1_0 join supplier s1_0 on s1_0.id=p1_0.supplier_id where s1_0.name=? order by p1_0.sku
[BOLT-7/FASTENER/80, BOLT-9/FASTENER/95/inactive, CAM-9/MOTION/2300]
-- 7. count / exists / delete --
Hibernate: select count(p1_0.id) from product p1_0 where p1_0.category=?
count structural = 2
Hibernate: select 1 from product p1_0 where not(p1_0.active) fetch first ? rows only
exists inactive = true
Hibernate: delete from product p1_0 where not(p1_0.active)
deleted inactive = 1
-- 8. Query by Example --
Hibernate: select p1_0.id,p1_0.active,p1_0.category,p1_0.price_in_cents,p1_0.sku,p1_0.supplier_id from product p1_0 where lower(p1_0.sku) like ? escape '\' order by p1_0.sku
[BOLT-7/FASTENER/80]
Hibernate: drop table if exists product cascade
Hibernate: drop table if exists supplier cascade
Hibernate: drop sequence if exists product_seq
Hibernate: drop sequence if exists supplier_seq

Read the SQL against the composition that produced it:

  1. One criterion becomes one predicate: where p1_0.category=?. The enum is a bound parameter, never spliced into the string.
  2. where(a).and(b).or(c) is evaluated left to right as (a and b) or c. Hibernate prints it without parentheses — category=? and price_in_cents between ? and ? or category=? — because SQL's and binds tighter than or, so the brackets would be redundant. If you meant a and (b or c), build b.or(c) first and pass it to and; the fluent chain will not guess. Specification.not becomes not(p1_0.active).
  3. anyOf joins its arguments with or; allOf with and. Notice like ? escape '': a Criteria cb.like with no escape character means a % or _ typed into a search box is a wildcard. A derived StartingWith (§3) escapes for you, emitting escape '\'; a hand-written spec does not.
  4. The null-tolerant filter with every argument null produced a query with no where clause at all — allOf of an empty list is "unrestricted", not where 1=1. With three arguments present, three predicates appear, joined by and. This is the pattern a search endpoint wants.
  5. Paging costs two statements: the page itself with offset ? rows fetch first ? rows only, then select count(p1_0.id) … where p1_0.active. Spring Data re-applies the same specification to a count query, so the total always matches the filter (§7).
  6. A join inside a spec — root.join("supplier") — becomes an inner join, and query.distinct(true) becomes select distinct. The guard if (query != null) matters: Spring Data 4 calls the same spec for count, exists and delete, where there is no CriteriaQuery to set distinct on.
  7. count, exists and delete reuse specs too. exists is select 1 … fetch first ? rows only — it stops at the first match. delete here takes a PredicateSpecification, Spring Data JPA 4's query-independent form (root, cb) -> …, and runs one bulk delete: no entities are loaded, no lifecycle callbacks fire, and the persistence context is not told (JPA §6).
  8. Query by Example turned a probe with sku = "bo", matched with startsWith and ignoring case, into lower(p1_0.sku) like ? escape '\'. Primitive fields are never null, so priceInCents and active would have become = 0 and = false — the matcher must ignore them explicitly. Only BOLT-7 comes back because step 7 deleted the inactive BOLT-9. While this page was being built, a probe with two fields (SKU and category) emitted its two predicates in a different order on different runs: Query by Example walks the entity's attributes in an order nobody promises. The rows are the same either way, but never write a test that asserts on its SQL text.

Build a filter

Compose a Specification from whichever criteria are present

The rows are the six products from the worked example, filtered in the browser by the same rules the database applies. The price range is "off" at its extremes, mirroring the null-tolerant factory: an absent bound contributes no predicate.

Which tool for which query

Choosing between derived queries, @Query, Specifications and Query by Example
The query is…Reach forWhy
Fixed, one or two conditionsDerived query (§3)The name is the documentation, validated at startup.
Fixed but complex: joins, aggregates, projections@Query (§4)One readable JPQL string, validated at startup.
Shape decided at runtime from optional inputsSpecificationComposable, typed, parameters always bound.
"Find things like this one", equality and string matching onlyQuery by ExampleZero query code; the probe is the filter.
Ranges, or across fields, nested properties of collectionsSpecificationQuery by Example cannot express them.
Reporting with grouping, window functionsNative @Query or jOOQCriteria becomes harder to read than the SQL it emits.

Treat specifications like small pure functions. Each factory knows one criterion and nothing else; the screen or service decides which to combine. That gives you criteria you can unit-test in isolation, reuse across repositories with the same attribute names, and name after the business rule — overdue(), restockCandidate(threshold) — rather than after the columns.

static Specification<Product> restockCandidate(int threshold) {
    return Specification.allOf(isActive(), stockBelow(threshold), not(discontinued()));
}
 
// the caller adds what the request supplied
Specification<Product> spec = restockCandidate(10);
if (req.category() != null) spec = spec.and(inCategory(req.category()));
List<Product> hits = products.findAll(spec, Sort.by("sku"));

Composition is immutable: spec.and(x) returns a new specification and leaves spec alone, so a shared base filter cannot be corrupted by one caller.

Query by Example needs only QueryByExampleExecutor, which JpaRepository already extends. The probe's non-null fields become predicates; the ExampleMatcher decides how strings compare (exact, starts with, contains, ends with, regex where supported) and whether case matters.

  • It can: equality on any property, including nested single-valued ones (supplier.name); string matching; ignoring paths; matchingAll versus matchingAny.
  • It cannot: ranges (between, >), in lists, or on the same property, conditions on collection elements, is null unless you opt in with withIncludeNullValues().
  • The primitive trap: an int field is 0, never null, so it is always included unless you ignore its path. Prefer wrapper types on probes, or ignore paths explicitly as the worked example does.

root.get("priceInCents") is a string. Rename the field and every spec still compiles, then fails at runtime with an IllegalArgumentException about an unknown attribute. Two cures:

  • The JPA static metamodel. Add hibernate-processor as an annotation processor and Hibernate generates Product_ with typed attributes, so the spec reads root.get(Product_.priceInCents) and a rename becomes a compile error. Not on this module's class path, so the worked example uses strings.
  • Querydsl generates QProduct and a fluent, typed predicate language (product.priceInCents.between(lo, hi)); Spring Data integrates it via QuerydslPredicateExecutor. It is a separate dependency and code generator — worth it on a large query surface, overkill for a handful of filters.
Specification gotchas
  • A fetch join in a spec breaks paging. root.fetch("lines") is reused for the count query, where Hibernate rejects fetching an association whose owner is not selected. Guard it with if (Long.class != query.getResultType()), or keep fetch plans in an @EntityGraph on the repository method (§6).
  • Joins multiply rows. A join to a collection returns one row per element; without distinct the same product appears several times, and the total in a Page counts the duplicates.
  • The fluent chain is left-associative. a.and(b).or(c) is (a and b) or c. Build the bracketed part as its own specification when you mean something else.
  • User input in like is a pattern. cb.like(root.get("sku"), prefix + "%") treats % and _ in prefix as wildcards. Escape them, or use the three-argument cb.like(expr, pattern, '\\').
  • Every filter combination is a different SQL string. Six optional filters can produce dozens of statement shapes, each parsed and planned separately by the database and each a separate entry in Hibernate's query plan cache. Usually fine; worth knowing when a database's statement cache starts thrashing.

Check yourself

1.A search endpoint receives no filters at all and calls products.findAll(Specification.allOf(List.of())). What SQL runs?

B. The worked example's step 4 shows it: allOf of nothing is the unrestricted specification, and Spring Data omits the where clause entirely. That is what makes the null-tolerant filter pattern work without special cases.

A would make the pattern unusable, and Spring Data deliberately allows it. C is what string-building code tends to produce, not what Criteria emits. D would be the result of anyOf semantics taken literally ("at least one of nothing"), which is not how an empty conjunction behaves.

2.You need: active products whose category is FASTENER or whose price is under 100 cents. Which composition is correct?

C. The or must be built first, then and-ed with isActive(): active and (category = ? or price < ?).

A groups left to right as (active and fastener) or cheap, so an inactive product under 100 cents is returned — exactly the shape step 2 of the worked example printed. B makes all three alternatives, returning every active product regardless of category or price. D is wrong: Hibernate faithfully renders the tree you built; it only omits parentheses that SQL precedence makes redundant.

3.Which of these can Query by Example express? Select all that apply.

A and D. String matching with a matcher, equality, and nested single-valued properties are exactly what a probe can describe. Step 8 of the worked example is the SKU half of case A; adding the category is one more field on the probe.

B: a probe holds one value per property, so there is no way to say "between". C: one property cannot hold two values, and matchingAny ors different properties, not alternatives for the same one. Both need a Specification.

Section 10

Validation and exception translation

Bad data reaches a data layer by two roads. Sometimes your own code produced it: a negative price, a blank SKU, a malformed e-mail. Sometimes the database refuses something that looked fine in Java: a duplicate key, a stale version, a foreign key to a row that has gone. Both deserve a clear, specific exception at the right place — and in a raw JPA application they arrive as an assortment of Hibernate, JDBC and driver types whose names change with the database you happen to run.

Spring addresses each road separately. Bean Validation (Jakarta Validation, implemented by Hibernate Validator) puts the rules on the fields — @NotBlank, @Positive, @Email or your own — and checks them both on entities when Hibernate flushes and on method parameters of any @Validated bean. Exception translation catches whatever the persistence provider throws as it leaves a repository proxy and rethrows it as one of Spring's DataAccessException subclasses, a hierarchy that means the same thing on H2, PostgreSQL and Oracle. This section provokes one of each and prints what arrives.

Worked example: five ways to be rejected

A Product with field constraints, including a custom @Sku; a @Validated service; a unique SKU column; and a @Version for the stale-update case. Every failure is caught and reported as "outer exception <- root cause". SQL echo is off for this program so the exceptions are not buried in DDL, and Hibernate's own SQL-error log category is switched off because H2's messages embed generated constraint names.

javaValidation.java
package lm.validation;
 
import jakarta.persistence.*;
import jakarta.validation.*;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.*;
import org.springframework.boot.CommandLineRunner;
import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.dao.DataAccessException;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaRepository;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.config.EnableJpaRepositories;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.transaction.PlatformTransactionManager;
import org.springframework.transaction.support.TransactionTemplate;
import org.springframework.validation.annotation.Validated;
 
import java.lang.annotation.*;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.TreeSet;
 
@SpringBootApplication
@EnableJpaRepositories(considerNestedRepositories = true)
public class Validation {
 
    /* A custom constraint: an annotation plus a validator. */
    @Documented
    @Constraint(validatedBy = SkuValidator.class)
    @Target({ElementType.FIELD, ElementType.PARAMETER})
    @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
    public @interface Sku {
        String message() default "must look like ABC-123";
        Class<?>[] groups() default {};
        Class<? extends Payload>[] payload() default {};
    }
    public static class SkuValidator implements ConstraintValidator<Sku, String> {
        @Override public boolean isValid(String value, ConstraintValidatorContext ctx) {
            return value == null || value.matches("[A-Z]+-\\d+");      // null is @NotBlank's job, not ours
        }
    }
 
    @Entity(name = "Product")
    @Table(name = "product")
    public static class Product {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE) Long id;
        @NotBlank @Size(max = 16) @Sku
        @Column(nullable = false, unique = true, length = 16) String sku;
        @Positive int priceInCents;
        @Email String supplierContact;
        @Version long version;
        protected Product() {}
        Product(String sku, int priceInCents, String supplierContact) {
            this.sku = sku; this.priceInCents = priceInCents; this.supplierContact = supplierContact;
        }
        @Override public String toString() { return sku + "=" + priceInCents + "c v" + version; }
    }
 
    public interface ProductRepository extends JpaRepository<Product, Long> {}
 
    public static class ProductNotFound extends RuntimeException {
        ProductNotFound(long id) { super("no product with id " + id); }
    }
 
    /* A service with method validation: @Validated on the class, @Valid / constraints on parameters. */
    @Service
    @Validated
    public static class CatalogService {
        private final ProductRepository repo;
        CatalogService(ProductRepository repo) { this.repo = repo; }
 
        public Product reprice(@Positive long id, @Min(1) @Max(1_000_000) int newPrice) {
            Product p = repo.findById(id).orElseThrow(() -> new ProductNotFound(id));
            p.priceInCents = newPrice;
            return repo.save(p);
        }
        public Product register(@Valid Product p) { return repo.save(p); }
    }
 
    static String rootOf(Throwable t) {
        while (t.getCause() != null && t.getCause() != t) t = t.getCause();
        return t.getClass().getSimpleName();
    }
    static void report(String label, Throwable t) {
        System.out.println(label + ": " + t.getClass().getSimpleName() + " <- root " + rootOf(t));
    }
    static void violations(Throwable t) {
        while (t != null && !(t instanceof ConstraintViolationException)) t = t.getCause();
        if (t == null) { System.out.println("  (no ConstraintViolationException in the chain)"); return; }
        TreeSet<String> lines = new TreeSet<>();
        for (ConstraintViolation<?> v : ((ConstraintViolationException) t).getConstraintViolations()) {
            lines.add("  " + v.getPropertyPath() + ": " + v.getMessage());
        }
        lines.forEach(System.out::println);
    }
 
    @Bean CommandLineRunner demo(ProductRepository repo, CatalogService catalog, PlatformTransactionManager txm) {
        return args -> {
            System.out.println("-- 1. entity constraints are checked at flush --");
            try {
                repo.save(new Product("bolt 7", -5, "not-an-email"));
            } catch (RuntimeException e) {
                report("save", e);
                violations(e);
            }
 
            System.out.println("-- 2. method validation on a service --");
            try {
                catalog.reprice(-1, 0);
            } catch (RuntimeException e) {
                report("reprice", e);
                violations(e);
            }
            try {
                catalog.register(new Product("", 10, null));
            } catch (RuntimeException e) {
                report("register", e);
                violations(e);
            }
 
            System.out.println("-- 3. a valid product, then a duplicate --");
            Product ok = repo.save(new Product("BOLT-7", 80, "sales@acme.example"));
            System.out.println("saved " + ok);
            try {
                repo.saveAndFlush(new Product("BOLT-7", 90, null));
            } catch (DataAccessException e) {
                System.out.println("duplicate: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName()
                        + " <- most specific " + e.getMostSpecificCause().getClass().getSimpleName());
            }
 
            System.out.println("-- 4. missing rows --");
            try {
                catalog.reprice(999, 100);
            } catch (ProductNotFound e) {
                System.out.println("lookup: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " (" + e.getMessage() + ")");
            }
            repo.deleteById(999L);
            System.out.println("deleteById(999) threw: false");
 
            System.out.println("-- 5. a stale update is translated --");
            TransactionTemplate tx = new TransactionTemplate(txm);
            Product stale = tx.execute(s -> repo.findById(ok.id).orElseThrow());       // detached copy, version 0
            tx.executeWithoutResult(s -> repo.findById(ok.id).orElseThrow().priceInCents = 85);  // someone else commits first
            try {
                stale.priceInCents = 70;
                repo.save(stale);                                                        // merge + flush → stale version
            } catch (RuntimeException e) {
                report("stale save", e);
            }
            System.out.println("db now " + repo.findById(ok.id).orElseThrow());
        };
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication app = new SpringApplication(Validation.class);
        app.setDefaultProperties(Map.of(
            "spring.main.web-application-type", "none",
            "spring.main.banner-mode", "off",
            "spring.main.log-startup-info", "false",
            "logging.level.root", "WARN",
            "logging.pattern.console", "%level %logger{0}: %msg%n",
            "spring.datasource.url", "jdbc:h2:mem:validation;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1",
            "spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto", "create-drop",
            "spring.jpa.show-sql", "false",
            "spring.jpa.open-in-view", "false",
            "logging.level.org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.error", "OFF"));   // H2 names its constraints; keep them out of stdout
        app.run(args).close();
    }
}
Expected output
-- 1. entity constraints are checked at flush --
save: TransactionSystemException <- root ConstraintViolationException
  priceInCents: must be greater than 0
  sku: must look like ABC-123
  supplierContact: must be a well-formed email address
-- 2. method validation on a service --
reprice: ConstraintViolationException <- root ConstraintViolationException
  reprice.arg0: must be greater than 0
  reprice.arg1: must be greater than or equal to 1
register: ConstraintViolationException <- root ConstraintViolationException
  register.arg0.sku: must look like ABC-123
  register.arg0.sku: must not be blank
-- 3. a valid product, then a duplicate --
saved BOLT-7=80c v0
duplicate: DataIntegrityViolationException <- most specific JdbcSQLIntegrityConstraintViolationException
-- 4. missing rows --
lookup: ProductNotFound (no product with id 999)
deleteById(999) threw: false
-- 5. a stale update is translated --
stale save: ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException <- root StaleObjectStateException
db now BOLT-7=85c v1

Five lessons, one per block:

  1. Entity constraints run at flush, so they surface at commit. Hibernate Validator hooks into Hibernate's pre-insert and pre-update events. repo.save only queued the insert; the flush happened as the repository's transaction committed, the validator threw ConstraintViolationException there, and Spring's transaction manager reported the failed commit as TransactionSystemException. If you catch only the inner type, you miss it. The three violations are printed sorted: @Sku, @Positive and @Email all failed, and they are reported together, not one at a time.
  2. Method validation runs before the method body. @Validated on the class makes Spring wrap the bean in a proxy that validates parameters on every call, so reprice(-1, 0) never reached findById. The violation paths read reprice.arg0: the build compiles without -parameters, so the real names are not in the bytecode. Spring Boot's Maven and Gradle plugins add that flag, and you would then see reprice.id. @Valid on register's parameter cascaded into the Product, which is why its field rules fired — two of them for the blank SKU.
  3. A duplicate key is translated. saveAndFlush forced the insert inside the repository call, H2 refused it, and what came out of the repository proxy was DataIntegrityViolationException — a Spring type you can catch on any database. getMostSpecificCause() still reaches the driver's own exception when you need the detail.
  4. Missing rows are your decision. findById returns an Optional; turning absence into a domain exception (ProductNotFound) is the service's job. deleteById of a missing id is silently ignored since Spring Data 3 — earlier versions threw EmptyResultDataAccessException, and code that relied on that now quietly succeeds.
  5. A stale update is translated too. The detached copy still had version 0; another transaction had already moved the row to version 1. save merged and flushed, Hibernate's where id=? and version=? matched no row, and Hibernate's StaleObjectStateException came out of the proxy as ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException, a subclass of OptimisticLockingFailureException. The first writer's 85 cents survived.

Match the failure to what you catch

Drag an exception onto its situation, or click one then click the other

Each situation reaches your service code through a repository or a transactional method. What arrives?

All four correct. Constraint breaches from the database are DataIntegrityViolationException; version conflicts are ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException; misuse of the API (here, a bulk update with no transaction to run in, which JPA reports as TransactionRequiredException) is InvalidDataAccessApiUsageException; and a validation failure that only happens at flush-on-commit is reported by the transaction manager as TransactionSystemException, with the ConstraintViolationException as its cause.

The translated hierarchy

Common DataAccessException subclasses and what causes them
Spring exceptionTypical causeUsual handling
DataIntegrityViolationExceptionUnique, not-null, check or foreign-key constraintMap to a domain error ("SKU already exists"); not retryable
DuplicateKeyExceptionA unique breach the translator could identify precisely (JDBC paths mostly)Same as above; a subclass, so catching the parent covers it
OptimisticLockingFailureException@Version mismatch (the ORM subclass is ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException)Reload and retry, or report a conflict to the user
PessimisticLockingFailureException, CannotAcquireLockExceptionLock timeout, deadlock victimRetry the whole transaction
InvalidDataAccessApiUsageExceptionWrong use of the API: bad JPQL, bulk update outside a transaction, null idA bug: fix the code
InvalidDataAccessResourceUsageExceptionThe SQL is wrong for this schema: missing table or columnA bug or a migration out of step
DataAccessResourceFailureExceptionThe database is unreachableFail fast; let a health check notice
QueryTimeoutExceptionA statement exceeded its timeoutInvestigate the query; maybe retry
TransactionSystemException (not a DataAccessException)The commit itself failed, often wrapping validation at flushInspect the cause chain

Validate at the boundary first. The request DTO a controller receives is where a user's mistake should be caught and reported field by field, before any transaction opens. Validate entities as the last line. Constraints on the entity catch bugs inside your own code — a service that computes a negative price — but they fire at flush, possibly at commit, far from the code that caused them.

  • @Valid (Jakarta) cascades into an object's fields; @Validated (Spring) on a class turns on method validation and can select groups, such as OnCreate versus OnUpdate.
  • Messages are interpolated from ValidationMessages.properties, so {jakarta.validation.constraints.Positive.message} can be translated without touching code.
  • Keep the database constraint too. Bean Validation cannot see other rows, so uniqueness is only ever enforced reliably by a unique index — a @Unique-style validator that runs a query has a race between the check and the insert.

Spring Data repositories are translated automatically: their proxies include a PersistenceExceptionTranslationInterceptor. Your own classes opt in by carrying @Repository, which PersistenceExceptionTranslationPostProcessor (registered by Spring Boot) wraps the same way.

The interceptor asks each PersistenceExceptionTranslator in the context — for JPA, the EntityManagerFactory bean, which delegates to Hibernate's dialect-aware SQL state mapping — to convert the exception. That is why a raw entityManager.flush() in a plain @Component throws Hibernate's own ConstraintViolationException, while the same failure through repo.saveAndFlush arrives as DataIntegrityViolationException (§11 shows exactly this).

Note the name clash: org.hibernate.exception.ConstraintViolationException (a database constraint) and jakarta.validation.ConstraintViolationException (a Bean Validation rule) are unrelated types with the same simple name. Import carefully.

  • Translate at the service edge. Catch DataIntegrityViolationException where you know what it means — registering a product — and throw SkuAlreadyExists. Callers should not have to know about constraints.
  • Retry only what can succeed on a retry. Optimistic and pessimistic locking failures can; integrity violations and API misuse cannot. A retry must start a new transaction, so it wraps the transactional method from outside (spring-retry's @Retryable, or a loop around a REQUIRES_NEW call as in §5), and the operation must be safe to repeat.
  • In a web layer a @ControllerAdvice maps domain exceptions to HTTP statuses — 409 for conflicts, 400 for validation, 404 for not found — so controllers stay free of try/catch. Spring MVC is out of scope here, but the mapping is only possible because the data layer threw specific types.
Validation and translation gotchas
  • The exception arrives at commit, wrapped. Entity validation fires at flush; if the flush is the commit, you get TransactionSystemException. Catching ConstraintViolationException around save alone catches nothing.
  • Method validation needs the proxy. @Validated constraints are ignored on self-invocation and on private methods, for the same reason @Transactional is (§5).
  • arg0 in messages means no -parameters. Builds outside Spring Boot's plugins often omit the flag; violation paths, @PathVariable without a name and @Param-less queries all depend on it.
  • A transaction that saw an exception is finished. After a DataIntegrityViolationException inside a @Transactional method, the transaction is marked rollback-only even if you catch the exception. Further work in it is wasted, and the commit raises UnexpectedRollbackException.
  • Do not log and rethrow at every layer. One stack trace per failure, at the edge that handles it; the translated exception keeps the original as its cause.

Check yourself

1.Outside any transaction, you call repo.save(new Product("BOLT-7", -5)) on an entity whose price is @Positive and whose id is SEQUENCE-generated. What do you catch?

C. Step 1 of the worked example printed exactly this. The repository opened its own transaction; persist only queued the insert; validation ran at flush, which happened during commit; the transaction manager wrapped the failed commit.

A would be true if validation ran at persist, but Hibernate validates on the pre-insert event at flush. B: the validator runs in the pre-insert event and stops the insert before the database ever sees the row, so no database constraint gets the chance to fire. D: Hibernate Validator is on the class path, so entity validation is on automatically.

2.A plain @Component (not @Repository) injects an EntityManager, persists a duplicate SKU and calls em.flush(). What reaches its caller?

B. Translation happens in an interceptor on repository proxies and on @Repository beans. A @Component has none, so Hibernate's exception passes through as-is. §11's harness hit exactly this until it switched to repo.saveAndFlush.

A overstates translation; it is opt-in by stereotype. C is the Bean Validation type with the same simple name — a different thing entirely. D: Hibernate already wrapped the JDBC exception in its own type before it left flush.

3.Which failures is it reasonable to retry automatically in a fresh transaction? Select all that apply.

A and C. Both are contention: another transaction got there first, and a fresh attempt that re-reads current state can succeed. The retry must wrap the transaction from outside and the operation must be safe to repeat.

B will fail identically every time — the SKU still exists — so it belongs in a domain error. D is a bug in the code; retrying only repeats it.

Section 11

Testing the data layer

Repository code fails in ways unit tests with mocks cannot see: a derived query whose name parses differently from what you meant, a mapping that produces the wrong SQL, an N+1 that only appears with real associations, a constraint the database enforces and your Java does not. So data-layer tests run against a real database, inside a real persistence context, through real repository proxies. Spring Boot's answer is the test slice @DataJpaTest: a cut-down application context with only the JPA machinery, an embedded database, and — the part that surprises people — every test method wrapped in a transaction that is rolled back at the end.

Rollback is what makes these tests fast and independent: no cleanup scripts, no ordering between tests, no leftover rows. It is also the source of the classic data-layer test bug, because a transaction that never commits may never flush, and a statement that is never sent cannot fail. JUnit cannot run inside this page's build, so the worked example reproduces what the test framework does, step by step, with a TransactionTemplate in a plain Spring Boot application. The real test classes follow it, unverified, as reference.

Worked example: what a test transaction actually does

Five experiments. Each is a "test body" run inside a transaction that ends in a rollback, exactly as @DataJpaTest would end it — except experiment 2, which commits for contrast.

javaRollbackHarness.java
package lm.testing;
 
import jakarta.persistence.*;
import org.springframework.boot.CommandLineRunner;
import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.core.io.ByteArrayResource;
import org.springframework.dao.DataAccessException;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaRepository;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.config.EnableJpaRepositories;
import org.springframework.jdbc.core.JdbcTemplate;
import org.springframework.jdbc.datasource.init.ResourceDatabasePopulator;
import org.springframework.transaction.PlatformTransactionManager;
import org.springframework.transaction.support.TransactionTemplate;
 
import javax.sql.DataSource;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.util.Map;
 
@SpringBootApplication
@EnableJpaRepositories(considerNestedRepositories = true)
public class RollbackHarness {
 
    @Entity(name = "Product")
    @Table(name = "product")
    public static class Product {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE) Long id;
        @Column(nullable = false, unique = true, length = 16) String sku;
        int priceInCents;
        protected Product() {}
        Product(String sku, int priceInCents) { this.sku = sku; this.priceInCents = priceInCents; }
        @Override public String toString() { return sku + "=" + priceInCents + "c"; }
    }
 
    public interface ProductRepository extends JpaRepository<Product, Long> {}
 
    @PersistenceContext EntityManager em;
 
    @Bean CommandLineRunner demo(ProductRepository repo, PlatformTransactionManager txm, DataSource ds) {
        JdbcTemplate jdbc = new JdbcTemplate(ds);
        TransactionTemplate tx = new TransactionTemplate(txm);
        return args -> {
            System.out.println("-- 1. what a test transaction does: run, assert, roll back --");
            tx.executeWithoutResult(status -> {
                repo.save(new Product("BOLT-7", 80));
                repo.save(new Product("NUT-3", 25));
                em.flush();
                System.out.println("inside the transaction, count = " + repo.count());
                status.setRollbackOnly();                       // what @DataJpaTest does for you at the end
            });
            System.out.println("after rollback, rows = " + jdbc.queryForObject("select count(*) from product", Long.class));
 
            System.out.println("-- 2. the same body, committed --");
            tx.executeWithoutResult(status -> {
                repo.save(new Product("BOLT-7", 80));
                repo.save(new Product("NUT-3", 25));
            });
            System.out.println("after commit, rows = " + jdbc.queryForObject("select count(*) from product", Long.class));
 
            System.out.println("-- 3. the flush trap: an assertion that cannot fail --");
            boolean detected = false;
            try {
                tx.executeWithoutResult(status -> {
                    repo.save(new Product("BOLT-7", 1));          // duplicate sku — but nothing is flushed
                    status.setRollbackOnly();                     // ...and the rollback discards it unflushed
                });
            } catch (DataAccessException e) { detected = true; }
            System.out.println("duplicate detected without flush: " + detected);
            String caught = "nothing";
            try {
                tx.executeWithoutResult(status -> {
                    repo.saveAndFlush(new Product("BOLT-7", 1)); // flush through the repository proxy
                    status.setRollbackOnly();
                });
            } catch (DataAccessException e) { detected = true; caught = e.getClass().getSimpleName(); }
            System.out.println("duplicate detected with flush: " + detected + " (" + caught + ")");
 
            System.out.println("-- 4. the first-level cache hides the database --");
            tx.executeWithoutResult(status -> {
                Product p = repo.save(new Product("CAM-9", 2300));
                em.flush();
                Product again = repo.findById(p.id).orElseThrow();
                System.out.println("same instance without clear(): " + (p == again));
                em.clear();                                       // TestEntityManager.clear()
                Product fresh = repo.findById(p.id).orElseThrow();
                System.out.println("same instance after clear(): " + (p == fresh));
                status.setRollbackOnly();
            });
 
            System.out.println("-- 5. what @Sql does: a script before the body --");
            String script = """
                insert into product (id, sku, price_in_cents) values (1001, 'SEED-1', 10);
                insert into product (id, sku, price_in_cents) values (1002, 'SEED-2', 20);
                """;
            new ResourceDatabasePopulator(new ByteArrayResource(script.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8))).execute(ds);
            System.out.println("rows after script = " + repo.count());
        };
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication app = new SpringApplication(RollbackHarness.class);
        app.setDefaultProperties(Map.of(
            "spring.main.web-application-type", "none",
            "spring.main.banner-mode", "off",
            "spring.main.log-startup-info", "false",
            "logging.level.root", "WARN",
            "logging.pattern.console", "%level %logger{0}: %msg%n",
            "spring.datasource.url", "jdbc:h2:mem:testing;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1",
            "spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto", "create-drop",
            "spring.jpa.show-sql", "true",
            "spring.jpa.open-in-view", "false",
            "logging.level.org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.error", "OFF"));   // H2 names its constraints; keep them out of stdout
        app.run(args).close();
    }
}
Expected output
Hibernate: create global temporary table HTE_product(priceInCents integer, rn_ integer not null, id bigint, sku varchar(16), primary key (rn_)) transactional

Hibernate: create table product (price_in_cents integer not null, id bigint not null, sku varchar(16) not null unique, primary key (id))
-- 1. what a test transaction does: run, assert, roll back --
Hibernate: select next value for product_seq
Hibernate: select next value for product_seq
Hibernate: insert into product (price_in_cents,sku,id) values (?,?,?)
Hibernate: insert into product (price_in_cents,sku,id) values (?,?,?)
Hibernate: select count(*) from product p1_0
inside the transaction, count = 2
after rollback, rows = 0
-- 2. the same body, committed --
Hibernate: insert into product (price_in_cents,sku,id) values (?,?,?)
Hibernate: insert into product (price_in_cents,sku,id) values (?,?,?)
after commit, rows = 2
-- 3. the flush trap: an assertion that cannot fail --
duplicate detected without flush: false
Hibernate: insert into product (price_in_cents,sku,id) values (?,?,?)
duplicate detected with flush: true (DataIntegrityViolationException)
-- 4. the first-level cache hides the database --
Hibernate: insert into product (price_in_cents,sku,id) values (?,?,?)
same instance without clear(): true
Hibernate: select p1_0.id,p1_0.price_in_cents,p1_0.sku from product p1_0 where p1_0.id=?
same instance after clear(): false
-- 5. what @Sql does: a script before the body --
Hibernate: select count(*) from product p1_0
rows after script = 4
Hibernate: drop table if exists product cascade
Hibernate: drop sequence if exists product_seq
  1. Run, assert, roll back. Inside the transaction two inserts were flushed and count() saw them. After setRollbackOnly() the template rolled back instead of committing, and a JDBC count — outside any transaction — found zero rows. That is the whole contract of a test transaction: the database ends every test exactly as it started.
  2. Committed, the rows stay. The same body without the rollback flag leaves two rows. A test annotated @Commit behaves like this, and every test after it then runs against those rows.
  3. The flush trap. The SKU BOLT-7 now exists, so saving another must fail — yet the first attempt printed detected without flush: false and no insert appeared in the SQL. The insert was queued, the transaction rolled back, and the queue was discarded unsent. A test asserting "saving a duplicate throws" would pass for the wrong reason, or a test asserting "this save works" would pass when production fails. With saveAndFlush the insert is sent inside the test, H2 rejects it, and the failure arrives — translated, because it came through the repository proxy — as DataIntegrityViolationException.
  4. The first-level cache. Within one persistence context, findById returned the very instance just saved, without touching the database (there is no select before the first fact). A test that saves, then loads, then asserts is checking the Java object it already had, not what the mapping wrote and reads back. After clear() the load is a real select and a new instance. This is what TestEntityManager.flush() plus clear() is for.
  5. Seeding with a script. ResourceDatabasePopulator ran two plain SQL inserts — the mechanism behind @Sql — and the count went from 2 to 4. Note the script wrote columns by their database names, price_in_cents: scripts see the schema, not the entity.

Step through a test method

Inside @DataJpaTest Simulated ← → to step
Test source
@DataJpaTest
class ProductRepositoryTest {
    @Autowired TestEntityManager tem;
    @Autowired ProductRepository repo;
 
    @Test
    void findsBySkuPrefix() {
        tem.persist(new Product("BOLT-7", 80));
        tem.persist(new Product("NUT-3", 25));
        tem.flush();
        tem.clear();
        var hits = repo.findBySkuStartingWithOrderBySku("BOLT");
        assertThat(hits).extracting(Product::sku).containsExactly("BOLT-7");
    }
}

The real test classes

These are JUnit 5 test sources. They are not compiled or run by this page's build; run them with spring-boot-starter-test (and spring-boot-testcontainers plus a Docker daemon for the last one) on the test class path.

Test source — run with JUnit, not verified by this build.

javaProductRepositoryTest.java
@DataJpaTest
class ProductRepositoryTest {
 
    @Autowired TestEntityManager tem;
    @Autowired ProductRepository repo;
 
    @Test
    void rejectsDuplicateSku() {
        tem.persistAndFlush(new Product("BOLT-7", 80));
 
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> repo.saveAndFlush(new Product("BOLT-7", 90)))
            .isInstanceOf(DataIntegrityViolationException.class);   // flushed, so it really ran
    }
 
    @Test
    void roundTripsThroughTheMapping() {
        Long id = tem.persistAndGetId(new Product("CAM-9", 2300), Long.class);
        tem.clear();                                               // defeat the first-level cache
 
        assertThat(repo.findById(id)).get()
            .extracting(Product::priceInCents).isEqualTo(2300);
    }
}

Test source — run with JUnit, not verified by this build.

javaOrderQueriesTest.java
@DataJpaTest(properties = "spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.generate_statistics=true")
@Sql("/orders-with-lines.sql")                       // runs before each test, inside its transaction
class OrderQueriesTest {
 
    @Autowired OrderRepository orders;
    @Autowired EntityManagerFactory emf;
    @Autowired TestEntityManager tem;
 
    @Test
    void listingIsOneStatementNotNPlusOne() {
        Statistics stats = emf.unwrap(SessionFactory.class).getStatistics();
        tem.clear();
        stats.clear();
 
        orders.findAllWithLines().forEach(o -> o.getLines().size());
 
        assertThat(stats.getPrepareStatementCount()).isEqualTo(1);   // a regression guard for §6
    }
}

A statement-count assertion is the cheapest N+1 regression test there is: someone removing the @EntityGraph turns it red immediately, long before a slow page is noticed in production.

Test source — needs Docker; not verified by this build.

javaPostgresRepositoryTest.java
@DataJpaTest
@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = AutoConfigureTestDatabase.Replace.NONE)   // keep the real DataSource
@Testcontainers
class PostgresRepositoryTest {
 
    @Container
    @ServiceConnection                                  // Boot wires the container's URL, user and password
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres = new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:17-alpine");
 
    @Autowired ProductRepository repo;
 
    @Test
    void pessimisticLockUsesForUpdate() {
        // H2 and PostgreSQL disagree on locking, sequences, case sensitivity and
        // JSON types; this test runs against the database production uses.
    }
}

@ServiceConnection replaces the older @DynamicPropertySource boilerplate. A static container is started once per test class; with Boot's context caching and a shared base class, it is started once per test run.

Test source — run with JUnit, not verified by this build.

javaInventoryServiceIT.java
@SpringBootTest
@Transactional                                       // same rollback-per-test behaviour as the slice
class InventoryServiceIT {
 
    @Autowired InventoryService inventory;
    @Autowired StockLevelRepository stock;
 
    @Test
    void reserveDecrementsAndCommits() {
        inventory.reserve("BOLT-7", 3);
        TestTransaction.flagForCommit();            // this test wants its effect to persist
        TestTransaction.end();                      // commit now, then assert in a new transaction
        TestTransaction.start();
        assertThat(stock.findBySku("BOLT-7").orElseThrow().onHand()).isEqualTo(7);
    }
}

Mock collaborators of a service with @MockitoBean; do not mock repositories in a data-layer test, because the repository is the thing under test. A test that mocks the repository is a test of Mockito.

What the slice gives you

What @DataJpaTest configures, replaces and leaves out
ConfiguredReplaced by defaultLeft out
DataSource, Hibernate, JpaTransactionManager, repositories, TestEntityManager, Flyway/Liquibase if presentYour configured database, by an embedded one (H2, HSQLDB or Derby on the class path) — unless replace = NONE@Service, @Controller and other @Component beans; web; security
SQL logging on (showSql attribute, default true)Every test method's transaction, rolled backYour CommandLineRunners
Testing gotchas
  • No flush, no failure. A test that saves and never flushes never sends SQL, so constraint, length and mapping errors cannot happen. Use saveAndFlush or tem.flush() before asserting on anything the database decides.
  • No clear, no round trip. Loading what you just saved returns the same Java object. Clear the persistence context so the test exercises the mapping.
  • H2 is not your production database. It accepts syntax PostgreSQL rejects, locks differently, and has its own sequence and identity behaviour. Keep a Testcontainers suite against the real engine for queries, locking and migrations.
  • Rollback hides commit-time behaviour. @TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT) listeners (§8), deferred constraints and commit-time validation never run in a rolled-back test. Test those with @Commit or TestTransaction.end(), and clean up after.
  • Each distinct test configuration is a new context. Spring caches contexts between test classes with identical configuration; every different properties, @MockitoBean or profile builds another, and a suite of fast tests becomes a slow one.

Check yourself

1.In a @DataJpaTest, a test does repo.save(new Product("BOLT-7", 1)) when BOLT-7 already exists, then assertThat(repo.count()).isEqualTo(1). The SKU column is unique. What happens?

B. count() is a JPQL query on Product, and with flush mode AUTO Hibernate flushes pending changes to that entity first so the query sees them (JPA §7). The insert is sent then, the database rejects it, and the exception appears on a line that looks innocent. Had the test asserted nothing that queried Product, it would have passed — the worked example's step 3.

A: with SEQUENCE ids, save only queues the insert. C is what happens with no query before the rollback. D would require the database to accept a duplicate under a unique index.

2.A test saves a Product with a 20-character SKU into a length = 16 column, then loads it with findById and asserts the SKU matches. It passes on H2. Why is it worthless?

C. findById by primary key checks the persistence context first and returned the object the test had just saved (step 4 of the worked example). The too-long value never met the column. saveAndFlush plus clear() would have produced a DataIntegrityViolationException.

A: H2 rejects values too long for a varchar(16); it was simply never asked. B: it runs in the test's transaction, which is precisely why it shares the cache. D invents a mode that does not exist.

3.Which of these will a default, rolled-back @DataJpaTest fail to exercise? Select all that apply.

A and D. An after-commit listener needs a commit, which a rolled-back test never performs. And the slice does not load @Service beans at all, so the service and its transactional proxy are absent — use @SpringBootTest for that.

B is exactly what the slice is good at: the query runs for real. C: with a flush, the statement reaches the database inside the test, so the constraint fires.

Section 12

Configuration, profiles and production settings

Every program in this module has passed the same dozen properties to setDefaultProperties, and so far that has been treated as boilerplate. It is not. A Spring Boot application is shaped by its configuration more than by its code: the same jar behaves as a laptop sandbox, a CI fixture or a production service depending on which properties reach it, from where, and which one wins when two sources disagree. Most production incidents in the data layer trace back to a property — a pool too big for the database, ddl-auto left at update, show-sql logging every statement under load, a password in a properties file.

This section covers the machinery: the property sources and their precedence, profiles that switch beans and settings, type-safe binding with @ConfigurationProperties, how spring.jpa.* reaches Hibernate, how the Hikari pool should be sized, and how SQL initialisation interleaves with Hibernate's schema generation. It ends with the property set each environment should actually run with.

Worked example: one application, every configuration path

The program writes a three-line seed script, sets one JVM system property, then starts with the dev profile active. The runner prints what each mechanism resolved to.

javaProfiles.java
package lm.config;
 
import com.zaxxer.hikari.HikariDataSource;
import jakarta.persistence.*;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.Min;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.NotBlank;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Value;
import org.springframework.boot.CommandLineRunner;
import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.context.properties.ConfigurationProperties;
import org.springframework.boot.context.properties.EnableConfigurationProperties;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Profile;
import org.springframework.core.env.Environment;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaRepository;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.config.EnableJpaRepositories;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import org.springframework.validation.annotation.Validated;
 
import javax.sql.DataSource;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
 
@SpringBootApplication
@EnableJpaRepositories(considerNestedRepositories = true)
@EnableConfigurationProperties(Profiles.WarehouseProps.class)
public class Profiles {
 
    // ── a tiny entity so the data source and the seed script have something to hit ──
    @Entity(name = "Product")
    @Table(name = "product")
    public static class Product {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE) Long id;
        @Column(nullable = false, unique = true, length = 16) String sku;
        int priceInCents;
        protected Product() {}
    }
    public interface ProductRepository extends JpaRepository<Product, Long> {}
 
    // ── one interface, two implementations, one of them active per profile ──
    public interface PricingPolicy { String describe(); }
 
    @Component @Profile("dev")
    public static class ListPricePolicy implements PricingPolicy {
        public String describe() { return "list price, no rounding (dev)"; }
    }
    @Component @Profile("prod")
    public static class ContractPricePolicy implements PricingPolicy {
        public String describe() { return "contract price with psychological rounding (prod)"; }
    }
 
    // ── type-safe, validated configuration ──
    @ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "warehouse")
    @Validated
    public record WarehouseProps(@NotBlank String region,
                                 @Min(1) int reorderThreshold,
                                 List<String> prioritySkus) {}
 
    @Bean CommandLineRunner show(Environment env, PricingPolicy pricing, WarehouseProps props,
                                 DataSource dataSource, EntityManagerFactory emf, ProductRepository products,
                                 @Value("${warehouse.currency:EUR}") String currency) {
        return args -> {
            System.out.println("active profiles = " + String.join(",", env.getActiveProfiles()));
            System.out.println("pricing policy  = " + pricing.describe());
            System.out.println("props           = " + props);
            System.out.println("currency        = " + currency + "   (not set anywhere: the @Value default)");
 
            HikariDataSource hikari = (HikariDataSource) dataSource;
            System.out.println("pool            = " + hikari.getPoolName() + ", max " + hikari.getMaximumPoolSize()
                    + ", min idle " + hikari.getMinimumIdle());
            System.out.println("batch_size      = " + emf.getProperties().get("hibernate.jdbc.batch_size")
                    + "   (reached Hibernate through spring.jpa.properties.*)");
 
            System.out.println("seeded rows     = " + products.count() + "   (inserted by the spring.sql.init script, not by Hibernate)");
 
            System.out.println("warehouse.site  = " + env.getProperty("warehouse.site")
                    + "   (default properties said 'default-properties')");
            System.out.println("warehouse.region= " + env.getProperty("warehouse.region")
                    + "   (only the default properties define it)");
        };
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        // a seed script Spring Boot will run after Hibernate has created the schema
        Path seed = Path.of("warehouse-seed.sql");
        Files.writeString(seed, """
            insert into product (id, sku, price_in_cents) values (1, 'BOLT-7', 80);
            insert into product (id, sku, price_in_cents) values (2, 'NUT-3', 25);
            insert into product (id, sku, price_in_cents) values (3, 'CAM-9', 2300);
            """);
        // a system property outranks the application's default properties
        System.setProperty("warehouse.site", "system-property");
        try {
            SpringApplication app = new SpringApplication(Profiles.class);
            app.setDefaultProperties(Map.ofEntries(
                Map.entry("spring.main.web-application-type", "none"),
                Map.entry("spring.main.banner-mode", "off"),
                Map.entry("spring.main.log-startup-info", "false"),
                Map.entry("logging.level.root", "WARN"),
                Map.entry("logging.pattern.console", "%level %logger{0}: %msg%n"),
                Map.entry("spring.profiles.active", "dev"),
                Map.entry("spring.datasource.url", "jdbc:h2:mem:config;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1"),
                Map.entry("spring.datasource.hikari.pool-name", "warehouse-pool"),
                Map.entry("spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size", "4"),
                Map.entry("spring.datasource.hikari.minimum-idle", "1"),
                Map.entry("spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto", "create-drop"),
                Map.entry("spring.jpa.show-sql", "true"),
                Map.entry("spring.jpa.open-in-view", "false"),
                Map.entry("spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.jdbc.batch_size", "20"),
                Map.entry("spring.jpa.defer-datasource-initialization", "true"),
                Map.entry("spring.sql.init.mode", "always"),
                Map.entry("spring.sql.init.data-locations", "file:warehouse-seed.sql"),
                Map.entry("warehouse.region", "eu-west"),
                Map.entry("warehouse.reorder-threshold", "25"),
                Map.entry("warehouse.priority-skus", "BOLT-7,GIRD-1"),
                Map.entry("warehouse.site", "default-properties")));
            app.run(args).close();
        } finally {
            Files.deleteIfExists(seed);
        }
    }
}
Expected output
Hibernate: create global temporary table HTE_product(priceInCents integer, rn_ integer not null, id bigint, sku varchar(16), primary key (rn_)) transactional
Hibernate: drop table if exists product cascade
