Read it top to bottom against the configuration that produced it:

  • The DDL, then nothing. Hibernate creates the table, and the three seed rows appear without a single insert in the log. They were executed by Spring's spring.sql.init machinery straight through JDBC, so Hibernate's show_sql never saw them. If your seed data seems to load "silently", that is why.
  • active profiles = dev and pricing policy = list price…: two @Component classes implement PricingPolicy, and the runner asks for exactly one. That works only because @Profile("prod") kept the other one out of the context. Start with prod and you get the other bean; start with neither and the injection fails with NoSuchBeanDefinitionException, which is the right behaviour — no environment should run with an implicit pricing rule.
  • props = WarehouseProps[…]: three properties bound into an immutable, validated record. Note warehouse.reorder-threshold (kebab-case in the source) landed in reorderThreshold, and the comma-separated string became a List. Breaking @Min(1) fails startup, not the first request.
  • currency = EUR: no source defines warehouse.currency, so @Value("${warehouse.currency:EUR}") fell back to its default. Without the :EUR the context would refuse to start.
  • pool = warehouse-pool, max 4, min idle 1: the spring.datasource.hikari.* keys bind directly onto the HikariDataSource Spring Boot created.
  • batch_size = 20: spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.jdbc.batch_size was stripped of its spring.jpa.properties. prefix and handed to Hibernate verbatim — it is visible in the EntityManagerFactory's own property map.
  • warehouse.site = system-property: the default properties said default-properties, but System.setProperty outranks them. warehouse.region, defined only in the defaults, shows the defaults still apply wherever nothing overrides them.

Where a property comes from, and who wins

Spring Boot assembles one Environment from an ordered list of property sources and, for each key, takes the first match from the top. The list below runs from highest to lowest priority, abridged to the sources a data application actually uses:

  1. Test overrides: @DynamicPropertySource, @TestPropertySource, @SpringBootTest(properties = …) (§11).
  2. Command-line arguments: --spring.jpa.show-sql=true.
  3. SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON — a whole JSON document in one environment variable or system property.
  4. JVM system properties: -Dwarehouse.site=… or System.setProperty.
  5. OS environment variables: SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL=….
  6. Config files, where profile-specific beats plain and outside-the-jar beats inside: application-prod.properties next to the jar, then application.properties next to the jar, then the same two packaged inside it.
  7. @PropertySource on a configuration class.
  8. Default properties — SpringApplication.setDefaultProperties, which is all the programs in this module use.

The rule of thumb behind the order: the closer a source is to the person deploying, the more it wins. The jar's packaged application.properties holds sensible defaults, the deployment overrides them with environment variables or an external file, and a command-line flag overrides everything for one run. YAML (application.yml) is interchangeable with .properties; if both exist at the same location, .properties wins.

The property-precedence sandbox in §1 lets you tick sources on and off and watch which one wins; it is worth a second visit with this list beside it.

Relaxed binding and environment variables

Property names are matched loosely: warehouse.reorder-threshold, warehouse.reorderThreshold and warehouse.reorder_threshold all bind to the same field. Environment variables cannot contain dots or dashes, so they follow a fixed recipe — replace dots with underscores, drop the dashes, upper-case the lot:

SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/warehouse
SPRING_DATASOURCE_HIKARI_MAXIMUMPOOLSIZE=8        # spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size
SPRING_JPA_OPENINVIEW=false                       # spring.jpa.open-in-view
WAREHOUSE_REORDERTHRESHOLD=25                     # warehouse.reorder-threshold
WAREHOUSE_PRIORITYSKUS=BOLT-7,GIRD-1              # a list, comma-separated

The recipe only works for keys bound to a @ConfigurationProperties class; a plain @Value("${warehouse.reorder-threshold}") looks up the canonical name, which still resolves from an environment variable, but uncommon forms are easy to get wrong. That is one of several reasons to prefer type-safe binding.

Profiles

A profile is a named switch. It does two jobs: it selects which beans exist (@Profile("dev") on a component or @Bean method, with negation @Profile("!prod") and expressions @Profile("dev & local")), and it selects which config files load (application-dev.properties layered over application.properties). Activate profiles with spring.profiles.active=prod — as an environment variable SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod in a real deployment.

  • Groups name a set: spring.profiles.group.prod=prod-db,prod-cache lets you activate prod and get both, so the deployment does not have to know the decomposition.
  • spring.profiles.include unconditionally adds profiles from inside a config file; groups are usually clearer.
  • Profiles are for environments, not features. A profile per customer or per feature flag multiplies combinations nobody tests. Use a @ConfigurationProperties flag for a feature, and keep profiles to dev, test, prod and the occasional local.

@ConfigurationProperties versus @Value

Comparison of ConfigurationProperties and Value injection
@ConfigurationProperties@Value
GranularityA group of related keys under one prefix, as a record or classOne key per field or parameter
Type safetyBinds to int, Duration (30s), DataSize (10MB), lists, maps, nested recordsString conversion per key; collections need SpEL
Validation@Validated + Bean Validation, checked at startupNone
Relaxed bindingFullLimited — use the canonical kebab-case name
IDE metadataGenerated by spring-boot-configuration-processor: autocomplete and docs in application.propertiesNone
Use it forAnything your application owns: warehouse.*A single value in a single place, with a default

A record is the natural shape: immutable, constructor-bound, no setters to call by accident. Register it with @EnableConfigurationProperties(WarehouseProps.class) as the program does, or with @ConfigurationPropertiesScan on the application class to pick up every annotated record in the package.

How spring.jpa.* reaches Hibernate

There are two families of keys and confusing them is a common, silent bug:

  • spring.jpa.* and spring.jpa.hibernate.* bind to Spring Boot's own JpaProperties class, which knows a fixed set: show-sql, open-in-view, database-platform, defer-datasource-initialization, hibernate.ddl-auto, hibernate.naming.*. Boot translates them into Hibernate settings.
  • spring.jpa.properties.* is a pass-through map. Everything after the prefix goes to Hibernate unchanged — spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.jdbc.batch_size becomes hibernate.jdbc.batch_size, as the output showed.

So spring.jpa.hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=20, which looks right, matches nothing: JpaProperties.Hibernate has no such field, and nothing complains. If a Hibernate setting from JPA §9 seems to have no effect, check the prefix first.

The connection pool

Spring Boot picks HikariCP when it is on the class path, which spring-boot-starter-data-jpa guarantees. The knobs that matter:

HikariCP settings and their meaning
Property (spring.datasource.hikari.…)DefaultWhat it controls
maximum-pool-size10The hard cap on open connections per application instance. The number to size.
minimum-idlesame as maxIdle connections kept ready. Hikari recommends leaving it equal to the maximum: a fixed-size pool never has to open connections during a traffic spike.
connection-timeout30 sHow long a thread waits for a free connection before SQLTransientConnectionException. Lower it so an exhausted pool fails fast instead of piling up waiting requests.
max-lifetime30 minRetires each connection after this long. Must be shorter than any timeout the database, firewall or proxy applies, or the pool hands out connections that were already cut.
idle-timeout10 minRetires idle connections above minimum-idle; irrelevant for a fixed-size pool.
leak-detection-thresholdoffLogs a stack trace when a connection is held longer than this — the way to find the code that never returns one. A diagnostic, not a permanent setting.

Bigger is not better. A database server with eight cores runs eight things at once; give it eighty connections and seventy-two of them queue inside the database instead of inside the pool, where they also contend for locks and memory. HikariCP's starting formula — cores × 2 + effective spindle count — is a budget for the whole database, so it must be shared by every instance of every service that connects to it. Then check the demand side with Little's law: connections busy at once equals requests per second times the database time per request.

Size the pool for this deployment

SQL initialisation and Hibernate's schema

Spring Boot can run SQL scripts at startup: schema.sql and data.sql from the class path by default, or the files named in spring.sql.init.schema-locations / data-locations. Two settings decide whether and when:

  • spring.sql.init.mode — embedded (the default: only for H2, HSQLDB and Derby), always, or never. The default is deliberate: scripts that recreate data are a convenience for an in-memory database and a hazard for a real one.
  • spring.jpa.defer-datasource-initialization — by default the scripts run before the EntityManagerFactory exists, which suits a hand-written schema.sql. If Hibernate generates the schema (ddl-auto), a data.sql that inserts into its tables needs true, or it runs against tables that do not exist yet. The program sets it for exactly that reason.

In production neither mechanism should own the schema: a migration tool should. Put Flyway or Liquibase on the class path and Spring Boot runs it before JPA starts, configured under spring.flyway.* or spring.liquibase.*, with migrations in db/migration. Combine it with ddl-auto=validate so Hibernate checks the migrated schema against the entities (JPA §10). Do not mix script-based initialisation with a migration tool; choose one owner for the schema.

A property set per environment

bashapplication-dev.properties
# a real database in a container (docker compose, or Boot's Testcontainers dev-time support)
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/warehouse
spring.datasource.username=warehouse
spring.datasource.password=dev-only-password
 
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate        # the migrations own the schema even locally
spring.jpa.open-in-view=false
spring.jpa.show-sql=false                     # use the logger below: it can be turned on per package
logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=debug         # every statement
logging.level.org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.bind=trace   # and its bound parameters
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.generate_statistics=true

Developing against the same database engine as production is the single cheapest way to avoid "works on H2" surprises. Statistics on locally means N+1 regressions show up in a log line, not a production graph.

bashapplication-test.properties
# the datasource itself comes from @ServiceConnection on a Testcontainers PostgreSQL (§11)
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate        # migrations run first; this proves they match the entities
spring.jpa.open-in-view=false
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.generate_statistics=true   # tests assert statement counts
spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=4  # tests are not load tests
logging.level.root=WARN

CI is where validate earns its keep: a migration that forgot a column fails the build, not the deployment.

bashapplication-prod.properties
# url, username and password arrive as environment variables or from a secret store — never here
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate        # or none; never update, never create
spring.jpa.open-in-view=false
spring.jpa.show-sql=false
 
spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=8  # sized for the database, divided by instance count
spring.datasource.hikari.minimum-idle=8
spring.datasource.hikari.connection-timeout=3000
spring.datasource.hikari.max-lifetime=1740000 # just under a 30-minute server or proxy timeout
 
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.order_inserts=true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.order_updates=true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size=16   # the N+1 safety net from §6
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.generate_statistics=false     # it has a cost; enable briefly to diagnose

Nothing here is environment-specific secret material, so the file can live in the repository. Health and pool metrics come from Spring Boot Actuator (/actuator/health, hikaricp.connections.* metrics) once it is added.

Secrets

A database password in application.properties is committed to version control, copied into every build artefact and readable by anyone with the jar. Supply it at runtime instead: an environment variable (SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD) injected by the platform, a mounted file imported with spring.config.import=configtree:/run/secrets/, or a secret store such as Vault through its Spring integration. The property name stays the same; only the source changes — which is precisely what the precedence list is for.

Configuration gotchas
  • Seed rows with explicit ids collide with the sequence. The program's script inserted ids 1, 2 and 3 directly. The first entity Hibernate persists afterwards asks product_seq for a value, gets 1, and fails on the primary key. Either let seed scripts call the sequence (next value for product_seq), restart the sequence after seeding, or seed through the application.
  • A misspelt key is silently ignored. spring.jpa.hibernate.jdbc.batch_size, spring.datasource.hikari.max-pool-size and spring.jpa.open_in_view all bind to nothing. Your own @ConfigurationProperties classes can opt into strictness with ignoreUnknownFields = false; Spring's own keys cannot, so verify the effective value, as the program does.
  • Every instance has its own pool. Ten pods with the default pool of 10 open 100 connections, which is PostgreSQL's entire default max_connections. A rolling deployment briefly doubles it.
  • spring.profiles.active in a packaged application.properties sets the profile for every environment that does not override it, including production if someone forgets. Leave it out of the jar and set it where the application is deployed.
  • An @Profile that matches no active profile removes the bean. If the only implementation of an interface is @Profile("prod"), every other environment fails at startup. That is usually what you want; make sure it is not a surprise.

Check yourself

1.warehouse.site is set in the packaged application.properties, as an environment variable WAREHOUSE_SITE, as a system property -Dwarehouse.site, and as a command-line argument --warehouse.site. Which value does Environment.getProperty return?

D. Command-line arguments sit above every other runtime source; only test overrides rank higher. The order follows who is closest to this particular run: the person typing the command beats the deployment, which beats the build.

A is the lowest of the four — a packaged file holds defaults meant to be overridden. B loses to system properties, which are more specific to one JVM than the process environment. C would win if the command-line argument were absent; the worked example showed a system property beating the default properties for the same reason.

2.An application uses spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=create-drop on H2 and has a data.sql that inserts into the product table Hibernate generates. It does not set spring.jpa.defer-datasource-initialization. What happens at startup?

B. By default script initialisation runs before the EntityManagerFactory is built, so the insert targets a table that does not exist and the context fails to start. Setting spring.jpa.defer-datasource-initialization=true moves the scripts after Hibernate's schema generation, which is why the worked example sets it.

A describes the deferred behaviour, not the default. C is wrong for H2: the default mode embedded does run scripts against an in-memory database; always is needed only for a real one. D gets the order backwards — and Hibernate's drop happens at shutdown, not after the scripts.

3.Which line actually changes Hibernate's JDBC batch size?

C. spring.jpa.properties.* is the pass-through map: the remainder of the key reaches Hibernate unchanged. The worked example read it back from the EntityManagerFactory as batch_size = 20.

A looks plausible but binds to Spring Boot's JpaProperties.Hibernate, which knows only ddl-auto and the naming strategies, so it is silently ignored. B is not a key anything binds to. D sits in Spring's Environment, but nothing copies arbitrary hibernate.* keys from the environment into the persistence unit — only the spring.jpa.properties prefix does that.

4.Twelve instances of a service each use Hikari's default pool against a PostgreSQL server with 8 cores and max_connections = 100. Response times rise sharply under load. Which changes help? Select all that apply.

A and D. Twelve pools of 10 ask for 120 connections from a server that can usefully run about 17 (8 × 2 + 1) and refuses beyond 100. Shrinking the pools moves the queue out of the database, where waiting connections compete for CPU and locks, into the pool, where waiting is cheap. Reducing database time per request lowers the demand side of Little's law directly.

B makes it worse: 600 requested connections, most refused, and the rest contending inside an overloaded server. C only lets requests wait longer before failing; it hides the saturation and lets threads pile up behind it.

Put it together

Hands-on lab: the warehouse as a Spring Boot service

Six steps that rebuild the JPA module's lab as a Spring application, each exercising a part of this module. Write each step before opening its solution. The steps share one application class, so by the end you have a single runnable program; the assembled version follows, compiled and run during the build of this page.

Starter
node tools/fetch-deps.mjs java-spring-data        # once: resolves Spring Boot 4.1.1 into build/lib/java-spring-data
mkdir -p lab/lm/lab && cd lab
# write lm/lab/SpringWarehouseLab.java as you go
javac -d classes -cp "../build/lib/java-spring-data/*" lm/lab/SpringWarehouseLab.java
java -cp "classes;../build/lib/java-spring-data/*" lm.lab.SpringWarehouseLab      # ':' instead of ';' on macOS/Linux

Start from the bootstrap shape every program in this module uses: @SpringBootApplication, @EnableJpaRepositories(considerNestedRepositories = true), a CommandLineRunner, and the deterministic property set from the How-to-use section. Add spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.generate_statistics=true; you will need it in step 4.

Step 1 — entities and derived queries §2, §3

Map Product (unique sku, name, a Category enum stored as a string, priceInCents, an active flag), StockLevel (sharing the product's primary key, with a @Version), and an order with lines kept in sync by a helper. Give ProductRepository three derived queries: look up by SKU, list a category sorted by SKU, and test whether a SKU exists.

Solution — step 1
@Entity(name = "StockLevel") @Table(name = "stock_level")
public static class StockLevel {
    @Id Long id;
    @OneToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY) @MapsId Product product;   // id = the product's id
    int onHand;
    @Version long version;                                        // optimistic locking in step 3
}
 
@Entity(name = "PurchaseOrder") @Table(name = "purchase_order")  // ORDER is a reserved word in SQL
public static class PurchaseOrder {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE) Long id;
    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "order", cascade = CascadeType.ALL, orphanRemoval = true)
    List<OrderLine> lines = new ArrayList<>();
    void addLine(Product p, int qty) { lines.add(new OrderLine(this, p, qty)); }   // sets both sides
}
 
public interface ProductRepository extends JpaRepository<Product, Long> {
    Optional<Product> findBySku(String sku);
    List<Product> findByCategoryOrderBySkuAsc(Category category);
    boolean existsBySku(String sku);
}

@MapsId makes the stock row's primary key the product's id, so there is no separate sequence and no join column to keep consistent. The entity is called PurchaseOrder because order is a reserved word; mapping a table called order works only with quoted identifiers, which then leak into every native query.

Step 2 — declared queries and projections §4

Add three repository methods: revenue per category as a record DTO, products whose stock is below a threshold as an interface projection, and a bulk reprice(category, delta) that adds delta cents to every product in a category and returns the row count.

Solution — step 2
public record CategoryRevenue(Category category, long cents) {}
public interface LowStock { String getSku(); int getOnHand(); }
 
@Query("select new lm.lab.SpringWarehouseLab$CategoryRevenue(p.category, sum(l.qty * p.priceInCents)) " +
       "from OrderLine l join l.product p group by p.category order by p.category")
List<CategoryRevenue> revenueByCategory();
 
@Query("select p.sku as sku, s.onHand as onHand from StockLevel s join s.product p " +
       "where s.onHand < :threshold order by p.sku")
List<LowStock> lowStock(@Param("threshold") int threshold);
 
@Transactional                                   // without it: TransactionRequiredException
@Modifying(clearAutomatically = true)
@Query("update Product p set p.priceInCents = p.priceInCents + :delta where p.category = :category")
int reprice(@Param("category") Category category, @Param("delta") int delta);

The @Transactional on reprice is not decoration. Spring Data runs a repository's query methods in a read-only transaction by default; an update or delete query there fails with No active transaction for update or delete query. The first draft of this lab hit exactly that. Either annotate the method, as here, or call it from a @Transactional service. The $ in the DTO's name is the binary name of a nested record (§4).

Step 3 — a transactional reservation with a retry §5

Write InventoryService.reserve(sku, qty): load the stock level, refuse with an exception if there is not enough, otherwise decrement — no explicit save. Then make a stale read fail and recover: one method loads the row, lets a second picker reserve the same SKU in its own committed transaction, then decrements. Wrap it in a gateway on a separate bean that retries once on OptimisticLockingFailureException.

Solution — step 3
@Service
public static class InventoryService {
    @Transactional
    public int reserve(String sku, int qty) {
        StockLevel level = stock.findByProductSku(sku).orElseThrow();
        if (level.onHand < qty) throw new OutOfStock("only " + level.onHand + " of " + sku);
        level.onHand -= qty;                 // dirty checking: update ... where id=? and version=?
        return level.onHand;
    }
 
    @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
    public int reserveElsewhere(String sku, int qty) { return reserve(sku, qty); }   // a second picker
 
    @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
    public int reserveWithInterference(String sku, int qty, Runnable interference) {
        StockLevel level = stock.findByProductSku(sku).orElseThrow();   // reads version 0
        if (interference != null) interference.run();                  // someone else commits version 1
        level.onHand -= qty;                                            // update where version=0: 0 rows
        return level.onHand;
    }
}
 
@Component
public static class ReservationGateway {           // a SEPARATE bean, so each attempt goes through the proxy
    public String reserveWithRetry(String sku, int qty, Runnable firstAttemptInterference) {
        for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
            try {
                int left = inventory.reserveWithInterference(sku, qty, attempt == 1 ? firstAttemptInterference : null);
                return "attempts: " + attempt + ", left: " + left;
            } catch (OptimisticLockingFailureException e) {
                if (attempt == 3) throw e;
            }
        }
    }
}

Three proxy rules from §5 decide whether this works. The interfering picker must be REQUIRES_NEW; a plain @Transactional method would join the attempt's transaction, share its persistence context and never conflict. The retry loop must live on another bean, or each attempt is a self-invocation that bypasses the proxy and runs in one transaction. And the exception surfaces at commit, which happens when reserveWithInterference returns through its proxy — so the catch belongs in the caller, not inside the method.

Step 4 — an N+1-free listing and a page of summaries §6, §7

List every order with its lines and their products, walking the whole graph, in one SQL statement — prove the count with Hibernate's statistics. Then return the first page of order totals, two per page, as an interface projection with an explicit count query.

Solution — step 4
@EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"lines", "lines.product"})
@Query("select o from PurchaseOrder o order by o.id")
List<PurchaseOrder> findAllWithLines();
 
public interface OrderSummary { Long getId(); long getTotal(); }
 
@Query(value = "select o.id as id, sum(l.qty * p.priceInCents) as total from PurchaseOrder o " +
               "join o.lines l join l.product p group by o.id order by o.id",
       countQuery = "select count(o) from PurchaseOrder o")
Page<OrderSummary> summaries(Pageable pageable);
 
// in the runner
Statistics stats = emf.unwrap(SessionFactory.class).getStatistics();
stats.clear();
List<PurchaseOrder> all = orders.findAllWithLines();
// ... walk o.lines and l.product ...
System.out.println("statements = " + stats.getPrepareStatementCount());   // 1

The entity graph turns the lazy lines and lines.product into joins on this one query only, leaving the mapping lazy everywhere else. The explicit countQuery matters for Page: Spring Data's derived count of a group by query would count groups through a subquery at best, and a fetch-joined page would be paginated in memory (§7).

Step 5 — auditing, events and a dynamic search §8, §9

Stamp createdAt and createdBy on products automatically, with a fixed auditor. Publish an OrderPlaced event from an order service and count deliveries in a listener that runs only after commit. Finally, search products with a Specification combining category, a price range and the active flag.

Solution — step 5
@EnableJpaAuditing                                   // on the application class
@EntityListeners(AuditingEntityListener.class)       // on Product
@CreatedDate Instant createdAt;
@CreatedBy String createdBy;
@Bean AuditorAware<String> auditor() { return () -> Optional.of("picker-bot"); }
 
@Transactional
public Long place(LocalDate placed, LinkedHashMap<Product, Integer> items) {
    PurchaseOrder order = new PurchaseOrder(placed);
    items.forEach(order::addLine);
    orders.save(order);
    events.publishEvent(new OrderPlaced(order.id, order.lines.size()));
    return order.id;
}
 
@TransactionalEventListener(phase = TransactionPhase.AFTER_COMMIT)
public void on(OrderPlaced event) { delivered.incrementAndGet(); }
 
public interface ProductRepository extends JpaRepository<Product, Long>, JpaSpecificationExecutor<Product> { … }
 
static Specification<Product> inCategory(Category c) { return (root, q, cb) -> cb.equal(root.get("category"), c); }
static Specification<Product> priceBetween(int lo, int hi) { return (root, q, cb) -> cb.between(root.get("priceInCents"), lo, hi); }
static Specification<Product> active() { return (root, q, cb) -> cb.isTrue(root.get("active")); }
 
products.findAll(inCategory(FASTENER).and(priceBetween(0, 50)).and(active()), Sort.by("sku"));

The event is published inside the transaction but the listener is held until commit. Had place thrown after publishEvent, the order would have rolled back and the listener would never have run — exactly the guarantee you want before sending a confirmation email. The LinkedHashMap is deliberate: Map.of has no defined iteration order, so line ids could differ between runs.

Step 6 — validation and configuration §10, §12

Put @NotBlank on the SKU and @Positive on the price, and show that an invalid product is rejected before it reaches the table. Bind the low-stock threshold used in step 2 from a warehouse.reorder-threshold property into a @ConfigurationProperties record.

Solution — step 6
@NotBlank @Column(nullable = false, unique = true, length = 16) String sku;
@Positive int priceInCents;
 
try {
    products.saveAndFlush(new Product("  ", "Nameless", Category.MOTION, 0));
} catch (ConstraintViolationException e) {
    List<String> paths = e.getConstraintViolations().stream()
        .map(v -> v.getPropertyPath().toString()).sorted().toList();     // [priceInCents, sku]
}
 
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "warehouse")
public record LabProps(int reorderThreshold) {}
@EnableConfigurationProperties(SpringWarehouseLab.LabProps.class)        // on the application class
// warehouse.reorder-threshold=20 in the properties

Hibernate Validator runs on the persist event, so the insert is never issued: the table still holds four products afterwards. Sorting the property paths keeps the output stable; a Set of violations has no defined order.

The finished thing

All six steps in one application. The program runs with show-sql off: four entities' worth of DDL plus every statement of every step would bury the results, and the two claims that depend on SQL — one statement for the listing, a retry after a stale write — are proved more precisely by Hibernate's statistics and by the exception the retry catches. Turn show-sql on locally to watch the versioned update fail.

javaSpringWarehouseLab.java

import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;
 
@SpringBootApplication
@EnableJpaRepositories(considerNestedRepositories = true)
@EnableJpaAuditing
@EnableConfigurationProperties(SpringWarehouseLab.LabProps.class)
public class SpringWarehouseLab {
 
    // ── step 1: entities ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
    public enum Category { FASTENER, STRUCTURAL, MOTION }
 
    @Entity(name = "Product") @Table(name = "product")
    @EntityListeners(AuditingEntityListener.class)
    public static class Product {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE) Long id;
        @NotBlank @Column(nullable = false, unique = true, length = 16) String sku;
        @Column(nullable = false) String name;
        @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING) @Column(nullable = false, length = 16) Category category;
        @Positive int priceInCents;
        boolean active = true;
        @CreatedDate Instant createdAt;
        @CreatedBy String createdBy;
        protected Product() {}
        Product(String sku, String name, Category category, int priceInCents) {
            this.sku = sku; this.name = name; this.category = category; this.priceInCents = priceInCents;
        }
        @Override public String toString() { return sku + "@" + priceInCents; }
    }
 
    @Entity(name = "StockLevel") @Table(name = "stock_level")
    public static class StockLevel {
        @Id Long id;
        @OneToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY) @MapsId Product product;
        int onHand;
        @Version long version;
        protected StockLevel() {}
        StockLevel(Product product, int onHand) { this.product = product; this.onHand = onHand; }
    }
 
    @Entity(name = "PurchaseOrder") @Table(name = "purchase_order")
    public static class PurchaseOrder {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE) Long id;
        @Column(nullable = false) LocalDate placed;
        @OneToMany(mappedBy = "order", cascade = CascadeType.ALL, orphanRemoval = true)
        List<OrderLine> lines = new ArrayList<>();
        protected PurchaseOrder() {}
        PurchaseOrder(LocalDate placed) { this.placed = placed; }
        void addLine(Product p, int qty) { OrderLine l = new OrderLine(this, p, qty); lines.add(l); }
    }
 
    @Entity(name = "OrderLine") @Table(name = "order_line")
    public static class OrderLine {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE) Long id;
        @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false) PurchaseOrder order;
        @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false) Product product;
        int qty;
        protected OrderLine() {}
        OrderLine(PurchaseOrder order, Product product, int qty) { this.order = order; this.product = product; this.qty = qty; }
    }
 
    // ── step 2: repositories, projections, a modifying query ─────────────
    public record CategoryRevenue(Category category, long cents) {}
    public interface LowStock { String getSku(); int getOnHand(); }
    public interface OrderSummary { Long getId(); long getTotal(); }
 
    public interface ProductRepository extends JpaRepository<Product, Long>, JpaSpecificationExecutor<Product> {
        Optional<Product> findBySku(String sku);
        List<Product> findByCategoryOrderBySkuAsc(Category category);
        boolean existsBySku(String sku);
 
        @org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.Query("select new lm.lab.SpringWarehouseLab$CategoryRevenue(p.category, sum(l.qty * p.priceInCents)) " +
               "from OrderLine l join l.product p group by p.category order by p.category")
        List<CategoryRevenue> revenueByCategory();
 
        @org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.Query("select p.sku as sku, s.onHand as onHand from StockLevel s join s.product p " +
               "where s.onHand < :threshold order by p.sku")
        List<LowStock> lowStock(@Param("threshold") int threshold);
 
        @Transactional                       // repository query methods are read-only by default
        @Modifying(clearAutomatically = true)
        @org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.Query("update Product p set p.priceInCents = p.priceInCents + :delta where p.category = :category")
        int reprice(@Param("category") Category category, @Param("delta") int delta);
    }
 
    public interface StockRepository extends JpaRepository<StockLevel, Long> {
        Optional<StockLevel> findByProductSku(String sku);
    }
 
    public interface OrderRepository extends JpaRepository<PurchaseOrder, Long> {
        @org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"lines", "lines.product"})
        @org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.Query("select o from PurchaseOrder o order by o.id")
        List<PurchaseOrder> findAllWithLines();
 
        @org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.Query(value = "select o.id as id, sum(l.qty * p.priceInCents) as total from PurchaseOrder o " +
                       "join o.lines l join l.product p group by o.id order by o.id",
               countQuery = "select count(o) from PurchaseOrder o")
        Page<OrderSummary> summaries(Pageable pageable);
    }
 
    // ── step 3: a transactional service with an optimistic retry ──────────
    public static class OutOfStock extends RuntimeException {
        OutOfStock(String msg) { super(msg); }
    }
 
    @Service
    public static class InventoryService {
        private final StockRepository stock;
        InventoryService(StockRepository stock) { this.stock = stock; }
 
        @Transactional
        public int reserve(String sku, int qty) {
            StockLevel level = stock.findByProductSku(sku).orElseThrow();
            if (level.onHand < qty) throw new OutOfStock("only " + level.onHand + " of " + sku);
            level.onHand -= qty;                       // dirty checking issues the versioned update at commit
            return level.onHand;
        }
 
        /* A second picker: its own transaction, committed before it returns. */
        @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
        public int reserveElsewhere(String sku, int qty) { return reserve(sku, qty); }
 
        /* Loads the row, then lets `interference` run in its own committed
           transaction, then updates — exactly what a concurrent picker does. */
        @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
        public int reserveWithInterference(String sku, int qty, Runnable interference) {
            StockLevel level = stock.findByProductSku(sku).orElseThrow();
            if (interference != null) interference.run();
            if (level.onHand < qty) throw new OutOfStock("only " + level.onHand + " of " + sku);
            level.onHand -= qty;
            return level.onHand;
        }
    }
 
    @Component
    public static class ReservationGateway {
        private final InventoryService inventory;
        ReservationGateway(InventoryService inventory) { this.inventory = inventory; }
 
        public String reserveWithRetry(String sku, int qty, Runnable firstAttemptInterference) {
            for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
                try {
                    int left = inventory.reserveWithInterference(sku, qty, attempt == 1 ? firstAttemptInterference : null);
                    return "attempts: " + attempt + ", left: " + left;
                } catch (OptimisticLockingFailureException e) {
                    if (attempt == 3) throw e;
                    System.out.println("  attempt " + attempt + " failed with " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ", retrying");
                }
            }
        }
    }
 
    // ── step 5: auditing, domain events, specifications ───────────────────
    public record OrderPlaced(Long orderId, int lineCount) {}
 
    @Service
    public static class OrderService {
        private final OrderRepository orders;
        private final ApplicationEventPublisher events;
        OrderService(OrderRepository orders, ApplicationEventPublisher events) { this.orders = orders; this.events = events; }
 
        @Transactional
        public Long place(LocalDate placed, LinkedHashMap<Product, Integer> items) {
            PurchaseOrder order = new PurchaseOrder(placed);
            items.forEach(order::addLine);
            orders.save(order);
            events.publishEvent(new OrderPlaced(order.id, order.lines.size()));   // delivered only after commit
            return order.id;
        }
    }
 
    @Component
    public static class OrderPlacedListener {
        final AtomicInteger delivered = new AtomicInteger();
        @TransactionalEventListener(phase = TransactionPhase.AFTER_COMMIT)
        public void on(OrderPlaced event) { delivered.incrementAndGet(); }
    }
 
    static Specification<Product> inCategory(Category c) { return (root, q, cb) -> cb.equal(root.get("category"), c); }
    static Specification<Product> priceBetween(int lo, int hi) { return (root, q, cb) -> cb.between(root.get("priceInCents"), lo, hi); }
    static Specification<Product> active() { return (root, q, cb) -> cb.isTrue(root.get("active")); }
 
    // ── step 6: configuration ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    @ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "warehouse")
    public record LabProps(int reorderThreshold) {}
 
    @Bean org.springframework.data.domain.AuditorAware<String> auditor() { return () -> Optional.of("picker-bot"); }
 
    /* Map.of has no defined iteration order; a LinkedHashMap keeps line ids stable. */
    static LinkedHashMap<Product, Integer> lines(Object... pairs) {
        LinkedHashMap<Product, Integer> m = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < pairs.length; i += 2) m.put((Product) pairs[i], (Integer) pairs[i + 1]);
        return m;
    }
 
    // ── the run ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    @Bean CommandLineRunner run(ProductRepository products, StockRepository stock, OrderRepository orders,
                                InventoryService inventory, ReservationGateway gateway, OrderService orderService,
                                OrderPlacedListener listener, LabProps props, EntityManagerFactory emf) {
        return args -> {
            Statistics stats = emf.unwrap(SessionFactory.class).getStatistics();
 
            // step 1 — seed through repositories
            Product bolt = products.save(new Product("BOLT-7", "Hex bolt M7", Category.FASTENER, 80));
            Product nut = products.save(new Product("NUT-3", "Nut M3", Category.FASTENER, 25));
            Product gird = products.save(new Product("GIRD-1", "Girder 1m", Category.STRUCTURAL, 120_000));
            Product cam = products.save(new Product("CAM-9", "Cam follower", Category.MOTION, 2_300));
            stock.saveAll(List.of(new StockLevel(bolt, 400), new StockLevel(nut, 12), new StockLevel(gird, 3), new StockLevel(cam, 30)));
            System.out.println("step 1  products        = " + products.count() + ", stock rows = " + stock.count());
            System.out.println("step 1  fasteners       = " + products.findByCategoryOrderBySkuAsc(Category.FASTENER));
            System.out.println("step 1  exists NUT-3    = " + products.existsBySku("NUT-3") + ", exists ROD-4 = " + products.existsBySku("ROD-4"));
            System.out.println("step 1  findBySku       = " + products.findBySku("CAM-9").map(p -> p.name).orElse("?"));
 
            // step 5 (events need orders) — place three orders
            orderService.place(LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 1), lines(bolt, 10, nut, 4));
            orderService.place(LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 2), lines(gird, 1));
            orderService.place(LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 3), lines(cam, 2, bolt, 5));
            System.out.println("step 5  events after commit = " + listener.delivered.get());
 
            // step 2 — projections and a modifying query
            System.out.println("step 2  revenue         = " + products.revenueByCategory());
            products.lowStock(props.reorderThreshold()).forEach(l ->
                System.out.println("step 2  low stock       = " + l.getSku() + " on hand " + l.getOnHand() + " (threshold " + props.reorderThreshold() + ")"));
            System.out.println("step 2  repriced rows   = " + products.reprice(Category.FASTENER, 5));
            System.out.println("step 2  after reprice   = " + products.findByCategoryOrderBySkuAsc(Category.FASTENER));
 
            // step 3 — reservations
            System.out.println("step 3  reserve 3 GIRD  = " + inventory.reserve("GIRD-1", 3) + " left");
            try { inventory.reserve("GIRD-1", 1); }
            catch (OutOfStock e) { System.out.println("step 3  refused         = " + e.getMessage()); }
            String outcome = gateway.reserveWithRetry("BOLT-7", 50, () -> inventory.reserveElsewhere("BOLT-7", 1));
            System.out.println("step 3  retry outcome   = " + outcome + "   (399 after the interfering picker, then 349)");
            System.out.println("step 3  version BOLT-7  = " + stock.findByProductSku("BOLT-7").orElseThrow().version);
 
            // step 4 — N+1-free listing and a projection page
            stats.clear();
            List<PurchaseOrder> all = orders.findAllWithLines();
            int lineTotal = 0;
            for (PurchaseOrder o : all) for (OrderLine l : o.lines) lineTotal += l.qty * l.product.priceInCents;
            System.out.println("step 4  orders          = " + all.size() + ", lines walked = " + all.stream().mapToInt(o -> o.lines.size()).sum()
                    + ", statements = " + stats.getPrepareStatementCount());
            Page<OrderSummary> page = orders.summaries(PageRequest.of(0, 2));
            System.out.println("step 4  page 0/2        = " + page.getContent().stream().map(s -> s.getId() + "=" + s.getTotal()).toList()
                    + ", total elements " + page.getTotalElements() + ", pages " + page.getTotalPages());
 
            // step 5 — auditing and specifications
            Product audited = products.findBySku("BOLT-7").orElseThrow();
            System.out.println("step 5  audit           = createdBy " + audited.createdBy + ", createdAt set " + (audited.createdAt != null));
            Specification<Product> spec = inCategory(Category.FASTENER).and(priceBetween(0, 50)).and(active());
            System.out.println("step 5  spec search     = " + products.findAll(spec, Sort.by("sku")));
 
            // step 6 — validation at the boundary
            try {
                products.saveAndFlush(new Product("  ", "Nameless", Category.MOTION, 0));
            } catch (ConstraintViolationException e) {
                List<String> paths = e.getConstraintViolations().stream().map(ConstraintViolation::getPropertyPath).map(Object::toString).sorted().toList();
                System.out.println("step 6  rejected        = " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " on " + paths);
            }
            System.out.println("step 6  products        = " + products.count() + "   (the invalid one never reached the table)");
        };
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication app = new SpringApplication(SpringWarehouseLab.class);
        app.setDefaultProperties(Map.ofEntries(
            Map.entry("spring.main.web-application-type", "none"),
            Map.entry("spring.main.banner-mode", "off"),
            Map.entry("spring.main.log-startup-info", "false"),
            Map.entry("logging.level.root", "WARN"),
            Map.entry("logging.pattern.console", "%level %logger{0}: %msg%n"),
            Map.entry("spring.datasource.url", "jdbc:h2:mem:springlab;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1"),
            Map.entry("spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto", "create-drop"),
            Map.entry("spring.jpa.show-sql", "false"),
            Map.entry("spring.jpa.open-in-view", "false"),
            Map.entry("spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.generate_statistics", "true"),
            Map.entry("warehouse.reorder-threshold", "20")));
        app.run(args).close();
    }
}
Expected output
step 1  products        = 4, stock rows = 4
step 1  fasteners       = [BOLT-7@80, NUT-3@25]
step 1  exists NUT-3    = true, exists ROD-4 = false
step 1  findBySku       = Cam follower
step 5  events after commit = 3
step 2  revenue         = [CategoryRevenue[category=FASTENER, cents=1300], CategoryRevenue[category=MOTION, cents=4600], CategoryRevenue[category=STRUCTURAL, cents=120000]]
step 2  low stock       = GIRD-1 on hand 3 (threshold 20)
step 2  low stock       = NUT-3 on hand 12 (threshold 20)
step 2  repriced rows   = 2
step 2  after reprice   = [BOLT-7@85, NUT-3@30]
step 3  reserve 3 GIRD  = 0 left
step 3  refused         = only 0 of GIRD-1
  attempt 1 failed with ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException, retrying
step 3  retry outcome   = attempts: 2, left: 349   (399 after the interfering picker, then 349)
step 3  version BOLT-7  = 2
step 4  orders          = 3, lines walked = 5, statements = 1
step 4  page 0/2        = [1=970, 2=120000], total elements 3, pages 2
step 5  audit           = createdBy picker-bot, createdAt set true
step 5  spec search     = [NUT-3@30]
step 6  rejected        = ConstraintViolationException on [priceInCents, sku]
step 6  products        = 4   (the invalid one never reached the table)

Every number can be derived by hand, which is the point of checking it:

  • Events before step 2. The orders are placed early because the revenue query in step 2 needs them; the step 5 line reports the three after-commit deliveries at that moment.
  • Revenue. Fasteners: 10 × 80 + 4 × 25 + 5 × 80 = 1300. Motion: 2 × 2300 = 4600. Structural: one girder at 120000.
  • Low stock below 20. GIRD-1 (3) and NUT-3 (12); CAM-9 has 30 and BOLT-7 400.
  • Reprice. Two fasteners, each 5 cents dearer: BOLT-7 85, NUT-3 30.
  • Reservations. Three girders leave 0, so the next request is refused. For BOLT-7, attempt 1 reads 400 at version 0; the interfering picker commits 399 at version 1; attempt 1's update … where version = 0 matches no row and fails. Attempt 2 reads 399 at version 1 and leaves 349 at version 2.
  • One statement for three orders and five lines, products included — the entity graph at work.
  • The page. Order 1 is 10 × 85 + 4 × 30 = 970, priced after the reprice: the summary query reads current prices, because the order lines store no price of their own. A real order should copy the unit price onto the line at placement — the first extension below.
  • The search. Fasteners between 0 and 50 cents that are active: only NUT-3 at 30 after the reprice.
Extensions worth attempting
  • A REST layer. Add spring-boot-starter-web and a controller that returns OrderSummary pages and accepts a PlaceOrderRequest record validated with @Valid. Never return an entity: the lazy associations and the @Version field are not part of your API. Copy the unit price onto OrderLine while you are there.
  • A Testcontainers test. Write a @DataJpaTest against PostgreSQL with @ServiceConnection that asserts the listing still takes one statement. Then run the reservation retry against it: PostgreSQL's locking differs from H2's, and the test will tell you whether your retry still holds.
  • A Flyway migration. Generate the schema once with Hibernate's script export (JPA §10), commit it as V1__init.sql, switch ddl-auto to validate, and add a V2 that introduces the unit-price column with a backfill.
